title: Plain-Language Front-Page Statement for Virgin Islands Leases
bodyText: Virgin Islands law on plain-language consumer contracts covers residential leases. It calls for a statement on the front page of the lease, captioned "PLEASE READ THIS" in 12-point bold capitals, that highlights every lease term that restricts or reduces the tenant's rights and every term designed to protect the landlord, printed in 10-point bold type that is not in all capitals (in a typewritten lease, the statement is underlined). Steinoak's lease builder is to print this statement for Virgin Islands leases from the clauses you choose; check that it appears and lists every restrictive or landlord-protective term in your lease, including any you add yourself. If the lease does not comply, the tenant can recover actual damages, punitive damages of up to $1,000 and reasonable attorney's fees and costs, unless both sides have fully performed the lease, you tried in good faith to comply (using a model plain-language form from a state or federal agency, the Commission on Uniform Laws or a national trade association is prima facie evidence of good faith), or the tenant supplied the language. You may ask the Attorney General for an opinion on whether your lease form complies. The law does not apply to contracts "involving amounts of more than $25,000"; because it is unclear whether that means a lease's total rent, treat every residential lease as covered.

title: Plain-Language Rules for Virgin Islands Residential Leases
bodyText: A Virgin Islands residential lease must be written in clear, simple, understandable and easily readable language. In judging that, a court or regulator weighs confusing cross-references, overlong sentences, double negatives and exceptions to exceptions, illogical order, and obsolete or Latin and French legal terms; and it considers whether sections are logically divided and captioned, whether a lease of more than 3,000 words has a table of contents or index, and whether conditions and exceptions to the main promises are given equal prominence with them and printed in at least 10-point type. Technical terms alone are not a violation. A lease may not waive these rights. A violation does not by itself make the lease void or give the tenant a defense to a claim for breach, unless enforcing the lease would be unconscionable, but it can make you liable for the tenant's actual damages, up to $1,000 in punitive damages and attorney's fees (see the front-page statement row). The Consumer Services Administration, a regulator or any interested person may also seek an injunction.

title: Payment-Method Fees and Electronic Payment in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands Payment Options law decides which rent payment methods you must accept, and the library's `acceptable-payment-methods-vi` clause applies it. Three points matter for fees and electronic payment. First, a covered business must offer at least two payment options, one of them cash and one a credit or debit card; the customer chooses among the options offered, and no business may induce or coerce a customer to use a particular method.

So if the law covers you, do not require rent to be paid only through an online portal, an electronic transfer, a check or a money order. Second, we found no Virgin Islands statute that bans or caps a surcharge or convenience fee for paying by card, but a fee that steers tenants away from a payment option you must offer could be treated as inducing a particular method, so the cautious course is no card surcharge and no extra fee for paying in cash.

You may set a minimum of up to $10 for card charges if you tell the customer in writing at the point of sale. Third, if a payment method you offer becomes unavailable, offer another one, and if it stays unavailable for more than five business days, tell the Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs in writing. The law reaches any individual or entity formed for profit, except commercial establishments doing less than $50,000 of business a year; whether a small landlord fits that exemption is not settled, so offering cash and card is the safe course. Fines start at $1,000 for a first offense.

title: No Algorithm-Specific Rent Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute specifically bans or regulates setting rents or lease terms with algorithmic pricing or revenue-management software, or landlords sharing rent data. General antitrust law still applies. The Virgin Islands Antimonopoly Law makes it a violation to contract or conspire with a competitor for the purpose or with the effect of fixing, controlling or maintaining the price or fee charged for a service, or otherwise to unreasonably restrain trade by agreement; the Attorney General may sue for an injunction and penalties of up to $50,000, and a person injured by price fixing may recover three times the actual damages plus attorney's fees. Federal antitrust law also applies in the territory. Set your rent independently: don't agree with other landlords, directly or through software that pools competitors' private rent, occupancy or lease-term data, on rents, concessions or lease terms, and don't treat a vendor's recommended rent as binding. During a Governor-declared state of emergency, separate price rules apply to rents (`edu-emergency-rent-pricing-vi`).

title: No Application-Fee Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute caps, bans or regulates a rental application or screening fee, requires you to refund an unused fee, or requires a written notice of your screening criteria before you take one. General rules still apply. Charge every applicant the same fee on the same terms: the territory's housing discrimination law bars discriminating in the terms of a rental because of race, creed, age, color, national origin, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability or political affiliation. Say in writing, before you take the fee, what it covers and whether any part is refundable, and keep it to your actual screening cost; a misleading statement about a fee can be a deceptive trade practice. If the Payment Options law covers you, let the applicant pay in cash or by card and offer a receipt for a fee of $5 or more (`edu-rent-receipts-vi`). FEDERAL: if you deny an application, or offer worse terms, because of a consumer report, give the adverse-action notice the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires.

title: How Payments Are Applied in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute sets an order for applying a tenant's payments to rent, fees and other charges, so the lease governs; the shared clause `application-of-payments`, tagged for the Virgin Islands, applies each payment to rent first. Without a lease term, the common law applies: Virgin Islands courts follow the common law as expressed in the Restatements unless local law or the Virgin Islands Supreme Court's own decisions say otherwise, and under those rules a debtor may direct how a payment is applied, and if the debtor doesn't, the creditor may choose.

Applying payments to rent first also protects an eviction case. A forcible entry and detainer case for nonpayment rests on unpaid rent, and if the rent-control subchapter is in force (its status is unsettled) a nonpayment case can be brought only if the rent claimed is no greater than the tenant's rent for the month before the default. Diverting a rent payment to a fee can leave rent unpaid that the tenant thought was paid and invite a defense.

Collect unpaid fees in a separate civil action or in small claims (up to $10,000), not in the eviction case.

title: Collection Fees and Costs in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute sets, caps or bans a fee a landlord may charge for collecting past-due rent or other amounts, and the territory has no general debt-collection practices act for landlords who collect their own debts. Two general rules apply. The Consumer Protection Law forbids deceptive or unconscionable practices in the collection of consumer debts, and money owed under a residential lease is probably a consumer debt, so demand only amounts the lease and the law allow, and describe them accurately.

In a lawsuit, the court may award the winning party a sum toward attorney's fees at its discretion, whatever the lease says about fees. If you want the tenant to pay a collection agency's reasonable costs, the lease must say so (`collection-costs-vi`, optional).

FEDERAL: a collection agency, or a lawyer who regularly collects debts, is a debt collector under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, which bars collecting any amount, including a fee or charge, unless the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes it or law permits it.

title: Amounts Due at Signing in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute limits what you may collect at signing: there is no cap on the security deposit, on first or last month's rent paid in advance, or on fees, and no rule on when each must be paid. Two rules matter. First, rent paid in advance protects the tenant's possession: a notice to quit does not let you bring an eviction case before the end of any period for which the tenant has already paid rent, so last month's rent collected at signing is rent for that month; label it as rent, keep it separate from the security deposit, and don't treat it as a fund for damage.

Second, if the Payment Options law covers you, the tenant may pay these amounts in cash or by credit or debit card, and you must offer a receipt for each payment of $5 or more. List each amount and its due date in the lease (`due-at-signing`, tagged for the Virgin Islands) and give a receipt showing how much is rent, deposit and fees.

title: No Fee-Disclosure or All-In Pricing Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires all-in rent pricing, a fee disclosure on the lease's first page, or a fee list in rental advertising, and none addresses automatically renewing leases. General consumer rules still shape how you present fees. Under the Consumer Protection Law, failing to state a material fact can be a deceptive trade practice if it deceives or tends to deceive, and the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices law bars unfair or deceptive acts in any trade or commerce, which includes dealing in real property, read in line with Federal Trade Commission interpretations; consumers may bring class actions in which a jury's damages are trebled. So show every mandatory fee, with its amount, wherever you advertise or quote the rent, and list every fee in the lease (`fees-and-charges-vi`). Two tax rules affect billing: you may not show the territorial gross receipts tax as a separate charge on a bill or invoice (build it into the rent), but on a rental shorter than 90 days the hotel room tax must appear as a separate item (`edu-rent-tax-vi`). The plain-language law also requires a residential lease to be clear and easily readable, with a front-page statement of provisions that restrict the tenant's rights (the lease builder prints it). FEDERAL: the Federal Trade Commission's rule on unfair or deceptive fees requires total-price display for short-term lodging.

title: Charging Only for Services You Provide in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute is worded as a general ban on charging a tenant for services you don't provide, but several rules reach that result for particular charges. If you charge a tenant for the public sewer system user fee, you may not charge more than the actual fee attributable to the tenant's unit (split equally among units when you pay for several), and you may not pass on penalties assessed against you. If you charge for water or electricity, the charge must be based on what the tenant actually uses, and unless you agreed otherwise in writing, a tenant may ask you to install a water or electric meter. You may not take any payment to permit cable television installation, or charge more rent because the tenant receives cable. You may not charge a blind tenant extra for a dog guide. More generally, charging for a service that does not exist or is not provided is likely a deceptive practice under the territory's consumer laws. Bill only for services you actually provide, at the amount the lease states.

title: Fees and Rent in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: Virgin Islands law has no general definition that turns fees into rent, and no statute lets a lease make a fee rent by calling it additional rent. The eviction statutes speak of rent: a forcible entry and detainer case for nonpayment lies when the tenant fails to pay rent due, and whether fees labelled additional rent count is for the courts to decide. One definition does sweep fees in: the rent-control subchapter, whose status is unsettled, defines rent as all consideration, including any bonus, benefit or gratuity, demanded or received for the use or occupancy of the unit. If that subchapter applies, mandatory charges for use or occupancy count toward the rent ceiling, and a nonpayment eviction can proceed only if the rent claimed is no greater than the tenant's rent for the month before the default, so charges that vary from month to month could defeat the case. A lease clause calling fees additional rent is lawful, but the library doesn't offer one for the Virgin Islands: it could tie an eviction to disputed fee amounts and may not work. Collect unpaid fees in a separate civil action or small claims (up to $10,000). If you want such a clause, add your own after taking legal advice.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no county or municipal governments that license or register rental units, and no rental registration law. It does have a territorial business license: a license from the Commissioner of Licensing and Consumer Affairs is required before engaging in a business on the licence fee list, which includes apartment houses (an annual fee set by your total number of units, one licence per owner), unless you own and live in an apartment house of fewer than five units. No statute says whether you may have a tenant reimburse a government fee charged to you, so the lease decides, within these limits. A public sewer system user fee may be charged to a tenant only up to the actual fee attributable to the tenant's unit, and penalties assessed against you may not be passed on. The gross receipts tax you owe on rent may not be shown as a separate charge on a bill or invoice; build it into the rent. The hotel room tax on rentals shorter than 90 days is the guest's tax, which you collect and itemize (`edu-rent-tax-vi`). The library does not offer the shared government-fee reimbursement clause for the Virgin Islands because it is written for local registration and licensing fees; recover your business licence fee and other territorial costs through the rent.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
One Virgin Islands rule bars passing a penalty to tenants: in the sewer-fee law, penalties assessed against the landlord or owner may not be passed on to the tenants. That sentence sits in the section on charging tenants for the public sewer user fee and could be read to reach other penalties too, so never pass on a penalty for a condition you are responsible for. For a fine the tenant caused, no statute bars or allows reimbursement; a tenant who breaks the lease answers for the loss the breach causes, and an optional clause makes the right express (`tenant-caused-fines-vi`).

Tenants have their own Housing Code duties: keep the part of the dwelling they occupy or control clean, safe and sanitary, dispose of garbage under Public Works rules, and use plumbing fixtures with reasonable care. Never charge a tenant for calling the police or emergency help in a domestic violence situation. Collect any reimbursement in a separate civil action or small claims, not in an eviction case.

title: Late Fees in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute caps late fees on residential rent, requires a grace period or a notice, or governs them at all, so the amount and timing come from the lease (`late-fee`, tagged for the Virgin Islands). A court may refuse to enforce a late fee that is a penalty rather than a fair estimate of your loss from late payment, under common law the Virgin Islands Supreme Court develops itself, so set a modest flat fee or percentage tied to your real costs, charge it once per late payment, and state the grace period.

Two statutes are close by. Money that has become due carries interest at the legal rate of 9% a year, and by express written agreement interest may run up to 18½% a year on amounts of $9,000 or less; if a fee works as interest, keep it within those limits, and don't charge both a late fee and interest on the same late payment. A late fee can't be collected in an eviction case; sue for it separately or in small claims.

No Virgin Islands statute contradicts the shared clause's sentence that accepting a late payment doesn't waive your rights, but whether repeatedly accepting late rent waives strict timeliness is a common-law question, so enforce the lease consistently. If a housing subsidy pays part of the rent, charge the late fee only on the tenant's own share.

title: No Late-Fee Cap in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute caps a residential late fee, sets a minimum grace period, limits how often a late fee may be charged, or requires notice before one is charged. The territory's late-fee statutes cover other transactions, such as rent-to-own contracts for goods, timeshare assessments and utility bills paid late by an energy assistance program, not dwelling rent. The limits that apply come from the common law on penalties and, if a fee works as interest, the 9% legal rate and the 18½% maximum written-contract rate; see `edu-late-fee-vi` for the cautious course.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires month-to-month and fixed-term tenants to get the same lease terms, or caps the rent difference between them. The differences that exist are in how tenancies end. A tenancy at will or by sufferance ends on three months' written notice, or, where rent is payable at shorter intervals, on notice equal to the interval between rent payments (one month for a month-to-month tenancy, one week for week-to-week); unpaid rent on a tenancy at will allows a fourteen-day written notice to quit. A fixed term ends when it expires, and a tenant who stays on after a notice to quit may be evicted. If the rent-control subchapter is in force (its status is unsettled), every possession case needs 30 days' written notice to quit and one of its four grounds, whatever the tenancy type (`edu-rent-control-vi`). You may price fixed-term and month-to-month leases differently for legitimate business reasons, but apply your pricing the same way to every applicant: the housing discrimination law requires equal terms regardless of the protected classes.

title: Time Limits for Rent and Damage Claims in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: A landlord's lawsuit for unpaid rent, damages or other money owed under a lease is an action on a contract and must be brought within six years after the claim accrues; a lease under seal gets twenty years. A claim for waste or trespass to the property, or for taking or damaging personal property, also has six years. Each unpaid rent installment generally accrues as its own claim on the day it fell due. If the tenant pays something toward the debt after it is due, the six years likely start again from that last payment. A promise or acknowledgment of the debt restarts or extends the period only if it is in a writing the tenant signed; an oral promise is not enough. A tenant's claims against you have their own periods: six years on the lease (including a deposit claim), two years for an injury not arising from the contract, and two years after paying usurious interest to sue for double the interest. Don't wait: file promptly, in small claims for amounts up to $10,000.

title: Rent Concessions in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute regulates rent concessions such as a free month, a move-in credit or a reduced rent for the first months. Write any concession into the lease with its amount and the rental periods it covers (`rent-concession-wi`, tagged for the Virgin Islands), and frame it carefully: keep the Monthly Rent at the full amount and describe the concession as a credit against named months, not as a lower rent. If the rent-control subchapter is in force (its status is unsettled), a nonpayment eviction can proceed only if the rent claimed is no greater than the tenant's rent for the month before the default, so a reduced rent in that month could limit your claim, and the subchapter counts any bonus or benefit you receive for occupancy as rent.

Say plainly whether any part of the concession must be repaid if the tenant leaves early; an undisclosed repayment term could be a deceptive practice.

title: Rent Control in the Virgin Islands: Status Unsettled
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has a rent-control law on its books, and whether it still applies is unsettled. The Code prints a 1947-era rent-control subchapter as current law. It covers housing and business accommodations throughout the territory, but not hotels or transient lodging houses, and it stays in force until the Legislature declares by resolution or act that the 1947 housing emergency has ended; we found no such declaration, and a territorial department is still charged with enforcing rent control. If it applies: maximum rents are tied to the rents in force on July 1, 1947, with a petition process before a Rent Control Officer; a tenant who paid more than the ceiling may sue for double the overcharge or $50, whichever is greater; no action to recover possession may be brought except on four grounds (the owner's good-faith personal use; good-faith demolition with plans complete; tenant nuisance, unreasonable damage or repeated serious misconduct; nonpayment of rent); every possession case needs 30 days' written notice to quit; and a tenant may defend a nonpayment case by claiming the rent is unjust and unreasonable. We found no evidence that a Rent Control Officer operates today, and the Virgin Islands Supreme Court applied the ordinary eviction statute in 2024 without discussing the subchapter. The cautious course: don't price at 1947 levels, but give at least 30 days' written notice to quit before any possession case and rely only on one of the four grounds. There is no local rent control: the territory has no municipal governments that make such rules. Separately, during a Governor-declared state of emergency, rents can be frozen and unconscionable rent prices are a crime (`edu-emergency-rent-pricing-vi`).

title: Collecting Rent for a Substandard Unit in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute expressly bars demanding or collecting rent for a substandard unit, or makes code violations a defense to a rent claim. Two rules point that way. The Housing Code makes it unlawful to rent to another any building or part of one for living, sleeping or cooking that does not comply with the Building Code or the Housing Code; the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority enforces it. And a dwelling found unfit for human habitation can be ordered repaired, or vacated and closed, or demolished; once a dwelling is ordered vacated and closed, don't rent it or collect rent for it. Whether a tenant may refuse rent, or recover rent paid, for a noncomplying unit is a common-law question (an illegal lease, an implied warranty of habitability) for the Virgin Islands Supreme Court. The cautious course: fix code violations promptly, don't rent a unit you know does not comply, and don't sue for rent for any period when the unit was closed or unfit to live in.

title: Rent Changes During a Lease in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute regulates rent escalation clauses, so during a fixed term the rent changes only as the lease provides: a schedule of new amounts or an index adjustment (`rent-escalation-la`), or an optional mid-term increase on 30 days' written notice with a right for the tenant to leave (`rent-increase-midterm-ky`), both tagged for the Virgin Islands. The territory has no landlord-tenant retaliation statute with a safe harbour tied to an escalation clause; its civil-rights law does forbid retaliating against anyone who complained of or opposed discrimination, so put increases in the lease rather than imposing them after a complaint.

If the rent-control subchapter is in force (status unsettled), a scheduled increase can't push rent above the ceiling, and a nonpayment eviction is maintainable only if the rent claimed is no greater than the tenant's rent for the month before the default; in the first month of a higher rent, claim only the earlier amount in an eviction case and collect the difference separately. During a declared state of emergency, increases are restricted.

title: Raising the Rent in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute sets a notice period or form for a rent increase. During a fixed term you may raise the rent only as the lease provides (`edu-rent-escalation-vi`). A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy has no separate rent-increase procedure: the rent changes when you end the current tenancy with the notice the law requires and the tenant stays on new terms. A tenancy at will ends on three months' written notice, or on notice equal to the rent interval when rent is paid more often than every three months (one month for a month-to-month tenancy). The cautious course is written notice of the new rent at least 30 days before it takes effect and, for a month-to-month tenancy, at least one full rental period ending on a rent day. If the rent-control subchapter is in force (status unsettled), rent above its ceiling can be challenged, and a nonpayment eviction for a newly increased rent may fail because the rent claimed must be no greater than the tenant's rent for the month before the default (`edu-rent-control-vi`). During a declared state of emergency, rent increases are restricted (`edu-emergency-rent-pricing-vi`). Never raise rent to retaliate against a tenant who complained of discrimination.

title: Rent During a Declared State of Emergency in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: During a state of emergency the Governor declares (for example after a hurricane), two Virgin Islands rules limit what you may charge for rent. First, the Governor may, through the Commissioner of Licensing and Consumer Affairs, freeze prices of goods and services at the level that existed just before the emergency proclamation, and rents are expressly included. Second, while the emergency lasts (including extensions and renewals), it is unlawful to rent or offer to rent essential goods or services, including those on the price-freeze list, at an unconscionable price: one showing a gross disparity from the average price in the 30 days before the declaration, unless the increase comes from documented added costs or market trends. Willfully charging an unconscionable price, or offering goods or services to the public during the emergency without a business license, is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $1,000 to $5,000 per violation, prosecuted by the Virgin Islands Department of Justice; the section gives no private right to sue. An increase approved by the Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs is not unconscionable. So during a declared emergency, don't raise rent on a renewal or a new lease above the pre-emergency level without documented cost increases, check whether a price-freeze order covers rents, and keep records of your costs. Proclamations and freeze orders are not in the Code; check the Governor's current orders.

title: Paying Rent in Installments in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute regulates paying rent in installments or says whether scheduled installments are partial payments, so the lease may set any schedule (`rent-installments-or`, tagged for the Virgin Islands). One effect to note: for a tenancy at will, notice to end the tenancy may equal the interval between rent payments when rent is paid more often than every three months, so splitting rent into two payments a month could arguably shorten that notice for both you and the tenant; give at least 30 days' written notice anyway. Apply any late fee to an installment only as the lease states, and give a receipt for each payment.

title: Paying Rent in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
Virgin Islands law sets no default due date, place of payment or weekend rule for rent; those terms come from the lease (`rent-payment`, tagged for the Virgin Islands).

What the law does say: anyone in possession of land from which rent is due is liable for the rent on the part they hold; rent may be recovered in a lawsuit, using the lease as evidence of the amount due; and you keep any other remedy the lease or the law gives. Rent the tenant has paid in advance protects the tenant from an eviction case until that period ends. Nonpayment supports an eviction only after a written demand or notice to quit (cautiously 30 days' notice), and the rent itself must be collected in a separate civil action or small claims, not in the eviction case.

If the Payment Options law covers you, accept cash and a credit or debit card and offer a receipt for each payment of $5 or more (`acceptable-payment-methods-vi`).

title: Receipts for Rent and Other Payments in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: If the Virgin Islands Payment Options law covers you, you must offer the tenant a receipt for every payment of $5 or more, whatever the payment method, and give one on request for smaller payments. The receipt must show what was paid for (for example, rent for a named month, the security deposit, or a fee), the amount paid for each item, the date, and your legal name and address (an individual's name as on the birth certificate or as declared by a court, or a business entity's name as reported in its formation documents). Keep a record of each day's transactions, with the amount and payment method, for at least seven years; the Bureau of Internal Revenue may inspect it. The law reaches any individual or entity formed for profit; the $50,000 small-business exemption appears in the payment-options section but not in the receipt section, so give receipts even as a small landlord. We found no Virgin Islands rule that a receipt for later rent presumes earlier rent was paid, and none making a missing receipt an eviction defense; a receipt is your best evidence, so note on it any amount still owed.

title: No Rent-Reporting Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute creates a rent-reporting program, requires you to offer positive rent reporting, bars requiring a tenant to join one, or requires notice before you report late rent to a credit bureau. If you do report, report accurately and describe the debt correctly: a false or misleading statement in collecting a consumer debt can be a deceptive practice under the Consumer Protection Law. FEDERAL: if you furnish payment information to a consumer reporting agency, the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires accurate information, correction of errors and investigation of disputes.

title: Taxes on Rent in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
Two Virgin Islands taxes reach rent. Gross receipts tax: anyone doing business in the territory, meaning any activity conducted for gain, profit or income, pays a 4% tax on gross receipts, including rentals. The tax is imposed on you, not on the tenant, and you may not state it, or any part of it, separately on a bill or invoice, so build it into the rent rather than adding a line item. If your annual gross receipts are under $225,000, the first $9,000 of gross receipts each month is exempt.

Hotel room tax: renting an apartment, condominium or residence to someone for less than 90 days makes the occupant a guest, and the guest owes a hotel room tax of 12.5% of the gross room rate or rental, which includes additional charges such as maintenance or service fees; you collect and remit it and must show it as a separate item on each statement, or the full charges are taxed plus penalties. A rental of 90 days or more is outside the room tax.

A month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy has no fixed length, and whether its 'period of time of the rental or lease is less than 90 days' (33 V.I.C. § 54(a)(3)) is not settled; ask the Bureau of Internal Revenue before renting periodically to a short-stay occupant. For a lease shorter than 90 days, use `hotel-room-tax-vi`. Check current rates and filing rules with the Bureau of Internal Revenue.

title: Listing Fees in a Virgin Islands Lease
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute requires a lease to list every fee or sets a notice period for adding a fee later. List them anyway (`fees-and-charges-vi`). Your right to a fee rests on the lease, so a charge the lease doesn't provide for is hard to collect; adding a fee during a fixed term needs the tenant's written agreement; failing to state a material fact about charges can be a deceptive practice; and the plain-language law requires a residential lease to be clear and easily readable.

Don't list the gross receipts tax as a fee (it may not be stated separately), and don't list charges the law forbids, such as a payment to permit cable television installation or an extra charge for a blind tenant's dog guide. For a month-to-month tenancy a new fee is a change of terms: give written notice at least one full rental period ahead, as for a rent increase.

title: Bounced Rent Payments in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute caps or sets the fee a landlord may charge for a bounced check or a failed electronic payment. The territory's dishonored-check fee rules apply only to certain lenders (consumer loans and insurance premium finance) and to a government agency, not to rent. So a returned-payment fee is a matter of contract: put it in the lease (`returned-payments-vi`) and keep it close to your actual bank charges and handling costs, because a court may refuse to enforce an excessive fixed charge as a penalty.

A bounced payment does not pay the rent; the rent stays owed and can be collected in a separate civil action or small claims. Knowingly writing a worthless check is also a crime, a matter for the police and prosecutors, not a lease remedy; if you think it applies, send the tenant prompt written notice that the check was not paid, because a drawer who doesn't pay within 10 days after such notice is presumed to have known the funds were insufficient.

If the Payment Options law covers you, keep offering cash and a credit or debit card even after repeated bounced payments, and don't require a single method: you may stop taking personal checks, but the tenant keeps the choice among your other payment methods; you may not require that all rent be paid only by cashier's check, certified check or money order (the library's `returned-payments-vi` clause is drafted this way).

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute delays rent, waives late fees or pauses evictions for federal or territorial government workers during a government shutdown or a lapse in appropriations. The lease's ordinary rent, late-fee and default terms apply. Consider a written payment plan for an affected tenant, and remember that an eviction needs a written notice to quit (cautiously 30 days, `edu-rent-control-vi`) and that rent itself is collected in a separate civil action or small claims, not in the eviction case. FEDERAL: the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act protects servicemembers on active duty, including a court stay of eviction for a dwelling whose rent is below the federal limit and a right to end a lease on military orders.

title: Virgin Islands Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Virgin Islands law sets few money limits on a residential lease. No statute caps the security deposit, the late fee, an application fee or an ordinary rent increase, and none requires a grace period. The limits that do exist: (1) Rent control: the rent-control subchapter, whose status is unsettled, ties maximum rents to July 1, 1947 levels with a petition process (`edu-rent-control-vi`). (2) Emergencies: during a declared state of emergency, rents may be frozen and unconscionable rent prices are a crime (`edu-emergency-rent-pricing-vi`). (3) Utilities: a sewer user fee charged to a tenant can't exceed the actual fee attributable to the unit, and water or electricity charges must reflect the tenant's actual use (`edu-fee-unprovided-service-vi`). (4) No charge to permit cable television installation, and no extra charge for a blind tenant's dog guide. (5) Interest: 9% a year on overdue money; by express written agreement up to 18½% a year on amounts of $9,000 or less (`edu-unpaid-damages-interest-vi`). (6) Payment options: a covered landlord must accept cash and card and may set a card minimum of no more than $10 (`edu-payment-method-fees-vi`). (7) Taxes: a 4% gross receipts tax you may not bill separately, and a 12.5% hotel room tax on rentals shorter than 90 days (`edu-rent-tax-vi`). (8) Small claims: up to $10,000.

title: No Rent-Proration Rule for Subsidized Units in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute sets a formula for reducing rent, the tenant's share or a housing authority's share, when part of a subsidized unit becomes unfit, and none gives any tenant a statutory rent-abatement or withholding remedy. What does apply: the Housing Code makes it unlawful to rent a dwelling that does not comply with it or the Building Code, enforced by the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority; and a dwelling found unfit for human habitation can be ordered repaired, or vacated and closed, or demolished. Whether a tenant may claim a rent reduction under the common law is for the courts. FEDERAL: under the Housing Choice Voucher program the housing authority may abate or stop its payments for a unit that fails housing quality standards, and the family is not responsible for the authority's share of the rent; follow your housing assistance payments contract. Fix defects promptly and document the repairs.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute addresses late fees when a housing subsidy pays part of the rent. A late fee rests on the tenant's own delay, so charge it only on the tenant's share, never because a housing authority or other program paid its share late, and write the late-fee clause that way. The territory's utility law takes the same approach for utility bills: no late charge may be assessed because an energy assistance program paid late (that rule binds utilities, not landlords). FEDERAL: under the Housing Choice Voucher program the family is not responsible for the housing authority's share of the rent, and the housing assistance payments contract and HUD's tenancy addendum control over the lease.

title: Passing Property Tax or Insurance Increases to a Virgin Islands Tenant
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute addresses a residential lease clause that passes real property tax or insurance increases to the tenant. The property tax is the owner's; a lease may shift an increase to the tenant only if it says so, which the optional `tax-insurance-escalation-la` clause (tagged for the Virgin Islands) does by stating the tenant's percentage share and refunding any later reduction. Three cautions. If the rent-control subchapter is in force (status unsettled), its definition of rent includes any benefit demanded for occupancy, so pass-through charges count toward the rent ceiling, and a nonpayment eviction can't claim more than the prior month's rent.

Don't pass through the gross receipts tax: it may not be shown separately on a bill or invoice. And during a declared state of emergency, a new charge could be treated as a price increase.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
Without any lease term, money that has become due in the Virgin Islands carries interest at the legal rate of 9% a year, as does money received for another's use and kept beyond a reasonable time without consent, and money due under a contract that names no rate. So a court can award 9% interest on unpaid rent or damages from the date due, and a tenant can claim 9% on a deposit balance you keep too long. A written lease may set a higher rate by express agreement, but not above 18½% a year on amounts of $9,000 or less (larger amounts have no maximum).

Taking more than the law allows is usury: the payer may sue within two years for double the interest received, and in a suit on the contract the entire interest is forfeited. To set a contract rate, use `unpaid-amounts-interest-vi`, and don't charge both interest and a late fee on the same late rent payment.

title: No Move-In or Move-Out Inspection Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a move-in inventory, a joint inspection, photographs, a move-out inspection, or a notice of inspection rights, and the territory has no security-deposit statute tying deductions to such records. Your claim against the deposit rests on the lease and on proof, so make the record yourself: at move-in, walk through the unit with the tenant, complete a written condition checklist, take dated photographs, and both sign it; give the tenant a few days to add items in writing; repeat at move-out and give the tenant a copy. The library's existing-condition clause supports this (`existing-condition`, tagged for the Virgin Islands). The only inspections in Virgin Islands housing law are official ones: the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority may inspect dwellings to enforce the Housing Code, with the occupants' consent or by due process of law.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets a lease preset what you will charge against the deposit for cleaning, carpet or repairs, or forbids it, because the territory has no deposit statute. A preset charge works only as an agreed estimate of a real loss: a court may refuse to enforce a fixed charge that operates as a penalty or that charges for ordinary wear and tear, under common law the Virgin Islands Supreme Court develops itself. If you list charges, tie them to typical actual costs, charge them only for damage or uncleanliness beyond ordinary wear and tear, and itemize every deduction. The tagged carpet-cleaning clause (`carpet-cleaning-ar`) follows that approach. When a domestic-violence victim ends the lease under the territory's release law, the deposit may not be kept for damage caused by an act of domestic violence (`edu-dv-deposit-timing-vi`).

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: If you can't return a security deposit refund because the former tenant can't be found or never cashes the check, the money does not become yours. The Virgin Islands Uniform Unclaimed Property Act lists security deposits and refunds as property, and you hold it for the tenant. A refund owed in your rental business is presumed abandoned if the tenant doesn't claim it or contact you about it for five years after the tenant's right to demand it arose (the catch-all period); if it were treated as money owed to a customer from a retail business transaction, the period would be three years, so check with the administrator, the Lieutenant Governor. Once a refund is presumed abandoned, report it before November 1 each year (covering the 12 months before July 1); if it is $50 or more and you have an address, send the tenant written notice 60 to 120 days before you file; then pay it to the administrator with the report. A lease clause that forfeits an unclaimed deposit to you doesn't work: the property is payable even though the tenant never demanded it, and a holder may deduct a dormancy charge only under a valid written contract it regularly enforces, in an amount that is not unconscionable. Failing to report or pay costs interest at 9% a year and a penalty of $200 a day (up to $5,000), or, if willful, $1,000 a day (up to $25,000) plus 25% of the value.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives tenants a right to pay a security deposit in installments or requires you to offer a plan, and the territory has no deposit statute, so you may require the full deposit when the lease says. You may agree to an installment plan; if you do, put the schedule in the lease, say what happens if an installment is missed, and give a receipt for each payment (`edu-rent-receipts-vi`). Offer any plan on the same terms to every tenant, since the housing discrimination law requires equal terms.

title: Security Deposit and Last Month’s Rent in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says whether a tenant may use the security deposit as the last month's rent, or whether you may apply it that way, and none restricts collecting last month's rent in advance. The lease decides. Keep the two separate and labelled. Money taken as last month's rent is rent paid in advance, and a notice to quit does not let you bring an eviction case before the end of any period for which rent was paid in advance. Money taken as a security deposit secures damage and other defaults; if the lease lets the tenant treat it as the last month's rent, you lose that security for damage found at move-out. The lease should say the tenant may not apply the deposit to rent without your written consent.

title: Move-Out Notice and the Deposit Refund in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no deposit statute, so no rule makes the refund depend on, or forbids conditioning it on, the tenant's advance notice of move-out, a forwarding address, a demand, or the return of keys by a deadline. The lease governs (`security-deposit-return-vi`). Ask for a forwarding address in writing at move-out and keep proof you mailed the refund to the last address you have. Don't hold the refund hostage to a missed notice: money received for another and kept beyond a reasonable time without consent carries interest at 9% a year, and an unclaimed refund must eventually be reported to the territory (`edu-deposit-escheat-vi`). A tenant leaving under the domestic-violence release gets the deposit back on termination (`edu-dv-deposit-timing-vi`).

title: Deposit Return After a Domestic-Violence Release in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence or domestic abuse may end a residential lease by giving at least 14 days' written notice, with a police report written within the 90 days before the notice, if the tenant seeks to leave out of fear of imminent danger to self or children; the notice names the termination date. When the lease ends that way, you must return the security deposit to the tenant victim upon termination of the lease. You may still keep part of the deposit for damage not caused by an act of domestic violence, but not for damage that was. The statute doesn't wait for other occupants to leave: any other tenant on the lease stays bound by it, and the person named in a court order as the perpetrator may be liable to you for your losses, including unpaid rent and repair costs. Where other tenants remain, the statute doesn't say how to divide the deposit; the cautious course is to refund the victim's share (or the whole deposit, if the victim paid it) promptly after the termination date, with an itemized list of any non-domestic-violence deductions, and to agree in writing with the remaining tenants how any new deposit will be held. You may not charge a fee solely because the lease ended this way.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no deposit statute, so there is no expedited or alternative deposit procedure: no faster refund in exchange for waiving an itemized statement, no fee for quicker processing, and no special track for a tenant who is evicted or abandons the unit. Handle every deposit the same way under the lease (`security-deposit-return-vi`): once you have possession back, apply the deposit only to the amounts the lease allows, send the balance with an itemized list, and collect anything more in a separate civil action or small claims (up to $10,000), not in the eviction case.

title: Fees in Lieu of a Security Deposit in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute or Code provision addresses deposit-alternative programs, such as a monthly or one-time fee, a surety bond or an insurance product taken instead of a security deposit, and the territory has no deposit statute. If you offer one, make it a real choice: offer every applicant a traditional deposit on the same terms, say in writing that the fee is not refundable and is not insurance for the tenant (unless it is), and that the tenant may still owe you for damage and unpaid rent, and explain any reporting to a credit bureau or collector before the tenant signs. Misdescribing what a program covers, or implying rights or obligations it doesn't involve, can be a deceptive practice. A product sold as insurance is regulated as insurance under Title 22; check the provider's licensing before you offer it.

title: Furnished Rentals in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute sets special rules for furnished dwelling rentals, a separate furniture deposit, or a furniture inventory; use the optional `furnishings-included-la` clause (tagged for the Virgin Islands) to list the items and their condition. Two rules can turn on whether, and for how long, you rent furnished. A residence rented furnished or unfurnished to someone for less than 90 days is a hotel for the hotel room tax, so the occupant owes a 12.5% room tax you collect and itemize.

And hotels and transient lodging houses are outside the rent-control subchapter, whose status is unsettled; an ordinary furnished apartment rented by the month is not a transient lodging house. The Housing Code applies to dwellings, apartments, rooming houses and hotels alike.

title: Holding Deposits Before a Virgin Islands Lease Is Signed
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute addresses a holding deposit, reservation fee or earnest money taken from an applicant before the lease is signed. Common law decides who keeps it if the deal falls through, so put the terms in writing before you take the money: the amount, how long you will hold the unit, that the deposit becomes part of the first month's rent or the security deposit if the lease is signed, when it is refunded (for example, if you reject the applicant or fail to offer the lease by the stated date), and whether you keep it if the applicant backs out. If you reject an applicant for credit reasons, refund it in full; the territory's consumer-fraud law, written for sales of goods, makes keeping a down payment as a credit-investigation fee after rejecting a credit application unlawful, and the same reasoning makes keeping a holding deposit risky. Give a receipt (`edu-rent-receipts-vi`) and treat every applicant alike.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: Because no Virgin Islands statute requires a move-in or move-out inspection or a notice of inspection rights, none sets a penalty, such as losing the right to withhold from the deposit or paying double damages, for skipping one. Your deductions still need proof, and a careful inspection record is the best proof you can have (`edu-no-condition-inspection-rule-vi`).

title: Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no deposit statute and no rule on nonrefundable deposits or fees, so whether money is refundable depends on what the lease says. Money given to secure the tenant's performance or against damage is a security deposit and should be refundable, less lawful deductions. A charge you mean to keep must be a fee for something, and the lease must say clearly that it is nonrefundable; the optional `nonrefundable-fees-wv` clause (tagged for the Virgin Islands) does this and treats all other security money as part of the deposit.

Calling security money nonrefundable, or describing a fee as refundable when it isn't, risks a deceptive-practice claim. Don't charge a blind tenant a pet fee or deposit for a dog guide.

title: No Separate Notice Rule for Nonrefundable Charges in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a separate written notice, at the time you collect money, that part of it is nonrefundable. State each nonrefundable fee in the lease (`nonrefundable-fees-wv`, `edu-nonrefundable-deposit-notice-vi`) and show it separately from the refundable deposit on the receipt; a receipt must list each item paid for and its amount (`edu-rent-receipts-vi`).

title: No Security Deposit Cap in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no security-deposit statute and sets no maximum deposit, no cap by tenancy type, no limit on extra deposits for pets, furniture or alterations, and no rule on raising a deposit later. The deposit is whatever the lease sets. Limits still apply: charge every tenant on the same terms (the housing discrimination law covers terms and conditions); don't charge a blind tenant any extra deposit or fee for a dog guide, though the tenant is liable for damage the dog causes; FEDERAL fair housing law bars extra deposits for assistance animals.

During a fixed term, you may raise the deposit only if the lease allows it. If the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), its definition of rent counts any bonus or benefit demanded for occupancy, so an unusually large deposit could be argued to be disguised rent; keep deposits proportionate to your real risk.

title: Holding a Security Deposit in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord who rents directly to keep tenants' deposits in a separate, escrow, trust or interest-bearing account, at a particular bank, or under a bond, or to tell the tenant where the deposit is held. Keep it in a separate, clearly labelled account anyway and record it on the receipt: the money is the tenant's, subject to your lawful deductions, and commingling makes it harder to prove what you held. If a licensed real estate broker manages the property and collects deposits, stricter rules apply to the broker: the Real Estate Commission may discipline a broker who commingles others' funds with the broker's own or fails within a reasonable time to account for or remit money belonging to others. A broker's definition includes acting for a client in the rental or management of real property and collecting escrow deposits.

title: No Interest Required on Security Deposits in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to pay interest on a residential security deposit, to hold it in an interest-bearing account, or to report deposit interest. If the deposit earns interest in your account, no statute says who keeps it; the lease may say. Two nearby rules: public utilities must pay interest on customer cash deposits (4¾% a year, or for the Water and Power Authority the average local bank savings rate), a rule for utilities only; and money received for another and kept beyond a reasonable time without consent carries interest at the legal rate of 9% a year, so a deposit balance you return late could carry interest from when it should have been returned.

title: Waiving Deposit Rights in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no deposit statute, so no statute makes deposit rights non-waivable; the lease governs the deposit. Limits still apply. The domestic-violence rule that the deposit goes back to a victim who ends the lease under the release statute is a statutory protection a lease can't override. The plain-language law, which covers residential leases, can't be waived. A lease term saying the tenant gives up rights the tenant has, or has rights or duties the deal doesn't involve, risks a deceptive-practice claim, and terms requiring consumers to waive legal rights are a factor the consumer agency weighs in declaring practices unconscionable. Don't ask tenants to waive the deposit's return; write fair deduction terms instead.

title: The Security Deposit When You Sell in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says what happens to tenants' security deposits when a rented property is sold: no duty to transfer them to the buyer, no notice requirement, and no rule releasing the seller. Under general property law a buyer usually takes the property subject to existing leases, but whether the buyer must return a deposit the buyer never received is a common-law question the courts decide. The cautious course for a seller: before closing, either refund each deposit to the tenant (less lawful deductions, with an itemized list) or transfer it to the buyer, with a written statement of each tenant's deposit and a notice to each tenant naming the buyer, the amount transferred and the buyer's address. As a buyer, get the deposits (or a closing credit) and a tenant-by-tenant schedule. Unclaimed refunds held by a successor follow the unclaimed property rules (`edu-deposit-escheat-vi`).

title: No Statutory Deposit Penalty in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no security-deposit statute, so there is no statutory penalty, such as double or triple damages or automatic forfeiture of your right to withhold, for mishandling a deposit. The deposit is governed by the lease and the general law. A tenant who claims you kept too much may sue for the balance, in small claims for up to $10,000, within six years; money kept beyond a reasonable time without consent carries interest at 9% a year; and the court may award the winning side a sum toward attorney's fees. If a misleading deposit term or statement is treated as a deceptive trade practice, consumer-protection remedies could follow, including trebled damages in a consumer class action under the consumer fraud law. Domestic-violence releases have their own deposit rule (`edu-dv-deposit-timing-vi`).

title: No Deposit-Return Statute in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no security-deposit statute, so no law sets a deadline for returning the deposit, requires an itemized statement, or penalizes a late or missing one. The library's Virgin Islands return clause states your own deadline and promises an itemized list (`security-deposit-return-vi`); keep it. Three statutes still touch the return. A tenant who ends the lease under the domestic-violence release gets the deposit back upon termination, less only damage not caused by domestic violence.

Money received for another and kept beyond a reasonable time without consent carries interest at 9% a year. And a refund you can't deliver becomes unclaimed property you must report, not money you keep. Return the balance promptly, with an itemized list of deductions, to the forwarding address the tenant gives you or the last address you have.

title: No Deposit-Standards Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to post or hand out the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if different tenants pay different deposits. The housing discrimination law still applies: you may not set a different deposit because of race, creed, age, color, national origin, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability or political affiliation. Write down your deposit criteria (for example, by credit result or number of pets), apply them the same way to everyone, and keep the record.

title: Using the Security Deposit in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute lists what a security deposit may be used for; the lease decides. The shared clause tagged for the Virgin Islands (`security-deposit-use`) lets you apply the deposit to unpaid rent and other defaults and to damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, and not to wear and tear or pre-existing conditions, which fits the general law. One statute limits use: when a tenant ends the lease under the domestic-violence release, you must return the deposit to the tenant victim and may keep part of it only for damage not caused by an act of domestic violence.

No statute lets a lease preset cleaning or repair charges. A deposit does not cap what the tenant owes; collect any larger amount in a separate civil action or small claims.

title: Utility Deposits in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute governs a utility deposit held by a landlord. If you collect money to secure utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease, treat it as part of the security deposit: say so in the lease, return it with the deposit, and itemize any utility charge you deduct; any water or electricity charge must reflect the tenant's actual use. Deposits a tenant pays directly to a public utility are different: the utility must pay interest on cash deposits it holds six months or more (4¾% a year, or for the Water and Power Authority the average local bank savings rate) and refund the deposit with interest when service ends, unless service ended for unjustified nonpayment; a utility deposit or refund not claimed within one year after it becomes payable is presumed abandoned. The tenant deals with the utility directly on those deposits.

title: Tenant alterations
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute governs whether a tenant may alter, improve or install anything in a rental home, who owns the result, or who pays for a disability-related modification, so the shared Alterations clause (`no-alterations`) and, if you want it, the optional improvements-ownership clause (`improvements-ownership-la`) work as written. Know the rules around them.
- (1) Housing Code: you as owner must care for the plumbing system and may not change its design or the arrangement of rooms so that required fixtures become inaccessible to occupants or lose their privacy, so do not approve tenant work that would do that; your Housing Code maintenance duties (walls, roof, windows, doors, floors, stairs, wiring) stay with you whatever the lease says.
- (2) Building Code: a permit is needed for construction, structural alteration, enlargement, conversion or demolition; no permit is needed for nonstructural work such as carpentry, plastering, like-for-like replacement of windows, doors, siding, roofing or flooring, or moving non-load-bearing interior partitions in residential buildings if no extra dwelling is created and ventilation is not harmed. If you approve work that needs a permit, require the tenant to get it.
- (3) Disability: Virgin Islands law says nothing requires a landlord to modify property to give a blind person a higher degree of care than anyone else; federal fair-housing law requires you to permit reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense, and you may make some interior modifications conditional on restoration. No Virgin Islands statute shifts that cost to owners of larger or assisted housing.
- (4) Cable television: you may not forbid a tenant's cable service or charge for allowing its installation, but you may require reasonable installation conditions.
- (5) A tenant for years who commits waste can be sued for treble damages.

For contractor liens from tenant work, see the construction-liens row.

title: Bed bugs and pests
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute deals with bed bugs or divides the duty and cost of pest treatment between landlord and tenant, so you may use the optional pest-cooperation clause (`pest-cooperation-la`) as written. The rules around it: under the Housing Code each occupant must keep the part of the dwelling he occupies or controls clean, safe and sanitary and dispose of garbage in a sanitary way, while you must keep openings screened, keep the shared areas of a building with two or more units clean, safe and sanitary, and supply garbage containers.

The territory's waste law forbids an owner or a lessee to let waste build up on premises he manages or controls if it may breed flies, mosquitoes or rodents. The Commissioner of Health may make regulations for treating premises for pests and vermin, with fees charged to owners that can be waived if the owner or tenant cannot pay.

Cautious course: treat promptly at your cost unless the tenant's fault caused the infestation, charge the tenant only reasonable actual costs you can show the tenant caused (collected in a separate civil action or small claims, not in an eviction case), and enter to inspect or treat only with the tenant's consent or as the lease allows.

title: Carpet cleaning at move-out
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute says whether a lease may require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, or on what condition, and the territory has no security deposit statute setting what may be deducted.

The optional carpet-cleaning clause (`carpet-cleaning-ar`) may be used; its condition (the carpets were professionally cleaned just before the tenancy) is a fairness safeguard, not a Virgin Islands rule, and keeping it makes the charge easier to defend. The Housing Code makes the tenant keep the part of the dwelling he occupies clean, safe and sanitary. Whether a charge for ordinary wear and tear is allowed rests on the common law; the cautious course is to charge only the reasonable cost you actually pay, back it with the receipt, and itemize it with any deposit deduction (see the Security Deposit topics).

title: Cold-weather vacate notice
bodyText: Not applicable in the Virgin Islands. No Virgin Islands statute requires a tenant to give notice or take freeze precautions before vacating or leaving a dwelling empty, and freezing pipes do not arise in the territory's climate. Related duties that do apply: the tenant must keep plumbing fixtures clean and use them with reasonable care, and a tenant who will be away for a long time may be asked by the lease to tell you (see `edu-no-extended-absence-notice-vi`).

title: Move-in condition
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute requires a move-in inspection, checklist or condition statement, or sets what a tenant's signed acknowledgment of condition does, so the shared Existing Condition clause (`existing-condition`) works as written. It cannot, though, relieve you of the Housing Code: no one may rent out a building or part of one for living, sleeping or cooking that does not comply with the Building Code or the Housing Code, and your duties to maintain the plumbing, walls, roof, windows, doors, floors, stairs, cistern system and wiring continue during the tenancy whatever the tenant acknowledged.

Cautious course: inspect with the tenant before move-in, record the condition in writing with dated photographs signed by both of you, and repair any Housing Code item rather than listing it as an accepted condition; the record is your best evidence in a later deposit or damage dispute.

title: Tenant absence
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute requires a tenant to tell you about an extended absence, requires the lease to contain such a term, or gives you a right to enter while the tenant is away. The shared absence-notice clause (`extended-absence-notice-ks`) may be used as a lease term; any damages for a willful failure to give notice are ordinary contract damages, claimed in a separate civil action or small claims.

What the law does say nearby: a notice to quit may be served by leaving it at the premises if the tenant is absent; entering another person's home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for the entry, so do not enter an absent tenant's home except as the lease allows or the tenant agrees; and no statute defines when an absent tenant has abandoned the home (see the Default & Termination topics).

title: Co-tenant liability
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute addresses whether co-tenants are jointly and severally liable under a lease, or whether accepting one co-tenant's share of the rent without a reservation releases that co-tenant, so the shared Joint Liability clause (`joint-liability`) works as written. Two statutes touch co-tenants. Every person in possession of land out of which rent is due is liable for the share of the rent due from the part he holds, even if it is only part of what was originally leased.

And when a tenant who is a domestic-violence victim ends the lease under the territory's release law, every other tenant under the lease stays bound, and a person named in a court order as the perpetrator may be liable to you for the resulting losses. Waiver by accepting partial payments is a common-law question; cautious course: when you accept a payment from one co-tenant, say in the receipt that you accept it as part payment and do not release any tenant.

Rent and damages are collected in a separate civil action or small claims, not in an eviction case.

title: Yard and irrigation
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute regulates which yard, landscaping or irrigation tasks a lease may give the tenant, and none requires a separate signed writing or extra consideration for them, so the shared Landscaping clause (`landscaping-irrigation`) works as written.

Keep in mind: the Housing Code makes you as owner keep roofs, gutters, spouting and pipes to cisterns tight and clean, keep openings screened and keep the pump and piping system working, so the cistern and its pump stay your responsibility even if the tenant waters the yard. The territory's waste law applies to whoever controls the yard, owner or lessee: no one may let waste build up that could breed flies, mosquitoes or rodents, burn waste in the open without the Waste Management Authority's permission, or dispose of waste other than at an authorized site, though a private compost pile is allowed if it is rodent-proof, holds no garbage and is not a nuisance. Tell tenants who keep the yard not to burn cuttings.

title: Occupancy limits
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands Housing Code sets occupancy by floor area, not by persons per bedroom. Every dwelling unit needs at least 150 square feet of habitable floor area for the first occupant, 100 more for each of the next three occupants and 75 more for each additional occupant (kitchens, bathrooms, closets, halls and foyers do not count). A room used for sleeping by one person needs at least 80 square feet; a room shared for sleeping needs 50 square feet for each occupant aged 12 or over and 35 for each occupant under 12; habitable rooms need 8-foot ceilings.

A unit with more sleepers than these figures allow is overcrowded and is occupied, used and rented in violation of the Housing Code, so both you and the tenant are exposed. The Housing Code covers all dwellings, apartments, rooming houses and hotels, but not owner-occupied rural dwellings under 600 square feet. The Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority enforces it on its own initiative or on complaints, so a neighbour or anyone else can complain, but no statute gives a neighbour a private action.

Use the shared Permitted Occupants clause (`permitted-occupants`) and set any occupancy cap from these figures. Do not set a cap tighter than the Housing Code requires without a sound reason: Virgin Islands law forbids discrimination in rental terms because of age (among other grounds), and federal fair-housing law protects families with children. No Virgin Islands statute lets a household member take over a lease when the tenant dies (see the Default & Termination topics on a tenant's death).

title: Tenant duties under Virgin Islands law
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no residential landlord-tenant act listing tenant duties, but several statutes bind tenants directly. (1) Housing Code: every occupant must keep the part of the dwelling he occupies or controls clean, safe and sanitary, dispose of his garbage in a clean and sanitary way under the Public Works rules, and keep the plumbing fixtures clean and use them with reasonable care; occupants also count toward the Housing Code's overcrowding limits, and the Housing Finance Authority may serve violation notices on occupants as well as owners (the Housing Code covers all dwellings except owner-occupied rural dwellings under 600 square feet). (2) Rent: every person in possession of land out of which rent is due is liable for the rent due from the part he holds. (3) Ending a tenancy at will or by sufferance: either party must give written notice (three months, or the rent interval if rent is paid more often). (4) Waste: a tenant for years who commits waste can be sued for treble damages and, in serious cases, lose the lease. (5) Waste law: an owner or lessee may not let waste build up that could breed flies, mosquitoes or rodents, leave a junked vehicle on property without the owner's consent, or burn waste in the open without permission. (6) Cannabis: consuming cannabis in a public place or a place open to public use is not protected. The library's Tenant Maintenance clause (`tenant-maintenance`) restates the Housing Code duties; breaches can support eviction only as the lease and the possession statutes allow (see the Default & Termination topics).

title: Tenant upkeep duties
bodyText:
The shared Tenant Maintenance clause (`tenant-maintenance`) matches the Virgin Islands Housing Code, which makes every occupant keep the part of the dwelling he occupies or controls clean, safe and sanitary, dispose of garbage in a sanitary way and use the plumbing fixtures with reasonable care. The Housing Code keeps the rest with you as owner: the plumbing system; weathertight walls, roof, windows and doors; floors, stairs and porches; roofs, gutters and pipes to cisterns kept tight and clean, openings screened and the pump and piping working; shared areas of buildings with two or more units; garbage containers; and safe wiring and fixtures.

The clause's exception for conditions the law requires you to repair keeps it consistent with those duties. Cisterns, wells and septic systems: no Virgin Islands statute was found that makes a tenant maintain a septic system or well, and the cistern system is yours under the Housing Code; the waste law forbids anyone to put waste into a sewer, storm drain or watercourse except as the Waste Management Authority allows.

A tenant for years who commits waste can be sued for treble damages, and unreasonable damage or a nuisance is one of the possession grounds in the rent-control subchapter (see the Default & Termination topics).

title: Acts the law forbids tenants
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no statutory list of acts a residential tenant must not do (like the uniform acts' list of prohibited conduct). Prohibitions are scattered: a tenant must not commit waste, must not let waste build up that breeds pests, leave a junked vehicle on property without the owner's consent, or burn waste in the open, and must not consume cannabis in a public place. Maintaining a nuisance, causing or permitting unreasonable damage, or repeatedly engaging in or permitting serious misconduct on the premises is one of the grounds on which possession may be recovered under the rent-control subchapter. The full list of statutory tenant duties, with citations, is in `edu-tenant-statutory-duties-vi`; the shared No Disturbance clause (`no-disturbance`) and Tenant Maintenance clause (`tenant-maintenance`) put the usual prohibitions into the lease. Remember that no lease term may let you end the tenancy or penalize a tenant for calling the police or emergency help in a domestic-violence situation.

title: Shifting repairs to the tenant
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute allows or forbids an agreement that the tenant will do repairs or chores, and none requires a separate writing, good faith or consideration for one. You may use the optional tenant-repair agreement (`tenant-repair-agreement-hi`) for specific tasks, but it cannot move your Housing Code duties as owner: the Housing Code puts the plumbing system, weathertight walls, roof, windows and doors, floors and stairs, roof gutters and cistern pipes, the pump and piping, shared areas and wiring on the owner, and the Housing Finance Authority enforces those duties against the owner whatever the lease says.

Use the agreement for tasks outside those duties (yard care, filters, light bulbs) or, if the tenant does owner work, stay responsible for the result. No statute gives a tenant a right to repair and deduct or withhold rent, and none lets you make a tenant do your repairs as a condition of the tenancy.

title: Residential-use covenant
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute sets what happens when a tenant uses a home for another purpose, so the shared Residential Use Only clause (`residential-use-only`) works as a lease covenant. Enforcing it: holding over contrary to a lease covenant after a notice to quit is an unlawful holding under the forcible entry and detainer statute, but that section is stated to be suspended while the rent-control subchapter is in effect, and under the cautious course a possession case needs one of that subchapter's grounds (owner's own use, demolition, nuisance, unreasonable damage or repeated serious misconduct, or nonpayment) and 30 days' written notice to quit.

A business use that is not a nuisance or serious misconduct may not be enough on its own; treat it first as a lease breach to be cured. Other laws that a non-residential use can trigger: a home rented out to guests for less than 90 days is a hotel for the 12.5 percent hotel room tax, collected by whoever rents or facilitates it; a home used as a hospice, child care, adult day care or health care facility becomes a public place under the Smoke-free Act; and zoning limits business uses in residential districts.

title: Subletting and assignment
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute limits a lease term requiring your consent before the tenant sublets or assigns, sets a standard for refusing consent, or treats your silence as consent, so the shared No Sublet or Assignment clause (`no-sublet-assign`) works as written.

Points to know: anyone in possession of the property owes the share of the rent due from the part he holds; the territory's housing discrimination law binds a tenant who sublets or assigns (it names sublessors and assignors), except for renting rooms in a home where the renter lives; a tenant who rents the home to guests for less than 90 days triggers the 12.5 percent hotel room tax, collected by whoever rents it out or facilitates the rental; and enforcing a breach by eviction is subject to the rent-control cautious course (a listed ground and 30 days' written notice to quit), so an unauthorized sublet that is not a nuisance or serious misconduct may be hard to use as the ground for possession.

title: Tenant forwarding legal papers
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute makes a tenant tell you about, or forward, papers in a proceeding against the property, and none deals with attornment (a tenant agreeing to recognize someone else as landlord). The shared forwarding clause (`tenant-forward-proceedings-ca`) is worth using because of one rule: when someone sues your tenant to recover the property, the tenant may answer that he holds only as your tenant and name you; you are made the defendant if you apply within the time the tenant has to answer, and if you do not, you lose the right to step in unless the plaintiff asks for it.

Once you are made the defendant, the judgment binds you as if the case had been brought against you from the start. Prompt notice from the tenant protects that window.
