title: Tenant insurance claims
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a tenant to carry renter's insurance, governs claims between a tenant's insurer and you, or limits a lease term on insurance or claims. A lease requirement to carry insurance is a matter of contract (see the tenant's-property insurance clause the library tags for the territory). Under the library's cautious course for the Virgin Islands, insurance clauses do not say that you are not liable for your own negligence, because whether such a term is enforceable in a residential lease rests on common law that was not searched.

title: Utilities and tenants
bodyText:
The shared Utilities clause (`utilities-responsibility`) works in the Virgin Islands, subject to these statutes.
- (1) Meters and charges: unless the lease says otherwise in writing, you must install a water or electric meter for a dwelling unit if the tenant asks, and whenever you charge a tenant for water or electricity the charge must be based on the amount the tenant uses.
- (2) Sewer fee: if you pay the public sewer system user fee, you may not charge a tenant more than the actual fee attributable to the tenant's unit, must divide a multi-unit fee equally between the units, and may not pass penalties on to tenants.
- (3) Cable television: you may not forbid a tenant's cable service, charge for allowing it, or raise rent because of it, though you may set reasonable installation conditions.
- (4) Utility accounts: under the Ratepayers' Bill of Rights a public utility may not refuse or cut off a new occupant's service because a former occupant from another household left a bill unpaid, and a customer may designate another person to receive notices about past-due bills and disconnection, so you can ask a tenant who holds the account to name you.

No Virgin Islands statute makes an owner liable for a tenant's unpaid electric or water bill or lets an unpaid bill become a lien on the property (see `edu-no-municipal-utility-lien-vi`), and no statute makes a tenant's unpaid utility bill a ground for eviction.

title: Meters and utility charges
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no regime for landlord submetering or reselling electricity, and no statute on interrupting submetered service; whether a landlord who re-bills metered electricity or water is itself a regulated public utility is not settled. It has one metering rule for all landlords of dwelling and commercial units: unless otherwise agreed in writing, when a tenant asks, you must install a water or electric meter to record what the tenant uses.

You may still charge the tenant for water or electricity, but only based on the amount the tenant uses. So if you bill tenants for utilities, bill from a meter reading rather than a flat or estimated share. A written lease term can relieve you of the duty to install a meter on request (see the optional clause `utility-meter-request-waiver-vi`), but no term relieves you of the usage rule if you charge separately. Shutting off a tenant's water or power to force payment or departure is not a lawful eviction method (see the Default & Termination topics on self-help).

title: Proof of utility payment
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives a landlord a right to proof that a tenant has paid utilities, or limits a lease term requiring it, so the shared clause (`utility-payment-evidence`) works as a contract term. A useful companion: the Ratepayers' Bill of Rights lets a utility customer designate another person to receive all information about the account, including past-due and disconnection notices, so you may ask a tenant who holds the account to designate you.

title: Keeping utilities on
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute makes a tenant keep utility service connected or lets you restore service at the tenant's cost, so the shared clause (`utility-service-continuity`) works as a contract term.

Related rules: the Ratepayers' Bill of Rights gives every public utility customer the right to a payment plan to avoid disconnection under the utility's terms, to avoid disconnection over a disputed bill while current on undisputed bills, to a 60-day medical hold, to keep service despite a former occupant's unpaid bill, to same-day restoration after paying, and to name another person (such as you) to receive disconnection notices.

The Housing Code makes you keep the plumbing, pump and piping and the wiring in working order, so a building-side failure is yours to fix. Cutting off a tenant's utilities yourself to force payment or move-out is not a lawful remedy (see the Default & Termination topics on self-help).

title: Smoking rules in rentals
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands Smoke-free Act bans smoking in enclosed areas of public places and places of employment, but it does not reach a private residence unless the home is used as a hospice, child care, adult day care or health care facility. So smoking inside a rented home is governed by the lease, and the shared Smoking Policy clause (`smoking-policy`) may be used. Points specific to the territory:
- (1) The Act's public places include hotels, resorts, guesthouses and inns and any place the public is invited or permitted (such as a lobby or leasing office open to visitors), and a place of employment includes the hallways and other areas your employees normally use, so in an apartment building with staff the enclosed common areas and the office must be smoke-free with the required signs, while the apartments themselves are not covered; smoking in a parking lot is allowed except within 20 feet of an entrance, window or vent of a public place or place of employment.
- (2) The Act defines smoking as a lighted product; it does not reach electronic cigarettes, and the cannabis law says vaporizing cannabis is not smoking, so a lease that means to ban vaping must say so, as the shared clause does.
- (3) Cannabis: no landlord may refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely because he is a registered medical-cannabis patient (unless federal law or a federal benefit requires it), but no landlord may be penalized for seeking a smoke-free environment. A ban on smoking cannabis is therefore safe; whether you may enforce a vaping ban against a patient's medical use inside the home is not settled, so take advice before acting on it, and never act on patient status alone. A patient may grow medical cannabis at home only with the landowner's express consent.
- (4) No Virgin Islands statute makes smoke drift a nuisance, prescribes a smoking-policy disclosure, or regulates adding a smoking ban mid-tenancy; a mid-term ban needs the tenant's agreement or a new lease term.

title: Landlord entry
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute gives a residential landlord a right to enter the tenant's home, sets a notice period, hours or purposes, or provides remedies for refused or abusive entry. Two statutes make consent essential: entering another person's home without the consent of the tenant is a crime (fine up to $200 or up to a year in jail) except where the law provides for the entry, and no one may enter land or a building except where the law allows, and then only peacefully, never by force.

No statute provides for a landlord's entry, so your authority to enter comes from the tenant's consent, given in the lease (the shared clause `landlords-access`, with 24 hours' notice) or at the time.

Cautious course: give the lease notice, enter at reasonable times for the lease's purposes, and if the tenant refuses entry at the door, do not force it; treat the refusal as a lease breach to be cured or taken to court. In a genuine emergency (fire, flooding, gas) entry to protect life or property rests on common law, so keep it to real emergencies and document them. A written maintenance request is good evidence that the tenant consents to entry for that repair, but no statute says so. No statute lets you relocate a tenant temporarily, governs showings, or requires a separate notice for scheduled services.

Government Housing Code inspectors may enter only with the occupants' consent or by due process.

title: Periodic inspections
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives you a right to inspect a rented home during the tenancy or at move-out, or limits how often you may. The shared Inspection clause (`inspection-rights`) gives you that right by the tenant's agreement. Because entering a home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for it, inspect only as the lease allows, on the lease's notice, and do not force entry if the tenant refuses at the time. Housing Code inspectors from the Housing Finance Authority also need the occupants' consent or court process to enter.

title: Entry for scheduled services
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute governs entry for regularly scheduled services (filter changes, pest treatment) or requires that a no-notice entry right be written conspicuously in the lease. The optional scheduled-services clause (`scheduled-services-entry-la`) works as the tenant's advance consent. Because entering a home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for it, state the services, schedule and notice plainly, stick to them, and do not enter over the tenant's objection at the time.

title: Showing the home
bodyText: Because the Virgin Islands has no statutory entry-notice period, there is nothing for a tenant to waive and no rule requiring a separate signed document to shorten notice for showings. The optional showing clause (`showing-notice-la`) sets a shorter notice for showings by agreement. Showings still depend on the tenant's consent: entering a home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for it, so follow the clause's hours and notice and do not show the home over the tenant's objection at the time.

title: Smart locks and app entry
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute regulates smart locks, keypad or app-based entry systems in rentals, the data they collect, or a tenant's right to a physical key. The territory's locksmith law does reach keyless devices: anyone whose trade is installing, servicing or opening locks, keys or keyless devices must be a licensed locksmith, although the owner or tenant of the premises may change a lock's mechanical adjustment or combination. Use a licensed locksmith or the device maker's authorized installer, and remember that remote entry is still entry: it needs the tenant's consent under the lease (see `edu-landlord-entry-vi`).

title: Key control
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute requires a key-control policy or background checks for employees with key access, for large complexes or anyone else. The locksmith law sets the nearby rules: only a licensed locksmith, or the owner or tenant of the premises, may open a lock whose key is lost, change a lock's mechanical adjustment or combination, or make an original key; master keys must be stamped "master", may be duplicated only on the signed order of the owner of the locks or the owner's authorized agent, and may be made only by a licensed locksmith; locksmiths and keymakers must log who orders master keys.

Violations are punishable by a fine of up to $500 or up to three months in jail.

Good practice: keep master keys in a log under your control, order duplicates in writing, and re-key between tenancies (the shared Keys clause, `keys`, lets you charge a tenant who does not return keys).

title: Lock changes for abuse victims
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute lets a domestic-violence victim require a landlord to change the locks, or sets who pays.

What the law does provide: a victim who seeks to leave out of fear of imminent danger to self or children may end the lease on at least 14 days' written notice with a police report written within the 90 days before the notice, without a termination fee; no lease term may penalize a tenant for calling police or emergency help in a domestic-violence situation; and a court protecting a victim may give the victim possession of a jointly leased home, exclude the abuser, and give the victim temporary possession of keys.

The locksmith law lets the owner or the tenant change a lock's mechanical adjustment or combination.

Cautious course: when a tenant shows you a protective order excluding a household member, change or re-key the locks promptly at the protected tenant's request, give no keys to the excluded person, and do not charge the victim a penalty for the change; waive the Keys clause's limit on duplicating keys for that purpose.

title: Assistance animals
bodyText:
Virgin Islands law protects one kind of assistance animal by name: a blind tenant's dog guide. A blind person with a dog guide is entitled to full and equal access to all housing offered for rent in the territory, may not be charged extra for the dog, and is liable for any damage the dog does; a no-pets term in a lease does not apply to a blind tenant's dog guide. The housing provision has no exemptions for small or owner-occupied buildings and no stated direct-threat exception, and the territory's guide-dog law has no documentation procedure, species rule or registration requirement for housing (the harness requirement applies to public places).

Denying or interfering with these rights is a misdemeanor. For every other disability, including emotional support animals and service animals of other kinds, the territory's civil-rights law bars housing discrimination because of disability, but no Virgin Islands statute sets out a reasonable-accommodation duty, documentation rules or fee rules for animals; those come from federal fair-housing law. Use the Virgin Islands Assistance Animal clause (`assistance-animal-accommodation-vi`): its no-fee and damage-liability terms match the dog-guide statute, and it never lets you withdraw a blind tenant's dog guide.

No statute gives a landlord immunity for injuries caused by an assistance animal it permits, and none makes misrepresenting an animal a crime.

title: Penalty for refusing a dog guide
bodyText:
Refusing a blind tenant's dog guide is a crime in the Virgin Islands. Anyone who denies or interferes with a blind person's right to rent housing on equal terms, or to keep a dog guide in housing without paying extra, commits a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $500 to $1,000, up to 60 days in jail, or both, and is liable to the blind person for actual and punitive damages or other relief in court. The blind person may also complain under oath to the Virgin Islands Commission on the Handicapped.

The housing right applies to all housing offered for rent in the territory, so it does not depend on whether a rental building counts as a public accommodation. It covers blind persons and their dog guides (and dog-guide trainers in public facilities); other assistance animals are protected through the general disability-discrimination law and federal law, which carry civil remedies but no criminal penalty for a refusal.

title: Fake service animals
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute makes it an offence to misrepresent an animal as a service, guide or assistance animal, in housing or anywhere else. The territory's protection is for a blind person (as defined by visual-acuity and field-of-vision standards) with a dog guide; for other animals the rules come from federal fair-housing law. If you doubt a request, use the documentation steps federal guidance allows (see the Virgin Islands Assistance Animal clause, `assistance-animal-accommodation-vi`), and do not refuse a blind tenant's dog guide, which is a crime (see `edu-service-animal-denial-penalty-vi`).

title: Pet fact sheet
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to give a tenant a fact sheet or notice about pets and eviction, or any other pet disclosure, with the lease. Pet terms are a matter of the lease (see `edu-pet-policy-vi` and the shared pet clause).

title: Pet deposits and pet rent
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute regulates pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent, and the territory has no security deposit statute defining a deposit or capping it, so a pet deposit or monthly pet rent is a matter of the lease (the shared pet clause treats pet rent as part of the rent and a pet deposit as a security deposit; see the Security Deposit topics for how deposits are handled). One firm rule: a blind tenant may not be charged extra for a dog guide, though the tenant is liable for damage the dog does.

Federal fair-housing law likewise bars fees for other assistance animals. If you charge pet rent as part of the rent, remember the library's cautious course on the rent-control subchapter (see the Rent & Payment topics).

title: Pet liability insurance
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute limits a lease term requiring a tenant with a pet to carry liability insurance, so the shared clause (`pet-insurance-requirement`) works as written. Its exception for assistance animals matters here: a blind tenant may not be required to pay extra compensation for a dog guide, and an insurance requirement aimed at the dog guide could be treated as an extra charge.

title: Towing and abandoned vehicles
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute authorizes or regulates towing ordered by a private property owner: there are no sign, written-authorization, rate-cap or kickback rules for private tows, and none bars towing for expired registration.

What the law provides is the abandoned motor vehicle chapter, re-enacted in December 2024.
- (1) A vehicle on privately owned property is abandoned if it is left unattended for more than 60 days or left there without the owner's permission. The property owner may presume it abandoned and claim ownership by giving notice to the owner of record and lienholders (by publication if they cannot be found) stating the vehicle's location, how long it has been abandoned and the intent to claim title; if it is not reclaimed within 30 days of the notice, ownership vests in the property owner, who may then get a new title from the Bureau of Motor Vehicles. An improper claim can bring fines of up to $1,000 and loss of the right to claim title.
- (2) The Police Department may take into custody and tow abandoned or derelict vehicles and vehicles that are a hazard; the vehicle's owner pays towing and storage and can be fined. A derelict vehicle includes an inoperable vehicle kept on private property outside an enclosed garage or storage building.
- (3) The waste law forbids anyone to leave or permit a junked or abandoned vehicle on property without the owner's consent.

In a rental, a tenant's own car parked with permission is not abandoned unless left unattended for more than 60 days, and whether the tenant's consent counts as the property owner's permission is not settled.

Cautious course: enforce parking rules through the lease (notice and cure); for an abandoned or derelict vehicle, call the Police Department or follow the claim procedure exactly; do not have a tenant's or guest's car towed by a private company on your own authority without legal advice, because the risk rests on common law.

title: Vehicle rules
bodyText:
The shared Vehicle Rules clause (`parking-vehicle-rules`) fits Virgin Islands law. Its ban on inoperable vehicles matches the abandoned-vehicle chapter, under which an inoperable vehicle intentionally kept on private property outside an enclosed garage or storage building is a derelict vehicle that its owner must dispose of (repairing a vehicle on a public street also makes it derelict). Its towing sentence works only through the phrase "in accordance with applicable law": no statute lets a landlord have a tenant's car towed for breaking a parking rule, and a tenant's car parked with permission is treated as abandoned only after 60 days unattended.

The waste law also forbids parking any vehicle in front of a waste storage point and leaving a junked vehicle on property without the owner's consent.

title: Parking terms
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute regulates parking terms in residential leases, so the shared Parking clause (`parking-ks-oh-ca`) works as written; it avoids saying you are not liable for your own negligence, in line with the library's cautious course for the territory.

Related rules: smoking is allowed in a parking lot except within 20 feet of an entrance, window or vent of a public place or place of employment; no vehicle may be parked in front of a waste storage point; and abandoned or derelict vehicles are dealt with under the abandoned-vehicle chapter. Federal fair-housing law may require an accessible or assigned space as a reasonable accommodation for a tenant with a disability.

title: Assigned parking
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute regulates assigning or reassigning a tenant's parking space, or changing parking rules during the term, so the shared clause (`assigned-parking-space`) works as written. Reassigning a space a tenant needs because of a disability may require a reasonable accommodation under federal fair-housing law.

title: Parking rules notice
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires parking or towing rules to be delivered before the lease is signed, prescribes a heading, limits mid-term changes or the vehicle information you may ask for, or ties a parking permit to the lease term. Give tenants your parking rules in writing with the lease so they bind as lease terms; a change during the term binds only as the lease allows (see `edu-parking-vehicle-rules-vi`).

title: Unbundled parking
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires parking to be offered or priced separately from the rent, or forbids it. If you charge separately for parking, state the charge in the lease; zoning off-street parking requirements for the building are a planning matter, not a lease term.

title: Storage space
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no self-service storage act, so no statutory lien-and-sale procedure applies to a storage locker that comes with a residential tenancy; the shared Storage clause (`storage-space-ks-oh-ca`) works as written. The territory's general storage lien belongs to a person who keeps or stores goods at the owner's request and lets that person hold the goods until paid; a locker the tenant controls under the lease is not that kind of storage, so do not treat the tenant's belongings as subject to a lien.

Belongings left after the tenancy ends are covered in the Default & Termination topics. The waste law forbids anyone to let waste build up on premises he controls if it may breed flies, mosquitoes or rodents, which supports the clause's ban on perishable materials.

title: EV charging right
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives a tenant a right to install or use an electric-vehicle charger, or requires you to provide one. Whether to allow a charger is your choice; if you do, use the optional installation clause (`ev-charger-installation-hi`), require any permit the Building Code needs, and remember that if you bill the tenant for the electricity it must be based on actual use (at no more than the rate the utility charges you, with no markup, because whether re-billing electricity is a public-utility service under 30 V.I.C. § 1(a)(3) is not settled; see `edu-no-submetering-disclosure-rule-vi`).

title: EV charger installation terms
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute sets conditions (insurance, licensed installers, removal, registration) for a tenant's electric-vehicle charger. The optional installation clause (`ev-charger-installation-hi`) works as a contract; add a requirement that the tenant obtain any building permit the work needs, and bill any electricity you supply only on actual use (at no more than the rate the utility charges you, with no markup, because whether re-billing electricity is a public-utility service under 30 V.I.C. § 1(a)(3) is not settled).

title: EV charger at move-out
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says who owns, removes or pays for a tenant-installed electric-vehicle charger when the tenancy ends. Settle it in the installation agreement (`ev-charger-installation-hi`) or the improvements clause (`improvements-ownership-la`); otherwise the common law of fixtures decides.

title: EV charging in shared areas
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives tenants a right to install electric-vehicle chargers in shared parking areas or sets rules for shared charging. Any shared-area charging is your decision, subject to building permits and, in a condominium, the association's rules.

title: Contractor liens from tenant work
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands construction lien law gives a contractor, subcontractor or sub-subcontractor who performs a real estate improvement contract a lien on the contracting owner's interest in the real estate being improved; an owner means the owner of any interest, so a tenant who hires the work is the contracting owner of the leasehold. Your own interest is bound only if you, in writing, requested that the improvement be made or agreed specifically that your interest may be bound by the lien.

So a lease that merely permits alterations with your consent should not expose your interest, but a lease or letter that requires or asks the tenant to make an improvement may. No lien arises for an unlicensed contractor. No statute lets a lease, recorded or not, keep your interest free of liens beyond that rule.

Cautious course: give consent to tenant work in writing, say that you are not requesting the work and do not agree that your interest may be bound, use the optional no-liens clause (`no-liens-ar`) so the tenant pays everyone it hires and clears any lien, and require licensed contractors.

title: Noise and disturbance
bodyText:
The shared No Disturbance clause (`no-disturbance`) works in the Virgin Islands, and the territory's noise law backs it up. It is unlawful to operate a sound-producing or amplification device that creates a noise disturbance, to run lawn mowers or other power machinery or repair vehicles in or near a residential zone between 8 p.m. and 7 a.m. so as to create a noise disturbance, and for anyone owning, occupying or having charge of a building or premises to cause, suffer or allow loud, unnecessary or unusual music or noise that can be heard 100 feet away.

Noise reaching a residential area may not exceed 65 dBA by day or 60 dBA at night. Note that the last rule reaches an owner or manager who allows the noise, so act on complaints. Maliciously disturbing the peace of a neighbourhood or person by loud or unusual noise is also a crime. For possession, a nuisance, unreasonable damage or repeated serious misconduct on the premises is one of the grounds in the rent-control subchapter (see the Default & Termination topics for the cautious course).

Never treat a tenant's calls to the police or emergency services in a domestic-violence situation as a disturbance: no lease term may penalize them.

title: Home businesses
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute makes a home-based business a use a lease cannot restrict, so the shared Residential Use Only clause (`residential-use-only`) may forbid or limit business use, and you may allow a specific business in writing. Zoning permits a home occupation in the residential districts: a use carried on entirely within the dwelling by those who live there, clearly incidental to living there, with no display or advertising of goods for sale on the premises and no more than one employee from outside the household (some uses, such as real estate brokers, tea rooms, cafes and animal hospitals, are excluded). That is a planning permission, not a right against you. A business listed in the territory's business licence law needs a licence from the Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs before it starts, so ask for it if you allow the business. A home used as a child care, adult day care or health care facility becomes a smoke-free public place and place of employment, and renting rooms to short-stay guests is a hotel use for the hotel room tax (see `edu-no-residential-use-remedy-vi`).

title: Child care in a rented home
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to allow a tenant to run a family child care home, or sets conditions such as liability waivers or insurance, so a lease may forbid or condition it (see `residential-use-only`). If you allow it: the territory's child day care licensure law covers family day care homes (3 to 6 children under 14) and group day care homes (7 to 12 children under 14), so require proof of whatever licence the Department of Human Services requires; zoning lists children's day care (nursery schools) among the uses in residential districts; and while the home is used for child care it is a smoke-free public place and place of employment under the Smoke-free Act, which binds everyone in it. You may require the tenant to carry liability insurance covering the child care, but under the library's cautious course do not make the tenant waive your liability for your own negligence.

title: Utility liens for tenant bills
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no municipal governments or municipal utilities, and no statute makes a tenant's unpaid electric or water bill a lien on your property or collectible from you, so there is no affidavit or lease procedure to use. Two charges work differently. (1) Waste: whoever possesses or controls premises must keep approved waste containers, apartment buildings of more than three units must provide proper waste storage, and if waste accumulates and the owner or occupant does not remove it after notice, the Waste Management Authority removes it, charges the cost to the tenant or the landowner, and may put a lien on the property; deal promptly with a tenant's accumulated waste. (2) Sewer: the public sewer system user fee is an owner-side charge levied and collected with the real property tax and a lien on the parcel; you may pass it on to tenants only up to the actual fee attributable to each unit, divided equally between units, and may not pass on penalties.

title: Caring for a tenant's animal
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute lets a landlord enter a rented home to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal, whether the tenant is away, in hospital or gone. Entering a home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for the entry, so get the tenant's consent (a lease term or a written authorization naming an emergency contact helps). If an animal seems abandoned or neglected, call the police, an animal warden or the animal shelter or humane society: abandoning an animal without providing for its care is a misdemeanor (fine up to $3,000), and those officers must take an apparently neglected animal and deliver it to a shelter, humane society or veterinarian, with notice to the owner and a hearing process.

Do not keep, sell or dispose of a tenant's animal yourself; if you take over its keeping, the territory's dog law can treat you as its owner.

title: Pets in rentals
bodyText:
Virgin Islands law lets a private landlord allow, limit or forbid pets by lease, and the shared pet clause (`pet-policy-or`) works as written; it gives you no power to seize or remove a tenant's pet, and the territory's statutes give none. The firm limit: a no-pets term does not apply to a blind tenant's dog guide, which you must admit without extra charge (the tenant is liable for damage it does). No statute gives elderly tenants a right to keep pets.

The territory's dog law also matters. Dog owners are liable for any damage their dogs do and for bites to people lawfully on the premises, whatever the dog's history, unless the person provoked the dog or a "Beware of Dog" or "Bad Dog" sign was prominently displayed. A dog an animal shelter designates as dangerous must be registered, kept in a locked enclosure of at least 5 by 10 feet with warning signs, and covered by a $50,000 bond or liability policy, or be euthanized.

Dogs and dangerous pets are banned in the territory's public housing projects except seeing-eye dogs. And the dog law's definition of an owner includes anyone who lets a domestic animal habitually stay about premises he lives in, so an owner who lives on the property should not take over keeping a tenant's dog. Revoking approval of a dangerous or nuisance pet is a lease matter; removing the animal is for its owner or the authorities.

title: No required habitability statement in the lease
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a residential lease to state that the home will be delivered or kept fit for habitation. Your duties apply whatever the lease says: the Housing Code forbids renting a building that does not comply with it or the Building Code, and lists the owner's maintenance duties. The shared maintenance clause (`landlord-maintenance`) states your repair promise and is tagged for the territory. Every lease you use must still meet the territory's plain-language rules for residential leases (see `edu-plain-language-vi`).

title: Health rules for rentals
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no health districts or local boards of health, and no statute requires you to give tenants copies of health regulations on request or to refer them to a health office. Health-related housing rules come from territorial agencies: the Housing Code (administered by the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority), the garbage rules of the Commissioner of Public Works that every occupant must follow, the Commissioner of Health's sewage, waste and pest regulations, and the Department of Public Works' power over dwellings unfit for human habitation. The regulations themselves (V.I. Rules and Regulations) were not searchable for this library. If a tenant reports a health hazard, fix it; a tenant may complain directly to the Housing Finance Authority, which may inspect with the occupants' consent.

title: Heating and cooling
bodyText: The Virgin Islands' tropical climate has no heating season, and no Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to supply heat or hot water, sets a minimum or maximum indoor temperature, or makes air conditioning an essential service, so the heating rules found elsewhere (including rules on shifting heat costs to a tenant) do not apply. The Housing Code instead requires light and ventilation: each habitable room must have a window or skylight that can be easily opened (or mechanical ventilation), and you must keep wiring and electrical equipment safe and operable. If the lease supplies air-conditioning units or a water heater, list them (see `appliances-included`): they become part of your lease promise, and air-conditioning equipment found not to conform to the adopted codes on inspection can be ordered corrected by the building Commissioner.

title: Tenant's remedies when a landlord breaches
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no statute giving a residential tenant remedies for a landlord's breach of the lease or of repair duties: no statutory right to end the lease after notice, to repair and deduct, to withhold or abate rent, to pay rent into court, or to recover statutory damages or attorney's fees. A tenant's private remedies (damages, ending the lease for a serious breach, constructive eviction, a defense to a rent claim) rest on case law not searched for this library. Public and statutory routes exist: a tenant may complain to the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority, which inspects, serves notice and orders repairs, and the tenant may appeal its orders; 25 residents may petition the Commissioner of Public Works to act on a dwelling unfit for human habitation; a tenant discriminated against may sue for compensatory and punitive damages with attorney's fees; and if rent control applies, a tenant sued for nonpayment may defend that the rent is unjust and unreasonable. In an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) case the tenant may raise defenses but not a counterclaim, and money claims either way go in a separate civil action or small claims.

title: Landlord's repair and maintenance duties
bodyText:
The shared maintenance clause (`landlord-maintenance`) is tagged for the territory and matches its Housing Code, which forbids anyone to rent a building that does not comply with it or the Building Code and makes the owner maintain: the plumbing system and required fixtures (kitchen sink, lavatory, water closet, tub or shower); foundation and exterior walls and the roof, weathertight and sound; floors, interior walls and ceilings; windows and exterior doors, weathertight and in working order; stairs and porches; impervious bathroom floors; roofs, gutters and pipes to the cistern, tight and clean, with openings screened and the pump and piping in working order; shared areas in buildings of two or more units, clean, safe and sanitary; garbage containers; and all wiring, fixtures and electrical equipment, with public halls and stairways lighted.

It applies to all dwellings, apartments, apartment houses, rooming houses and hotels (not owner-occupied rural dwellings under 600 square feet). The Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority enforces it with notices, 90-day orders to repair, vacate or demolish, Attorney General actions and fines after conviction; separately, the Commissioner of Public Works may repair or close a dwelling unfit for human habitation and record the cost as a lien on the land.

No statute lets a lease shift these duties, gives the tenant a self-help remedy, makes air conditioning an essential service, or lets a tenant end the lease because the unit is uninhabitable at the start; those questions rest on case law.

title: Shifting maintenance duties to the tenant
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets a lease shift any of the owner's Housing Code duties to the tenant, with or without conditions, and none lists particular duties (such as common-area garbage removal) that may be shifted. The code itself splits the work: the tenant keeps the part of the home the tenant occupies or controls clean, safe and sanitary, disposes of the tenant's garbage under the Public Works rules, and uses plumbing fixtures with reasonable care; the owner keeps the structure, plumbing, cistern system, pump, wiring and (in buildings of two or more units) the shared areas, and in all cases provides garbage containers. A tenant may agree to do specific tasks outside those owner duties, such as yard care or changing filters, using the optional `tenant-repair-agreement-hi` clause (see `edu-no-tenant-repair-agreement-vi`), but if the tenant does owner work you remain answerable to the Housing Finance Authority for the result.

title: Facilities you must provide
bodyText: The Virgin Islands Housing Code sets the facilities a rental must have and the owner must keep up: (1) in each dwelling unit, a kitchen sink, lavatory, water closet and tub or shower, inside the unit, with the toilet and bathing fixture private; a rooming house needs one lavatory, water closet and tub or shower for every five rooms or ten occupants; (2) a plumbing system and a potable water supply, which may be a cistern; a building not connected to the public water system must have a well or a rainwater collection area and cistern (a cistern of the required capacity, kept watertight and mosquito- and rodent-proof), with the gutters, cistern pipes, pump and piping maintained; (3) screened openings in the roof, gutter and cistern system; (4) in each habitable room a window or skylight facing outdoors of at least 15 percent of the floor area, with at least 8 percent openable (or mechanical ventilation), and bathroom light and ventilation; (5) wiring, fixtures and receptacles installed to code and kept safe and operable, and lighted public halls and stairways in multi-unit buildings; (6) garbage storage containers; and (7) minimum floor area per occupant and sleeping-room sizes, with 8-foot ceilings. No statute requires a stove, refrigerator, mailbox or laundry facilities.

title: Promises to repair
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, carry a completion date, or be made before the lease is signed. Whether an oral or pre-lease promise binds you is a question of contract law (case law not searched for this library). Three reasons to write promises into the lease anyway: an untrue statement to win a tenant may be treated as a deceptive practice under the territory's consumer protection law; a residential lease must be clear and easily readable under the plain-language law; and a written promise with a date avoids disputes about what was agreed. Promised work does not replace the Housing Code duties, which apply regardless.

title: Quiet possession
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute puts a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment into residential leases; the covenant comes from common law, which the territory's courts apply under rules the Virgin Islands Supreme Court shapes itself (case law not searched for this library). Statutes protect the tenant's possession in other ways: no one may enter land or a building except where the law allows it, and then only peacefully, never by force; entering another person's home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for the entry; a lease may not penalize a tenant for calling police or emergency help in a domestic-violence situation; and if rent control applies, you may recover possession only on a listed ground after written notice. Cautious course: treat the tenant's quiet enjoyment as part of every lease, enter only as the lease allows (see `edu-landlord-entry-vi`), and never lock out a tenant or cut off services to force a move.

title: Who keeps the repair duty when rent is collected by someone else
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says expressly that whoever receives the rent keeps the habitability duty whatever a lease, assignment, deed or security instrument says. The Housing Code reaches the same people another way: it puts the maintenance duties on the owner and defines the owner to include anyone who owns or controls the property or part of it, the owner's authorized agent or attorney, a purchaser, devisee or fiduciary, and anyone with a vested or contingent interest, so a manager collecting rent, a buyer under contract or a trustee can each be held to the code. No statute lets an owner escape those duties by assigning the rents. If you hire a manager, your management agreement should say who handles repairs, but you remain answerable.

title: Government inspections of rentals
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no rental registration, rental licensing inspection or periodic rental inspection program. Inspections reach rentals three ways: (1) the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority may inspect on its own initiative or on a complaint, entering residential premises with the occupants' consent and never by force without due process; (2) the building Commissioner may enter and inspect buildings, plumbing and wiring at all reasonable hours, again never by force without due process; and (3) the Commissioner of Public Works, investigating a dwelling unfit for human habitation, may enter with the least possible inconvenience to the occupants and must get a court order if entry is refused. No statute says a lease may give that consent in advance. A lease term in which the tenant agrees to admit government inspectors is a promise to you; whether it counts as the occupants' consent at the door is for the courts (case law not searched for this library), so ask the tenant to cooperate and let the inspector deal with any refusal through due process. Separately, renting out property may need a territorial business license (see `edu-no-government-fee-passthrough-vi`).

title: No small-landlord repair-remedy exemption
bodyText: Some states let a landlord with few units opt out of tenant rent-escrow or repair remedies by giving a notice. The Virgin Islands has no statutory rent escrow, repair-and-deduct or rent-withholding remedy, so there is nothing to opt out of and no notice to give. The only statutory deposit of rent in court in Virgin Islands landlord-tenant law is a condition of a court's stay of eviction under the rent-control subchapter, which is not a repair remedy. The Housing Code applies to every rental regardless of the number of units (except owner-occupied rural dwellings under 600 square feet).

title: How tenants give repair notice
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says how or when a tenant must tell you about a needed repair, or whether a lease may require repair requests in writing. The tagged maintenance clause (`landlord-maintenance`) asks for prompt written notice; treat that as a record-keeping request, not a condition of your duty. Your Housing Code duties do not depend on notice from the tenant, the Housing Finance Authority acts on its own inspections or on complaints however made, and no statutory tenant defense turns on written notice. So act on any notice you actually receive, by phone, text, e-mail or in person, and confirm it in writing. The Housing Code's own definition of written notice (personal delivery, or delivery or registered or certified mail to the last business address) governs only notices under that chapter.

title: No security-device or re-keying statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a residential landlord to install deadbolts, peepholes or door viewers, window latches or security bars, or to re-key locks between tenants, at any building size or construction date. What applies: the Housing Code makes you keep every window and exterior door weathertight and in good working order and repair; the Building Code requires jalousie windows and openings to meet the adopted codes' emergency escape and rescue opening rules and wind-borne debris rules, so security grilles or bars must not block a required escape opening; and the locksmith law limits who may open, change or duplicate locks and master keys (see `edu-no-key-control-mandate-vi`). No statute gives a domestic-violence victim a lock-change right (see `edu-no-dv-lock-change-vi`). Good practice: re-key or change locks at every turnover and keep doors and windows lockable.

title: No staff work card for senior housing
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a work card, licence or background check for staff of senior (55-plus or 62-plus) apartment buildings or any other ordinary rental housing. The territory's statutes on housing for elderly persons concern government support for non-profit projects, not staff rules. See `edu-no-employee-screening-rule-vi` for the related licensing and key-control rules; age is a protected class in Virgin Islands housing, so any senior-only housing must also fit the federal housing-for-older-persons exemption.

title: Services and utilities you provide
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute lists services a landlord must furnish, so the lease decides which utilities and services you provide, and the tagged clause `services-utilities-provided-ks-oh` (you provide only what the lease lists and what the law requires) works.

What the law requires of you as owner whatever the lease says: a potable water supply (a cistern or a public water connection) with the roof, gutters, cistern pipes, pump and piping kept in working order; a working plumbing system and fixtures; wiring and electrical equipment kept safe and operable; lighted public halls and stairways in multi-unit buildings; clean shared areas in buildings of two or more units; and garbage containers.

If you charge tenants for utilities: water or electricity may be charged only on the tenant's own use, and you must install a meter on request unless the lease says otherwise in writing (see `edu-utility-meter-vi` and `utility-meter-request-waiver-vi`); a public sewer system user fee may be passed on only up to the actual fee attributable to the unit; and you may not forbid cable television or charge for allowing it.

title: No stove or refrigerator requirement
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to supply a stove, range or refrigerator in a rental home or says who maintains one. The Housing Code requires a kitchen sink in each dwelling unit and defines a dwelling unit as one with facilities used or intended for living, sleeping and cooking, but it does not name cooking appliances. If you supply a stove or refrigerator, list it (`appliances-included`) and maintain it; if the tenant supplies one, say so (`appliances-excluded-vi`). A gas stove connection and its piping must meet the adopted codes.

title: Repair orders for substandard rentals; no receivership
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets tenants or the government ask a court to appoint a receiver to collect rents and repair a substandard rental building, at any building size. Repair orders do exist, for buildings of every size: (1) the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority serves written notice of a Housing Code violation and, if no action is taken within 90 days, orders repair, vacating or demolition; if the order is not obeyed the Attorney General must sue to correct the violation or stop the occupancy, and fines of up to $50 a day of wilful violation follow conviction; (2) on a petition by the housing agency or by 25 residents, the Commissioner of Public Works holds a hearing and may order a dwelling unfit for human habitation repaired, vacated and closed, or demolished, may do the work himself if the owner does not, and the cost becomes a lien on the land, foreclosable in court; and (3) the building Commissioner allows 45 days to comply with a written Building Code order, with fines of up to $500 a day after conviction and Attorney General actions to stop unlawful use or occupancy. The receivership statutes found concern public housing authority bonds, disputed estates and condominium foreclosures, not code enforcement.

title: Cable television and antennas
bodyText: Virgin Islands law limits what you may do about cable television. You may not forbid or prevent a tenant from receiving cable television service, may not demand or accept any payment as a condition of allowing it to be installed in the tenant's home, and may not charge different rent or otherwise discriminate against tenants who subscribe. You may require the installation to meet reasonable conditions to protect the safety, functioning, appearance and value of the premises and the convenience, safety and well-being of other tenants, and a cable company installing facilities for a tenant must agree to indemnify you for damage caused by installing, operating or removing them. No Virgin Islands statute addresses satellite dishes, broadband or other telecommunications access in multifamily buildings. Federal rules protect a tenant's right to install a small satellite dish or antenna in an area the tenant exclusively uses, such as a balcony, subject to reasonable safety restrictions.

title: No statutory tenant repair remedy
bodyText: The Virgin Islands Code gives a residential tenant no self-help remedy when you fail to make repairs: no repair-and-deduct, no rent withholding, no rent abatement, no payment of rent into court or escrow while a unit is unfit, and no statutory right to end the lease. The tenant's routes are public enforcement (a complaint to the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority, which inspects, serves notice and orders repairs, and whose orders the tenant may appeal; or a petition by 25 residents to the Commissioner of Public Works about a dwelling unfit for human habitation) and private claims that rest on case law not searched for this library (such as damages for breach of a lease repair promise or of an implied warranty of habitability, or a defense to a rent claim). Because the tagged maintenance clause (`landlord-maintenance`) promises repairs, a tenant may sue for breach of it in a civil action or small claims. Fix Housing Code items promptly; a tenant who withholds rent over repairs may raise the condition as a defense under case law even though no statute provides for it.

title: Utilities you pay
Dividing shared utility bills
bodyText: The Virgin Islands restricts how you divide utility costs among tenants. Water and electricity: you may charge a tenant for them, but only based on the amount of water or electricity that tenant uses, and unless the lease says otherwise in writing you must install a meter if the tenant asks, so dividing a master-metered water or electric bill by a formula (square footage, number of occupants, equal shares) is not a safe method; bill from a meter that records the tenant's own use, or include the utility in the rent. This rule has been law since 1998 and applies to every lease, old or new. Sewer: if you pay the public sewer system user fee for more than one unit, the amount attributable to each unit must be prorated equally between the units, you may not charge a tenant more than that, and you may not pass on penalties. No statute covers dividing other shared costs (such as bottled gas or garbage service), so a lease formula for those is lawful if stated clearly. If a utility account a tenant pays also serves a common area, credit the tenant or move the common load to your own account (see `edu-common-area-lighting-vi`).

title: Utility disconnection notices: the tenant may name you
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute gives an owner a right of its own to be told when a tenant's utility service is about to be disconnected, or lets an owner authorize the utility, in a separate document, to send it such notices. The right is the customer's: under the Ratepayers' Bill of Rights every public utility customer may designate another person to receive all information about the customer's services, including notices of past-due bills and disconnection.

So a lease may ask a tenant who holds a utility account in the tenant's own name to designate you, as the optional clause `utility-shutoff-notice-designee-vi` does. The Water and Power Authority's procedure for designations was not reviewed for this library. Use what you learn only to protect the property and the tenant's service, and remember the tenant's other protections: payment plans, no cut-off over a disputed bill while undisputed bills are paid, a 60-day medical hold, no cut-off or late charge for an energy-assistance program's late payment, and same-day restoration after payment.

title: When you hold the utility account
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute deals with a utility account held by the landlord for a tenant's home: none bars the utility from cutting off the tenant's service for your unpaid bill, requires notice to each unit before a building-wide shut-off, offers the tenant service in the tenant's own name, lets tenants pay the utility and deduct from rent, or lets tenants seek a rent receiver. The Ratepayers' Bill of Rights protects the customer, which is you if the account is in your name. One rule helps a tenant who later opens an account: a utility may not refuse or cut off service because a former occupant from a different household left a bill unpaid. Your other duties continue: the Housing Code makes you keep the water supply, pump, piping and wiring working, and a utility you agreed to pay is a lease promise. Keep accounts in your name current, and give tenants early warning of any planned interruption.

title: Utility shut-off limits
bodyText: The Virgin Islands limits public utility shut-offs through the Ratepayers' Bill of Rights, which binds the utilities (including the Water and Power Authority), not landlords: a customer may negotiate a delayed payment plan to avoid disconnection under the utility's terms; may not be cut off for a disputed bill while current on undisputed bills (with a deposit of half the 12-month average if the dispute runs two or more months); gets 60 days' protection from disconnection for nonpayment on a Virgin Islands doctor's written certification that disconnection would be life-threatening for the customer or a permanent household member; may not be cut off or charged late fees because an energy-assistance program paid late; may not be refused or cut off because a former occupant from a different household did not pay; must be restored the same business day after paying (within 24 hours if paid after 4 pm); and may name another person to receive disconnection notices. No statute adds a winter, weather, storm or hurricane moratorium. During a Governor-declared emergency the Governor may freeze prices for goods and services including water, fuel and rents, which reaches utility charges you bill to tenants. You may never shut off a tenant's utilities yourself to force payment or departure (see the Default & Termination topics on self-help).

title: No utility submetering disclosure rule
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute prescribes a lease disclosure, type size or separate signed page for submetered, ratio-billed or landlord-billed utilities, sets building-size thresholds, or limits late fees or disconnection for landlord utility billing. The rules that do apply: you may bill a tenant for water or electricity only on the tenant's own use, and must install a meter on the tenant's request unless the lease says otherwise in writing (see `edu-utility-meter-vi`); ratio billing of water or electricity is therefore not a safe method (see `edu-utility-apportionment-vi`); and the sewer user fee pass-through is capped at the actual fee for the unit. One open question: the territory regulates as a public utility anyone who provides electric power service or water supply service (other than retail deliveries) for compensation, and no statute says whether a landlord who re-bills metered electricity or water to tenants is covered; the cautious course is to bill only metered use at no more than the utility's own rate, with no markup. Good practice: state in the lease which utilities you bill, how each is metered, the rate, and when bills are due.

title: No landlord utility cut-off for non-transfer
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute gives you a procedure to cut off a utility still in your name when a tenant does not transfer it into the tenant's own name, and none sets a transfer deadline. Cutting off service to make a tenant act is a self-help remedy the territory's possession laws do not provide (see the Default & Termination topics), so the library does not offer an opt-in cut-off clause; a landlord who wants one should take advice first.

Use the optional clause `utility-transfer-vi` instead: it sets a transfer date and has the tenant reimburse the bills for the property's own meter in the meantime, without markup, which fits the rule that water and electricity may be charged only on the tenant's own use. Treat a failure to transfer as a lease breach, collectable in a civil action or small claims.

title: Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms
bodyText: No section of the Virgin Islands Code requires a residential landlord to install, test or maintain smoke alarms or carbon monoxide alarms in a rental home, gives the tenant a statutory duty to maintain them, sets placement rules, or gives a landlord any evidence or insurance protection for having installed them. Two gaps remain open. First, the territory adopts the International Building Code and the International Residential Code by reference and applies them to new and existing buildings, and the Building Code is administered together with the Fire Prevention Code; those model codes carry smoke-alarm and carbon-monoxide-alarm rules for construction and alteration, but their text is not printed in the Code and was not read for this library, so check them (through the Department of Planning and Natural Resources) before building, converting or substantially repairing a rental. Second, the Housing Code makes you keep all wiring, fixtures and equipment in a safe, operable condition, which reaches hard-wired alarms. Cautious course: equip every rental with working smoke alarms outside each sleeping area and on each level, and a carbon monoxide alarm wherever there is a fuel-burning appliance (such as a gas stove or water heater, or a generator kept near the home) or an attached garage; test them at move-in and record the test. You may use the optional detector-care clause (`detector-care-la`), which has the tenant leave alarms connected, report faults and pay for damage the tenant causes; it is your own rule, not a statutory one.

title: Alternate housing during repairs
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to provide or pay for alternate housing while a rental is repaired or after a hurricane, fire or other casualty, whether or not the tenant asks, and none gives a tenant a statutory right to substitute housing or to stop paying rent while the home is unusable. What does exist: the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority, which enforces the Housing Code, may order a non-complying dwelling repaired, vacated or demolished after written notice and 90 days, and the Commissioner of Public Works may order a dwelling found unfit for human habitation repaired or vacated and closed; neither statute makes the owner rehouse the tenants. The Housing Code also forbids renting a building that does not meet it. If rent control applies (see `edu-rent-control-vi`), a court that lets you recover a home for your own use or for demolition must stay the eviction for up to 6 months at a time if the tenant cannot find suitable housing despite reasonable efforts. Whether rent is owed for a period the home cannot be lived in rests on case law not searched for this library. Cautious course: do not charge rent for any period the tenant cannot lawfully or safely occupy the home, put your casualty and repair-period terms in the lease (see the casualty topic in the Default & Termination group), and if a project uses federal funds, check federal relocation rules before displacing a tenant.

title: Appliances you leave but do not supply
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute presumes that an appliance left in a rental is yours to maintain, and none lists appliances a lease may not exclude. The Housing Code draws the line instead: each dwelling unit must have a kitchen sink, lavatory, water closet and tub or shower, and you must care for and maintain the plumbing system, the roof gutters and pipes to the cistern, the pump and piping, and all lighting fixtures, receptacles, equipment and wiring, so none of those can be excluded.

Other items, such as a washer, dryer, freezer, microwave or a window air-conditioning unit left by a prior occupant, may be excluded by a clear lease term listing them.

Use the optional clause `appliances-excluded-vi` for that; the listed appliance clause (`appliances-included`) covers what you do supply.

title: Appliances you supply
bodyText:
The shared clause listing the appliances you supply (`appliances-included`) works in the Virgin Islands. No statute lists appliances a landlord must furnish, such as a stove, refrigerator or air conditioner. The Housing Code requires only plumbing fixtures in each dwelling unit (a kitchen sink, lavatory, water closet and tub or shower), which you must care for along with the plumbing system, the pump and piping, and all wiring, fixtures and electrical equipment.

Anything you list in the lease becomes part of what you promise; whether a broken listed appliance gives the tenant a remedy beyond damages rests on case law, and no statute gives the tenant a repair-and-deduct or rent-withholding remedy. List every appliance you will maintain, and use `appliances-excluded-vi` for items you leave but will not maintain.

title: Lighting of halls and stairways
bodyText: The Virgin Islands Housing Code requires every public hall and stairway in multiple dwelling units and in rooming houses to be adequately lighted at all times, and makes the owner keep all lighting fixtures, receptacles, equipment and wiring in a safe, operable condition. In a building with two or more units you must also keep the shared or public areas clean, safe and sanitary. The code applies to all dwellings, apartment houses and rooming houses (but not to owner-occupied rural dwellings under 600 square feet), and the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority enforces it. No statute says whether a tenant may be made to pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric meter. The territory's metering law points against it: if you charge a tenant for electricity, the charge must be based on the amount the tenant uses. Cautious course: keep hall and stair lighting on a house meter you pay; if an existing hallway light runs through a tenant's meter, rewire it or credit the tenant for it, and say so in the lease.

title: Rent after a repair, vacate or closing order
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute expressly bars you from collecting rent after a dwelling is ordered vacated, closed or condemned. But the Housing Code forbids anyone to rent to another a building that does not comply with the Building Code or the Housing Code, and the government can order a non-complying or unfit dwelling repaired, vacated and closed, or demolished: the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority after written notice and 90 days (with daily fines after conviction and an Attorney General action to stop the occupancy), the Commissioner of Public Works after a hearing on a dwelling found unfit for human habitation, and the building Commissioner, who may have the Attorney General stop the use or occupancy of a building in violation of the Building Code. An order is posted on the property, and Public Works can repair or close the dwelling itself and record the cost as a lien on the land. Collecting rent for a home the law forbids you to rent invites a refund claim and a deceptive-practice complaint; whether a lease is unenforceable for that period rests on case law not searched for this library. Cautious course: stop charging rent from the date an order requires the home to be vacated or closed, refund rent paid in advance for that period, and return the deposit as the lease provides (see also `edu-rent-demand-bar-vi`).

title: Habitability: what Virgin Islands law has and lacks
bodyText: How the Virgin Islands compares on habitability features found elsewhere. Present: (1) a Housing Code that forbids renting a building that does not meet it and makes the owner maintain the plumbing system and fixtures, weathertight walls, roof, windows and doors, floors, stairs, gutters and cistern pipes, the pump and piping, wiring and fixtures, lighted public halls and stairways, and clean shared areas in buildings of two or more units, and supply garbage containers; (2) occupant duties to keep the occupant's own part clean, safe and sanitary, dispose of garbage properly and use plumbing fixtures with reasonable care; (3) minimum floor-area, sleeping-room, window and ceiling standards, with overcrowding a violation; (4) public enforcement by the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority (inspection on complaint with the occupants' consent, written notice, 90 days, orders to repair, vacate or demolish, Attorney General action, fines after conviction, and a right of appeal for the owner or the tenant), plus the Commissioner of Public Works' power to repair, close or demolish dwellings unfit for human habitation on a petition of 25 residents; (5) water and electricity charges only for the tenant's actual use, and a water or electric meter on the tenant's request unless otherwise agreed in writing. Absent from the Code: a statutory implied warranty of habitability (it rests on case law not searched for this library), tenant repair-and-deduct, rent withholding, rent abatement or rent escrow, a statutory right to end the lease for uninhabitable conditions, a statutory list of essential services, heat or cooling rules, smoke or carbon monoxide alarm rules, security-device rules, protection against retaliation for housing complaints, and a rental registration or inspection program. See the individual Landlord Responsibilities rows for each.

title: Who makes repairs
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute lets a tenant make repairs at your expense, deduct repair costs from rent or withhold rent, so there is no statutory procedure for designating who does that work, and no statute requires a landlord to use a licensed or approved repairer for rental repairs. A lease may name your repair contact and say the tenant will not make repairs at your cost without your written consent; the optional clause `designated-repairer-vi` does that.

Two cautions: the Housing Code duties to maintain the plumbing, roof, walls, windows, doors, cistern system, pump and wiring stay with you whoever does the work, and whether a tenant may recover the cost of an emergency repair you failed to make rests on case law, so the clause leaves emergencies to the tenant's reasonable judgment after trying to reach you. Work that needs a building, electrical or plumbing permit needs one whoever does it.

title: Disability: accommodations and modifications
bodyText: Virgin Islands civil-rights law makes it unlawful for an owner, lessor, sublessor or managing agent to refuse to rent to a person, or to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or in the facilities or services provided with it, because of disability, and lets the person sue for compensatory and punitive damages with attorney's fees. It does not cover a building with housing for no more than two families where the owner or the owner's family lives in one, or rooms rented in a home where the owner or occupant lives. Unlike federal law, the territory's statutes do not spell out a duty to make reasonable accommodations in rules or services or to permit reasonable modifications, do not require a lease to state that a modification may be conditioned on restoring the unit, and do not provide for an interest-bearing restoration deposit. The territory's blind-persons statute even says it does not require an owner to modify property to give a blind person a higher degree of care than anyone else. The accommodation and modification duties come from the federal Fair Housing Act: you must make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services, and must let a disabled tenant make reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense, and for a rental you may, where reasonable, condition an interior modification on the tenant's agreement to restore the unit (with an escrow of restoration funds in limited cases). The federal exemptions differ from the territory's, so treat every rental as covered unless counsel confirms an exemption. A blind tenant's dog guide is protected by its own statute (see `edu-assistance-animals-vi`). The territory's visitable-housing design program is voluntary, binding only owners who claim its tax incentives.

title: Renting part of a room
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute forbids letting part of a room to more than one household, or gives an abatement or whole-room remedy when a room is double-let. The Housing Code still limits it: every room used for sleeping must have at least 80 square feet for one occupant, or 50 square feet for each occupant 12 or older and 35 for each younger occupant, and a dwelling or rooming unit with more sleepers than its rooms allow is overcrowded and occupied, used and rented in violation of the code; rooming houses must have shared bathroom fixtures for every five rooms or ten occupants. A civil-rights exemption also lets you restrict all rooms in a housing accommodation to one sex. Cautious course: rent each room or unit to one household under one lease, and check the floor-area limits before allowing additional occupants (see `edu-permitted-occupants-vi`).

title: Screening staff who enter units
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord or property manager to run background checks on employees, managers or contractors who have access to tenants' homes, or sets standards for doing so. Related rules: (1) a person who, for compensation, acts as agent for others in showing, leasing, renting or managing real property is a real estate broker and needs a licence, while the current licensing section exempts an owner or lessor acting in the regular course of managing its own property; (2) the locksmith law controls master keys (see `edu-no-key-control-mandate-vi`); (3) entering a tenant's home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for it, so staff should enter only under the lease's entry terms (see `edu-landlord-entry-vi`). Good practice: screen anyone who will hold keys, keep a key log, and supervise entries.

title: How serious a defect must be
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute sets a materiality threshold for a tenant's habitability claim or lists which defects count, because the Code gives tenants no statutory habitability remedy. The nearest yardsticks are public-law ones: any Housing Code violation can lead to a Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority notice and order, and the Commissioner of Public Works may find a dwelling unfit for human habitation where conditions are dangerous or injurious to the health or safety of the occupants, including fire and accident hazards, lack of ventilation, light or sanitary facilities, dilapidation, disrepair, structural defects, uncleanliness, overcrowding, inadequate exits or drainage, or any violation of health, fire, building or zoning rules. Whether a private claim needs a material defect rests on case law not searched for this library. Treat every Housing Code item as one you must fix, and fix promptly anything on that list.

title: Can a lease change Housing Code duties?
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says whether a lease may waive or modify a landlord's habitability duties, and none lets a lease shift them. The Housing Code duties are public-law duties on the owner, enforced by the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority whatever the lease says, and the code forbids renting a building that does not meet it, so a lease term cannot relieve you of them; tenant-side duties (keeping the tenant's own part clean, safe and sanitary, disposing of garbage, using plumbing fixtures with reasonable care) may be restated in the lease. Water is a common Virgin Islands case: the code's potable water supply may be a cistern rather than a public water connection, and a building without a connection to the public water system must have a well or a rainwater collection area and cistern, any cistern kept watertight and mosquito- and rodent-proof, with the roof, gutters, cistern pipes, pump and piping maintained by you. No statute lets a lease waive that. What a lease may do is say who pays for trucked water when the cistern runs low in a dry spell, since retail water deliveries are outside public-utility regulation; state it plainly as a cost term, not as a waiver of your cistern and pump duties. Whether a lease may waive the common-law implied warranty of habitability rests on case law not searched for this library.

title: No presumption of repair breach
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute presumes that a landlord breached a repair or habitability duty, or took too long to repair, from a code citation, a government notice or the passage of time, and none sets a repair deadline running from a tenant's request. The only fixed periods are in public enforcement: after the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority serves written notice of a Housing Code violation, it orders repairs, vacating or demolition if no action is taken within 90 days; the building Commissioner allows 45 days to comply with a written Building Code order; and an owner may appeal a Housing Code order within 45 days, which stays it. Fines run only after conviction. In a private dispute the tenant must prove the breach under case law not searched for this library. Keep dated records of every repair request and of what you did.

title: Belongings Left Behind by a Tenant in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no statute on a tenant's belongings left behind. There is no notice-and-storage procedure, no waiting period, no safe-harbor sale, no rule that a unit is abandoned after unpaid rent or a utility shut-off, no required notice about what happens to left-behind property, and no special procedure for a mobile home on a rented lot.

What the law does say:
- (1) You may not take back the unit or remove a tenant's belongings while the tenant still has possession. Entry onto real property is allowed only where the law gives it, and then only peaceably, and entering someone's home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for it. Get possession back through a written surrender (keys returned) or a court judgment carried out by the marshal. A lease for more than one year can be surrendered only in writing or by operation of law.
- (2) Under a court rule, personal property the Marshal takes into custody by court order is stored by the Marshal's office, which charges the owner storage fees after notice, and the Court may dispose of uncollected property after at least 10 days' written notice (the rule is written for property whose ownership has been transferred, so how it applies to an evicted tenant's belongings is not settled); you do not handle property in the Marshal's custody.
- (3) Vehicles left on your property follow the abandoned-vehicle law (see the towing topic).
- (4) The Hotelkeepers law gives a hotel a lien on guests' baggage and a six-month auction procedure; it covers places renting three or more rooms for pay to transient or permanent guests, and whether it reaches a rooming house is unsettled, so take advice before relying on it.

Everything else is common law, which the Virgin Islands Supreme Court decides: throwing away or keeping items of value without notice risks a claim for their value.

Cautious course: once the tenant has surrendered or been removed, list and photograph what is left, discard only trash and perishables, store the rest safely, send written notice to the tenant's last known address and any forwarding or e-mail address describing the items and giving at least 15 days to collect them, and only then sell, donate or dispose of them. Keep any sale proceeds, less reasonable costs, for the tenant, and claim rent or damages separately (from the deposit, or in a civil or small-claims action).

Return identity papers, medicines and personal papers on request, and call animal control or the humane society for an animal left behind.

The optional `abandoned-property-procedure-vi` clause puts this procedure in the lease; the shared Surrender clause (`surrender-end-of-term`) already says left-behind property may be treated as abandoned only to the extent the law allows.

title: Early Move-Outs and Re-Renting in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute says what happens when a tenant moves out before the lease ends: none says the lease stays enforceable for the rest of the term, none requires you to try to re-rent, and none ends the lease if you do or don't.

What the law does say: every person in possession is liable for the rent, and you may sue for it; you keep your other remedies for rent; a lease for more than one year can be surrendered (given up) only in writing or by operation of law; a forcible entry and detainer case recovers possession only, so unpaid rent and other losses must be claimed in a separate civil action (or small claims up to $10,000), within the six-year limit for contract claims.

Whether you must try to re-rent (mitigate) and how a court measures your loss are common-law questions the Virgin Islands Supreme Court decides; courts elsewhere differ.

Cautious course: if a tenant leaves early, make reasonable, documented efforts to re-rent at a fair rent, credit any rent you receive from a new tenant against what the old tenant owes, and get any agreement to end the lease in writing.
