If you accept the keys and re-rent without a written agreement, a court may treat the lease as surrendered. The shared Default by Tenant clause (`default-by-tenant`) already promises reasonable efforts to mitigate where the law requires it, and the Early Termination clause (`early-termination-ks`) gives a fixed-term tenant a paid way out.

A domestic-violence victim who ends the lease under the statute owes nothing further and no fee.

title: Attorney's Fees in Virgin Islands Lease Disputes
bodyText: In the Virgin Islands, attorney's fees follow a general court statute rather than the lease. The amount a party pays its own lawyer is left to that party's agreement with the lawyer, but the court allows the prevailing party in a civil action a sum it fixes in its discretion as indemnity for attorney's fees. That rule works both ways: a tenant who wins can recover fees from you just as you can from the tenant, whatever the lease says. It does not apply to personal-injury cases, where fees may be awarded only if the claim or defense is frivolous. No Virgin Islands statute requires a lease fee clause to be mutual, caps a landlord's fees, limits the fees a lease may charge for an eviction, or bans a lease fee clause, and we found no statute on collection costs for leases. Points to know: (1) the court decides the amount, so a lease cannot guarantee full recovery; (2) a forcible entry and detainer case is a quick possession case and the statute puts the court fees and costs for those summary proceedings at $2.00, so do not expect a fee award there; claim fees with the rent and damages in a separate civil action (in small claims, neither side may have a lawyer, so fees are rarely an issue); (3) some statutes give tenants fees regardless of the lease: a successful civil-rights housing claim (mandatory fees), a claim under the plain-language contract law, and a rent-control overcharge claim. The shared Default by Tenant clause (`default-by-tenant`) contains a mutual prevailing-party fee sentence that matches the statute; do not add a one-sided fee clause.

title: Fire, Storm and Other Damage to a Rental in the Virgin Islands
Converting Rentals to Condominiums or Short-Term Use in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute regulates converting rental housing to condominiums, cooperatives, hotels or short-term rentals: there is no conversion notice, no lease statement about conversion, no tenant right to buy first, and no ban on converting or demolishing rental housing for transient use. The Condominium Act deals with creating and running condominiums, not with existing tenants. A conversion does not by itself end existing leases: a fixed-term lease runs to its end date, and a periodic tenancy must be ended with the written notice the law requires (see the termination topics). If the rent-control subchapter still applies (its status is unsettled), you can recover possession only on a listed ground; converting is not one, though recovering the unit in good faith for your own personal use, or to demolish it and build new with plans complete, are grounds, and a unit recovered for your own use may not be re-let to someone else without first offering it back to the evicted tenant in writing by registered mail. Converting to rentals shorter than 90 days brings the hotel room tax (see `hotel-room-tax-vi`) and a business license.

title: Criminal Activity by Tenants in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
Virgin Islands law has one landlord duty tied to a tenant's crime: if, after signing a lease, you discover that the building or unit has been turned to use for prostitution, pandering, lewdness or assignation, you must notify the Police Commissioner in writing, and you have the right and the responsibility to seek the tenant's eviction. If you do not notify the Police Commissioner, the law treats you as having knowingly leased for prostitution, a crime punishable by a fine of up to $100, up to 180 days in jail, or both.

Apart from that, no Virgin Islands statute sets a special rule for drug or other criminal activity by tenants: there is no fast-track eviction, no duty to evict for drugs, no right for police, prosecutors or tenant groups to bring the eviction, and no required lease wording. A criminal-activity clause (the library's optional `criminal-activity-ky`) is enforced like any other lease term: serve a written notice to quit and go to court.

If the rent-control subchapter applies (its status is unsettled), maintaining a nuisance, causing unreasonable damage, or repeatedly engaging in or permitting serious misconduct on the premises is one of the listed grounds for possession, with 30 days' written notice to quit. Never treat a tenant's call to the police for help in a domestic-violence situation, or the tenant's status as a victim, as a violation.

title: Drug Labs and Disorderly Houses on Rental Property in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
Two Virgin Islands crimes can reach an owner who lets a rental be used for illegal purposes.
- (1) Anyone who knowingly maintains or operates premises used to manufacture methamphetamine, LSD, PCP or a Schedule I or II narcotic drug (or an analog), or who knowingly aids, promotes, finances or otherwise takes part in maintaining or operating them, faces 10 to 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $500,000 or five times the street value of the drugs, whichever is greater.
- (2) Anyone who keeps, or has any interest in keeping, a house of ill-fame or assignation, a place for unlawful sexual or indecent purposes, or a disorderly house or place that disturbs the peace, comfort or decency of the neighbourhood faces a fine of up to $200, up to one year in jail, or both.

The drug-premises crime requires knowledge; the disorderly-house crime reaches anyone who has 'any interest in keeping' (14 V.I.C. § 1624) such a place, and whether owning the building is enough is not settled. Once you know, do not let it continue: report it to the police, serve a written notice to quit for the breach (at least 30 days under the cautious course), and file for possession. For prostitution use you also have a written-notice duty to the Police Commissioner.

title: Notice and Cure Before Eviction in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no statute giving a tenant a set time to fix (cure) a lease violation after notice, and no separate cure tracks for nonpayment and other breaches. The possession statutes instead set notices to quit:
- (1) Nonpayment: failing or refusing to pay rent due, or failing to give up possession for three days after you demand it, is unlawful holding; for a tenant at will (no fixed term), fourteen days' written notice to quit for nonpayment ends the tenancy.
- (2) Holding over at the end of the term, breaching a lease condition or covenant, or staying without a written lease: you may sue after a written notice to quit has been served at least three days before filing.
- (3) Ending a tenancy at will without a breach: three months' written notice, or notice equal to the rent interval when rent is paid more often (one month for month-to-month).

Notices of 14 days or less are counted in business days (weekends and legal holidays don't count). Where the old nonpayment statute applies, a tenant who pays the rent owed with interest and costs before judgment, and performs the other lease terms, keeps the lease. But the rent-control subchapter may still be in force (its status is unsettled), and if it is, it suspends the unlawful-holding section behind items (1) and (2) (including the three-day rules, but not the fourteen-day and periodic notices for a tenancy at will) and that pay-before-judgment rule, and instead requires one of four grounds (owner's personal use, demolition with plans complete, nuisance/damage/serious misconduct, or nonpayment) and 30 days' written notice to quit before filing.

Cautious course in every case: serve a written notice to quit at least 30 days before filing, state the ground, and accept full payment of arrears with costs before judgment if offered. The shared Default by Tenant clause (`default-by-tenant`) leaves cure periods to applicable law; you may give a longer cure period in the notice if you choose.

title: Leases After a Declared Disaster in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute ends a lease, or excuses rent, because a disaster has been declared or because the home cannot be reached. Two emergency rules do affect rent: during a Governor-declared state of emergency the Governor may freeze rents at the level in effect just before the proclamation, and it is a crime to rent or offer to rent essential goods or services (rents included) at an unconscionable price while the emergency lasts (see `edu-emergency-rent-pricing-vi`). The Governor may also suspend some health, safety and zoning rules for up to 60 days to provide temporary housing for disaster victims, and public-housing tenants displaced by a disaster get first preference to return. Whether rent is owed for a home that is damaged or cannot be reached is a common-law question we did not research; follow the cautious course in `edu-no-casualty-statute-vi` and the optional `casualty-termination-vi` clause. Check executive orders issued for the particular emergency, which this library did not search.

title: Drug-Free Housing Addendums in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires, authorizes or limits a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, and none lets a homeowners' association or a government require one. You may use the library's optional criminal-activity clause (`criminal-activity-ky`), which covers drug activity on the property and protects domestic-violence victims and calls for police help, as the law requires. Enforce it like any other lease term: written notice to quit, then court. Federal rules require drug-related criminal-activity terms in public-housing and many federally assisted leases; follow the program's own lease addendum if your unit is in one. A registered medical-cannabis patient may not be refused a lease or penalized solely for that status unless federal law or a federal benefit would be lost, so do not write an addendum that treats lawful patient status as drug activity.

title: Domestic Violence and Eviction in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: Virgin Islands law protects tenants who are victims of domestic violence in four ways. (1) No residential lease may let you end the lease or impose a penalty because a tenant called the police or other emergency help in a domestic-violence or domestic-abuse situation, and the tenant cannot waive the right to call. (2) Nothing in the domestic-violence law lets you end a tenancy or evict a tenant solely because the tenant is a victim. (3) You may still end the tenancy of a victim through the ordinary possession process for conduct unrelated to the domestic violence, and you may seek possession against the person who committed the violence or abuse that damaged the premises or broke the lease. (4) A court protecting a victim may give the victim possession of a jointly owned or leased home and exclude the abuser, without changing either party's interest in the home. Practical points: do not count police calls, protective-order incidents or damage caused by the abuser against the victim; if a court order excludes a household member, honor it and do not hand that person keys (see `edu-no-dv-lock-change-vi`); serve any notice to quit for the abuser's own conduct on the abuser. The victim's right to end the lease is in `edu-dv-lease-termination-vi`, and the deposit rule is in `edu-dv-deposit-timing-vi`.

title: Domestic-Violence Lease Release in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: A residential tenant who is a victim of domestic violence or domestic abuse may end the lease early. The tenant must give you at least 14 days' written notice stating the termination date, together with a police report written within the 90 days before the notice, and must be leaving out of fear of imminent danger to self or children. You must then release the tenant, who owes nothing further except as the statute provides: the tenant is not liable for damage to the unit after the release date and may not be charged any fee solely because the lease ended this way. The release covers only the victim: any other tenant on the lease stays bound by it, so the lease does not end for co-tenants. The person named in a court order as the perpetrator is treated as having interfered with the lease, whether or not that person signed it, and may be liable to you for your economic losses from the early termination, including unpaid rent, early-termination fees, repair costs and rent concessions the victim received. The statute does not define domestic violence or limit who the abuser must be (the abuser need not be a co-tenant); the territory's domestic-violence chapter defines it by a list of acts (including stalking) committed by a family or household member or intimate partner, which is a sensible guide. It gives no separate route for a tenant abused by the landlord, and no route for victims of stalking or sexual assault by someone outside those relationships, so treat such requests carefully and take advice. Deposit: see `edu-dv-deposit-timing-vi`. Count the 14 days generously: if the notice gives at least 14 calendar days, honor it.

title: Proof Needed for a Domestic-Violence Release in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: For a domestic-violence lease release, the Virgin Islands statute names one form of evidence: a police report written within the 90 days before the tenant's written notice. It does not list protective orders, court records, or statements from a doctor, counselor or victim advocate as substitutes, and it sets no form for the notice beyond being in writing, giving at least 14 days and stating the termination date. You may accept other reliable proof (such as a protective order) if you choose, but do not demand more than the police report the statute names, and keep the documents confidential and share them only with people who need them. If a tenant gives notice without a qualifying police report, tell the tenant in writing what the statute requires rather than simply refusing.

title: Leases and Condemnation in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute says whether a tenant's rent ends or shrinks when the government takes the property by eminent domain, or lets the condemnation court cancel a lease. Condemnation cases follow the territory's eminent-domain chapter and the civil rule for condemning property, which require the government to name owners of interests in the property; how a tenant's leasehold shares in the compensation, and whether rent continues, are otherwise left to the courts and the lease.

Because the law is silent, decide it in the lease: the optional `eminent-domain-vi` clause ends or adjusts the lease on a taking and says who receives the award, while leaving the tenant any separate payment for moving costs or personal property.

title: Who Can Appear in Court for a Landlord Company in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: In the Small Claims Division of the Superior Court (claims up to $10,000), neither side may be represented by a lawyer and parties must appear in person, except that a corporation, association or partnership may appear through a personal representative, so an employee or officer can present a company landlord's small-claims case for unpaid rent or damages. Outside small claims, appearing in court as the representative of another person, firm or corporation is the practice of law, which only members of the Virgin Islands Bar may do unless a law or Supreme Court rule provides otherwise, and we found no such exception for forcible entry and detainer (eviction) cases. Cautious course: an individual landlord may file for himself or herself, but an entity landlord should file and appear in an eviction case through a Virgin Islands attorney, and a property manager who is not a lawyer should not sign or argue court papers for the owner.

title: Environmental Hazards and Ending a Lease in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets a landlord (or tenant) end a residential lease because of an environmental event such as mold, contamination, a chemical spill, sewage overflow or a similar hazard, and none sets an opt-in termination right for one. If a hazard makes the home unfit, the Housing Code still applies: you must keep the dwelling fit to live in, and the Housing Finance Authority (or Public Works, for dwellings unfit for human habitation) can order repairs or order the unit vacated. If you want the right to end the lease when a hazard makes the home unusable, use the optional `casualty-termination-vi` clause, which covers damage from any casualty you did not cause; otherwise follow the cautious course in `edu-no-casualty-statute-vi`.

title: Delays and Hardship Stays in Virgin Islands Evictions
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no general hardship stay of evictions, no seasonal or holiday moratorium, and no stay tied to a rental-assistance application. The delays that do exist: (1) If the rent-control subchapter applies (its status is unsettled) and you recovered the unit because you need it for your own use or to demolish and rebuild, the court must, on the tenant's application, stay the eviction order for up to six months at a time if the tenant has tried and failed to find another home or would suffer extreme hardship, and applies in good faith; the tenant must deposit in court, or pay you, the reasonable rent for the stay plus any rent already owed. This stay does not apply to evictions for nonpayment or for the tenant's misconduct. (2) In a forcible entry and detainer case, a continuance can be no longer than two days unless the tenant gives a secured undertaking to pay the rent that accrues and costs if you win. (3) To appeal a possession judgment, the tenant must also give an undertaking with two sureties to pay twice the rental value from judgment until the appeal ends. (4) Landlord-tenant cases are heard on the return day unless the court adjourns them. Federal law adds its own delays in some cases (bankruptcy, servicemembers, and the CARES Act notice).

title: How an Eviction Works in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: In the Virgin Islands you recover possession through a forcible entry and detainer (FED) case, a fast possession-only case heard by the Magistrate Division of the Superior Court. Steps: (1) Notice to quit: serve a written notice to quit by handing it to the tenant, or leaving it at the premises if the tenant is absent (e-mail alone is not enough). The statutory periods are three days for holdover or a lease breach, fourteen days for nonpayment by a tenant at will, and three months or the rent interval to end a tenancy at will; because the rent-control subchapter may still apply (status unsettled), the cautious course is at least 30 days' written notice and a listed ground (see `edu-for-cause-eviction-vi`). You cannot sue for possession before the end of any period for which the tenant paid rent in advance. (2) Complaint: describe the premises, state that the tenant is in possession and unlawfully holds it, and that you are entitled to possession; the court's form also asks which lease condition was broken and when and how the notice to quit was served. (3) Summons: it must be served and returned within 3 days, and the tenant must appear within 3 days after service; if the tenant does not appear, judgment is entered by default. Landlord-tenant cases are heard on the return day unless adjourned. (4) Hearing: the case cannot be joined with any other claim and the tenant cannot counterclaim, but may raise any defense; the court does not decide who owns the property. A continuance is limited to two days unless the tenant gives security for the rent that accrues and costs. (5) No money: the FED judgment gives possession only; rent, late fees and damages must be claimed in a separate civil action or in small claims (up to $10,000), and the court cannot hand you rent paid into court in the FED. Court fees and costs in the summary proceeding are $2.00. (6) Judgment and removal: the marshal executes the judgment and removes the tenant; the clerk issues a writ of execution or assistance on a judgment for possession. Never change the locks, remove belongings or cut utilities yourself: entry must be peaceable and as the law allows, and entering a tenant's home without consent is a crime. (7) Appeal: a tenant who appeals must give an undertaking for twice the rental value until the appeal ends. Short periods (14 days or less) are counted in business days. No Virgin Islands statute adds a pay-into-court or escrow rule, a wage-attachment limit specific to leases, a federal-shutdown continuance, or a ban on recording service; collecting a money judgment follows the general execution and garnishment chapters, and a wage garnishment for a rent or damages judgment may take only 10% of the tenant's gross weekly wages above $30.

title: Sealing Eviction Records in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute or court rule seals, expunges or removes eviction records as such: dismissed cases are not automatically expunged, records are not removed after a set number of years, and no rule gives a landlord a right to object to sealing. The court rules let the court seal the record of any case it deems sensitive (a case-number cross-reference stays available to the public), so a tenant may ask, and you may oppose, in a particular case. If you screen applicants, remember that the territory's expungement law treats a person whose criminal record was expunged as not having been arrested, and federal consumer-reporting law limits how old eviction and other records may be reported by screening companies.

title: Who Receives Eviction Papers in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets a lease name a person to accept a notice to quit or the court summons for the tenant, and there is no address-confidentiality program that changes where papers for a protected person are served. The notice to quit must be delivered to the tenant (or the person in possession) or left at the premises if the tenant is absent, and the summons is served under the court's rules and must be served and returned within 3 days of filing. Do not rely on a lease clause naming an agent for service; serve each adult tenant and occupant in possession directly.

title: No Fast-Track Eviction for Crime in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no expedited eviction for drug or violent crime: no shorter notice, no bar on a cure, and no right for police, prosecutors or tenant groups to bring the case. The ordinary forcible entry and detainer case is already fast (the tenant must appear within 3 days after service), so use it: serve a written notice to quit for the breach (at least 30 days under the cautious course) and file. If the rent-control subchapter applies, maintaining a nuisance, causing unreasonable damage or repeatedly engaging in or permitting serious misconduct on the premises is a listed ground. If you discover the unit is being used for prostitution, you must notify the Police Commissioner in writing and seek the tenant's eviction (see `edu-criminal-activity-vi`). Never base the case on a tenant's call for police help in a domestic-violence situation.

title: Do You Need a Reason to Evict in the Virgin Islands?
bodyText: Whether a Virgin Islands landlord needs a reason (cause) to recover a rental is unsettled, so follow the cautious course. The Code still prints a 1947 rent-control subchapter that stays in force until the Legislature declares the housing emergency over, and we found no such declaration. While it is in force, no action to recover possession of rented premises may be brought except on one of four grounds: (1) you seek the unit in good faith for your own personal use; (2) you want in good faith to demolish it and build a new building, with plans completed and ready to build; (3) the tenant maintains a nuisance, causes or permits unreasonable damage, or repeatedly engages in or permits serious misconduct on the premises; or (4) the tenant fails to pay rent due (and for nonpayment you must show the rent is no more than the tenant owed for the month before the default). You must also serve a written notice to quit at least 30 days before filing, and after recovering a unit for your own use or demolition the court may stay the eviction up to six months and you must offer the unit back before re-letting it. The subchapter covers housing and business rentals but not hotels or transient lodging houses. In 2024 the Virgin Islands Supreme Court applied the ordinary three-day notice-to-quit statute without addressing the rule that suspends it while rent control is in force, which suggests courts may treat the subchapter as dormant. If it is not in force, there is no just-cause rule: a fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term, and a tenant who holds over after a written notice to quit (served at least three days before filing) may be evicted; a tenancy at will ends on three months' written notice, or notice equal to the rent interval (one month for month-to-month), without any reason. No Virgin Islands statute adds a good-cause rule for particular groups (older or disabled tenants, mobile-home lots, long tenancies), lets a fixed term end only with special lease options, or protects tenants after a first year. Cautious course for every eviction: state one of the four grounds, give at least 30 days' written notice to quit, and never end a tenancy in retaliation or for a discriminatory reason. Federally assisted housing (vouchers, public housing, tax-credit units) has its own good-cause rules. See `edu-rent-control-vi`.

title: Tenants When a Rental Is Foreclosed in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute protects residential tenants when the landlord's property is foreclosed: none requires you to disclose a pending foreclosure, makes a lease survive the sale, or sets a notice period for the buyer. Federal law does: under the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, after a foreclosure of a federally related mortgage loan on residential property, the new owner takes subject to a bona fide lease until the end of its term (except that a buyer who will live in the unit may end it on 90 days' notice) and must give a bona fide tenant without a lease, or with a month-to-month tenancy, at least 90 days' notice to vacate. A buyer who wants possession must still use the Virgin Islands notice-to-quit and court process. Tell tenants promptly about a foreclosure that may affect them, and direct rent as the court or the new owner instructs once the sale is complete.

title: Tenants After a Court Sale of the Property in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: When Virgin Islands real property is sold under a court judgment (an execution sale, which is also how a mortgage foreclosure judgment is enforced), the buyer, and anyone who later redeems the property, is entitled to possession from the sale (or redemption) until a resale or redemption, unless a tenant holds the property under an unexpired lease. In that case the lease is not cut off by this rule; instead the buyer or redeemer is entitled to collect the rent, or the value of the use and occupation, from the tenant for that period. If your rental is sold this way, tell the tenant in writing whom to pay from the sale date, and expect the tenant to pay the buyer. How long the lease survives a foreclosure that wipes out later interests is a common-law question we did not research; federal law separately protects bona fide tenants after a foreclosure (see `edu-foreclosure-tenants-vi`).

title: Paying Up to Keep the Lease in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: A Virgin Islands statute lets a tenant sued for possession for nonpayment keep the lease by paying before judgment: if, at any time before judgment, the tenant (or a successor) pays you or brings into court the rent then in arrears, with interest and the costs of the action, and performs the other lease terms, the tenant may stay in possession under the lease. The statute is printed as suspended while the rent-control subchapter is in force, and that subchapter's status is unsettled; the cautious course is to accept a full tender of arrears, interest and costs made before judgment and dismiss the nonpayment case. There is no statutory right to reinstate a lease after a possession judgment, and no relief-from-forfeiture procedure like some states'. Two related rules: the court may forfeit a tenant's lease for waste only if the injury equals the value of the unexpired term or was done in malice, and a notice to quit does not allow a possession case before the end of a period for which rent was paid in advance. If your property is sold for unpaid real property taxes, a tenant may redeem it within one year and deduct the redemption money from the rent.

title: Lease Guarantors in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute deals specifically with guarantors of residential leases: none limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a maximum amount or end date, or limits what a guarantor may be asked to deposit. The general statute of frauds applies: a promise to answer for another person's debt or default is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor (or an agent with written authority).

Whether a guaranty covers renewals, extensions or a month-to-month holdover depends on its wording; under general suretyship principles a guarantor may be released by changes made without the guarantor's consent. Get the guaranty in writing and signed, and if it is to cover renewals, say so expressly and have the guarantor consent in advance; the optional `guaranty-vi` clause does this.

title: Tenants Who Stay Past the Lease in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no holdover-damages statute: no double rent, no multiple of rent, and no statutory per-day figure for a tenant who stays after the lease ends.

What the law does provide: a tenant who stays after the end of the term, after a written notice to quit, is unlawfully holding and can be removed in a forcible entry and detainer case once the notice has been served at least three days before filing (30 days under the cautious course while the rent-control subchapter's status is unsettled); a tenancy at will or by sufferance ends on three months' written notice, or notice equal to the rent interval.

Your loss for the extra days (normally the fair rental value, plus any other actual damage) is claimed in a separate civil action or small claims, not in the possession case. The only 'twice the rental value' figure in the statutes is the undertaking a tenant must give to appeal a possession judgment; it is not a holdover charge. The shared Holdover clause (`holdover-ca`) lets you recover actual damages, including the reasonable rental value, or accept rent and continue month to month; an optional agreed daily charge is in `holdover-rate-vi`.

If you accept rent for a period after the lease ends, expect a court to treat the tenancy as continuing month to month.

title: Waiving Exemptions From Collection in a Virgin Islands Lease
bodyText: Virgin Islands law protects some property from sale to pay a judgment. The homestead exemption covers a family's owned home (up to $300,000 in value and limited acreage), so it rarely matters for a renter. More relevant to tenants: necessary clothing, the tools or library a person needs to earn a living, and, for the head of a family, household goods, furniture and utensils in use up to $3,000 in value are exempt from execution if the debtor selects and reserves them at or after the levy and before sale. The exemptions do not protect an item from a judgment for its own price. No Virgin Islands statute lets a tenant waive these exemptions in a lease or sets words for a waiver, and the only statute we found on waiving an execution exemption forbids it (for workers' compensation benefits). Do not put a homestead or exemption waiver in a residential lease: its effect is doubtful, it would have to be highlighted on the lease's plain-language front page as a term that reduces the tenant's rights, and it may be challenged as deceptive or unconscionable. Collect a rent or damages judgment through the court's ordinary execution and garnishment process, which respects these exemptions.

title: Ending a Lease for Illness, Disability or Age in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets a tenant end a lease early because of illness, disability, age or a move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care, and none addresses ending a lease when a tenant dies. The only statutory early exit for tenants is the domestic-violence release (see `edu-dv-lease-termination-vi`), and federal law gives servicemembers their own right. A tenant with a disability may, however, ask for a reasonable accommodation, and federal fair-housing law can require you to let a tenant out of a lease (or reduce the early-termination charge) where that is reasonable because of the disability; Virgin Islands law also bars disability discrimination in rental terms. Treat such requests individually, in writing, and take advice before refusing. The optional Early Termination clause (`early-termination-ks`) gives every fixed-term tenant a paid way out.

title: No Landlord's Lien on a Tenant's Belongings in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands gives an ordinary residential landlord no lien on a tenant's furniture or other belongings for unpaid rent, and no court-issued distress for rent; the territory's personal-property liens cover people who repair, store or carry goods at the owner's request, not landlords. The Hotelkeepers law gives a hotel (a place renting three or more rooms for pay to transient or permanent guests, whose guests include tenants) a lien on guests' baggage and valuables with a six-month public-auction procedure; whether a rooming house fits that definition is unsettled. Some Virgin Islands commercial leases create a contractual lien on the tenant's property, enforceable by self-help, repossession or distress. The library does not offer such a clause for homes, and you should not use one: you may not enter a tenant's home or take belongings without the tenant's consent or a court order (entry must be peaceable and as the law allows, and entering a tenant's home without consent is a crime); a security interest in household goods would have to meet the territory's commercial-code rules; exemption laws protect some property from collection; and a lien term would have to be highlighted on the lease's plain-language front page and could be attacked as deceptive or unconscionable. A landlord who still wants one should take legal advice and add its own clause. Collect unpaid rent from the security deposit or through a civil or small-claims judgment.

title: Landlord's Remedies When a Tenant Defaults in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: When a Virgin Islands tenant breaks the lease, your remedies are possession and money, and you pursue them through the courts. (1) Possession: you recover the home only by a court judgment, normally in a forcible entry and detainer (eviction) case after a written notice to quit (see `edu-eviction-process-vi` and `edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-vi`); never by changing the locks, removing belongings or cutting off utilities. (2) Money: the eviction judgment gives possession only. Unpaid rent, late fees and damages must be claimed in a separate civil action, where either side may ask for a jury, or in small claims up to $10,000. The law makes the person in possession liable for the rent, lets you sue for it using the lease as evidence, and keeps any other remedy your lease or the law gives you. A general action to recover possession of real property, brought as an ordinary civil action, may combine possession with damages for withholding it, limited to the three years before suit. (3) You may sue for rent that is already due without ending the lease. No Virgin Islands statute deals with rent acceleration (making all future rent due at once), with a claim for rent not yet due, or with how your loss is measured after the lease ends; those are common-law questions the Virgin Islands Supreme Court decides, and we did not search case law. The library offers no acceleration clause, because a demand for all future rent sits badly with a likely duty to credit what you earn by re-renting. Cautious course: claim rent as it falls due, or after the tenancy ends claim your actual lost rent less what you receive from re-renting, make reasonable documented efforts to re-rent (see `edu-no-mitigation-statute-vi`), and ask the court for attorney's fees under the general fee statute (see `edu-attorney-fees-vi`). A tenant who commits waste can owe treble damages (see `edu-tenant-caused-damage-vi`). A domestic-violence victim who ends the lease under the statute owes nothing further (see `edu-dv-lease-termination-vi`).

title: No Statutory Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach and Bill It in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute lets a landlord fix a tenant's breach (cleaning, repairs the tenant must make, garbage, damage) and bill the cost as rent or as an extra charge. A right to do so comes only from the lease. Two statutes limit how you use it. First, you may enter the home only where the law allows, and then only peacefully, and entering a tenant's home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for it; your entry rights therefore come from the tenant's consent in the lease (`landlords-access`) or at the time, and you may never force entry.

Second, the Housing Code makes the owner, not the tenant, responsible for the building's plumbing, roof, wiring, structure and shared areas; the tenant must keep its own part clean, safe and sanitary, dispose of garbage properly and use plumbing fixtures with reasonable care, so a self-cure right should reach only duties the tenant actually has. Do not label repair costs as rent: if the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), a nonpayment eviction requires proof that the rent claimed is no more than the tenant owed for the month before the default, and extra charges added as rent could defeat the case.

Collect unpaid costs in a separate civil action or small claims, not in the eviction case.

The optional clause `landlord-self-cure-vi` gives you a self-cure right on written notice, without forced entry, billing actual and reasonable costs as a separate charge.

title: Agreed Damages for a Tenant’s Breach in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute permits, sets or caps an agreed (liquidated) damages amount for a residential tenant's breach, and no rule like some states' consumer regulations expressly allows a landlord to keep one. The Code's liquidated-damages provisions cover sales and leases of goods, construction contracts, government contracts and a consumer's down payment on a rejected credit application, not residential leases. Whether an agreed amount (an early-termination fee, a lease-break charge, a forfeited deposit) is enforceable is a common-law question the Virgin Islands Supreme Court decides; courts generally enforce an amount that is a reasonable estimate of the landlord's likely loss and refuse one that works as a penalty.

Two statutes limit agreed amounts: a tenant who ends the lease under the domestic-violence law owes no fee solely because of the termination, and the Consumer Protection Law forbids deceptive or unconscionable practices in consumer leases, so describe any fee accurately.

Cautious course: use only the library's fixed-term buyout (`early-termination-ks`), set any amount at a reasonable estimate of your actual loss (for example one or two months' rent), never call the security deposit a penalty, and do not apply any fee to a domestic-violence release.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets a residential landlord lock a tenant out, change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or cut off utilities because rent is late, and a lease clause cannot create that right. The law says no one may enter land or a building except where the law gives the right, and then only peacefully; entering a tenant's home without the tenant's consent, or using force to enter or hold property, is a crime (a fine of up to $200 or up to a year in jail) unless the law provides for it. A tenant who is forced out may bring its own forcible entry and detainer case to get back in. The only lawful way to remove a tenant for unpaid rent is a written notice to quit followed by a court judgment carried out by the Marshal (see `edu-nonpayment-notice-vi` and `edu-eviction-process-vi`). The library offers no lockout clause, and a lease term that claims one would also have to be listed on the plain-language front page as a provision designed for your protection. See `edu-self-help-eviction-vi`.

title: Minors as Tenants and in Eviction Cases in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: In the Virgin Islands a person reaches majority at 18. No statute deals specifically with leases signed by minors or bars naming a minor in an eviction case. Under the general common law (which the Virgin Islands Supreme Court decides. The Code lets a minor be emancipated by parental consent or by court order, but an emancipated minor may still be limited: under one emancipation section, until 18 the minor cannot take on an obligation larger than one year of the minor's income. Ask for the emancipation document and check that the lease's total rent fits within that limit. If a minor is sued, the court rules provide for a guardian ad litem, and the Code has a special rule for serving papers on a minor. Age is also a protected class in Virgin Islands housing law, so never refuse an adult (18 or older) because of age. Cautious course: sign leases only with adults or documented emancipated minors; if a minor must be a tenant, have a parent or guardian sign as co-tenant or guarantor; list minor household members as occupants, not tenants; and in an eviction name the adult tenants (the judgment for possession covers everyone who holds under them).

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
Before suing to evict for unpaid rent in the Virgin Islands you need a written notice to quit. The statutes:
- (1) a tenant who fails or refuses to pay rent due, or to give up possession for three days after you demand it, is unlawfully holding;
- (2) a tenant at will (no fixed term) who neglects or refuses to pay rent can be ended by fourteen days' written notice to quit;
- (3) where the old nonpayment statute applies, suing for possession for nonpayment counts as a demand for the rent, and a tenant who pays the arrears with interest and costs before judgment, and keeps the other lease terms, keeps the lease.

But the rent-control subchapter may still be in force (its status is unsettled), and if it is, it requires a written notice to quit served at least 30 days before you file, and you must prove the rent claimed is no more than the tenant owed for the month before the default. No statute prescribes the notice's wording, a state form, a move-in acknowledgment, a limit on how often a tenant may cure by paying, extra days for mailing, or a waiver of the notice in the lease.

How to serve: hand the written notice to the tenant, or leave it at the home if the tenant is absent; e-mail or text alone is not enough. Periods of 14 days or less are counted in business days; 30 days counts every day. You cannot sue for possession before the end of any period for which rent was paid in advance.

Cautious course: serve a written notice to quit at least 30 days before filing, stating the amount due, the months it covers, that the tenancy will end and you will file for possession if the tenant does not pay or leave, and how to pay; keep a signed record of delivery; accept full payment of arrears, interest and costs offered before judgment. Unpaid rent itself is collected in a separate civil action or small claims. For federally backed properties the federal CARES Act 30-day notice also applies.

title: Charging for Notices in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets a landlord charge a tenant for preparing or serving a notice (a late notice, a notice to quit, a lease-violation notice), and none bans such a charge. A fee comes only from the lease, and the territory has no closed list of permitted fees. In court, the costs of an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) case are fixed by statute at a total of $2.00, and in other civil actions the court may award costs such as officers' fees, publication of notices and postage for mailed service, plus a discretionary sum toward attorney's fees, whatever the lease says. Because the Consumer Protection Law forbids deceptive or unconscionable practices, any charge must be stated in the lease and match its description. Cautious course: the library offers no notice fee; recover the cost of serving court papers as court costs, and if you charge anything for notices, list it in the lease's fee schedule (`fees-and-charges-vi`) at a reasonable amount tied to your actual cost, and never charge for a notice the law requires you to give before you may sue.

title: Waiving or Shortening the Notice to Quit in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says a lease may waive or shorten the notice to quit, and none expressly forbids it either. The statutes, however, make the notice a condition of the court case: an action for holding over or breach may be brought when the notice to quit has been served for 3 days before filing, and, if the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), written notice to quit must have been served 30 days before any action for possession. The court's eviction complaint form asks when and how the notice was served. A court is unlikely to treat a lease waiver as a substitute for a statutory precondition; whether it would is a common-law question the Virgin Islands Supreme Court decides. The domestic-violence statute separately says a tenant may not waive the right to call for police or emergency help. The library never waives or shortens a notice to quit, and you should not add a waiver: serve a written notice to quit in every case, at least 30 days before filing under the cautious course (see `edu-nonpayment-notice-vi` and `edu-termination-notice-vi`).

title: Seasonal and Short-Stay Rentals in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no special rules for seasonal residential tenancies. A lease for a season is an ordinary lease with an agreed term: state exact start and end dates, because a fixed term ends on its last day, while a rental with no fixed term is a tenancy at will that needs written notice to end (see `edu-tenancy-at-will-vi`). If the occupant stays past the season, you still need a written notice to quit and a court order to remove them. Shorter stays bring other rules: (1) a renter of an apartment, condominium or residence for less than 90 days is a hotel guest for the hotel room tax, which you collect and show separately (`hotel-room-tax-vi`); (2) the rent-control subchapter does not apply to hotels or transient lodging houses; (3) the Hotelkeepers chapter, with its own guest-eviction and lien rules, covers a place held out to the public as furnishing sleeping accommodations for pay in three or more rooms, and whether it reaches a villa or guest house is unsettled, so take advice before relying on it; (4) a territorial business license may be needed: the license fee list includes apartment houses, cottage rentals, rooming houses and hotels and guest houses (see `edu-landlord-registration-vi`). Farming and agricultural leases, which are often seasonal, need six months' notice to quit, and the farm tenant keeps access to harvest crops planted before the notice.

title: Self-Help Evictions Are Unlawful in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: In the Virgin Islands you may not evict a residential tenant yourself. No one may enter land or a building except where the law gives the right, and then only peacefully, never by force. Entering a tenant's home without the tenant's consent, or using force to enter or to hold property, is a crime (a fine of up to $200 or up to a year in jail) unless the law provides for it. So changing or plugging the locks, removing doors, windows or belongings, cutting off water or electricity, or keeping the tenant out is unlawful. A tenant who is forced out may bring a forcible entry and detainer case against you to be restored to possession, and may sue for damages in a separate civil action. No statute sets a fixed money penalty for an ouster or a separate violation for a utility shut-off, and the public-utility shut-off rules bind the utilities, not landlords (see `edu-utility-shutoff-rules-vi`). The lawful route is a written notice to quit, a court judgment and removal by the Marshal (`edu-eviction-process-vi`). A narrow exception applies to hotels: a hotelkeeper may evict a guest who breaks the rules or overstays, after notice, and the police must help remove a person illegally on hotel property; it covers places held out to the public as furnishing rooms for pay (three or more rooms), not ordinary residential leases.

title: Servicemembers’ Lease and Eviction Rights in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: Servicemember protections in the Virgin Islands come from the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA), which applies in the territory. The Virgin Islands has no law of its own adding to it: no territorial lease-termination right, no shorter notice for military tenants, no rule on deciding servicemember applications, and no extension of the federal protections to National Guard members on territorial active duty (the National Guard provisions found cover pay, leave and insurance). Federal rules to follow: (1) a servicemember who enters military service, or receives orders for a permanent change of station or a deployment of 90 days or more, may end a residential lease by written notice with a copy of the orders; for a lease with monthly rent, the termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date, and you must refund rent paid in advance and the deposit (less lawful charges) and may not charge an early-termination fee; (2) a court must stay an eviction of a servicemember or dependents, on request, where military service materially affects the ability to pay and the rent is under the federal ceiling (adjusted each year); (3) before a default judgment in any case, including an eviction where the tenant does not appear, you must file an affidavit stating whether the defendant is in military service. The library's Early Termination clause (`early-termination-ks`) keeps these rights.

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments and Eviction in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a continuance, gives a defense or reinstates a tenancy when rent is late because a Social Security check, public-assistance payment, housing voucher or other government benefit was delayed. The ordinary rules apply: a written notice to quit before suing, the 30-day notice and listed grounds if the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), a continuance of no more than two days unless the tenant gives security for accruing rent and costs, and, where that statute applies, the tenant's right to keep the lease by paying the arrears, interest and costs before judgment. Utility customers (not tenants) have a statutory protection when an energy-assistance program pays late, but it binds the utilities, not landlords. FEDERAL: the federal programs have their own rules (for example, a public-housing or voucher landlord may not hold the tenant responsible for the housing authority's share). Cautious course: when you know a tenant's rent depends on a delayed benefit, give time before serving a notice to quit, and accept full payment of arrears before judgment.

title: When a Tenant May End a Lease Early Under Virgin Islands Law
bodyText:
A Virgin Islands tenant has few statutory ways to end a fixed-term lease early.
- (1) Domestic violence: a tenant who gives at least 14 days' written notice with a police report written within the 90 days before the notice, and seeks to leave out of fear of imminent danger to self or children, must be released; the tenant owes no fee for ending the lease and is not liable for damage after the release date, other tenants stay bound, and a perpetrator named in a court order is liable to you for your losses.
- (2) Military service: FEDERAL law lets a servicemember end a lease on entering service or receiving qualifying orders.
- (3) A periodic or at-will tenant may always end the tenancy by the statutory notice.

No Virgin Islands statute lets a tenant end a lease because of the landlord's fraud or misrepresentation, a casualty, a move to a nursing home or care facility, a disability, age, a job transfer or the tenant's death, and none releases accrued rent because a lease left out a required statement. The plain-language law gives damages, not a right to end the lease, when a lease is not in plain language. Your own fixed-term buyout is in `early-termination-ks`.

title: The End of the Lease Term in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
A fixed-term Virgin Islands lease ends on its last day, and the shared clause `surrender-end-of-term` asks the tenant to leave then "unless applicable law entitles Tenant to remain". That qualifier matters here. If the rent-control subchapter is in force (its status is unsettled), no action to recover rented premises may be brought except on one of its four grounds (your good-faith personal use, demolition with plans complete, the tenant's nuisance, damage or serious misconduct, or nonpayment), so the end of the term alone may not let you recover the home, and you need 30 days' written notice to quit.

If the subchapter is not in force, a tenant who stays after the term may be evicted after a written notice to quit served at least 3 days before filing. Either way you cannot remove a tenant who stays without a court judgment, and accepting rent after the term may create a new periodic tenancy (`holdover-ca`). A lease for more than one year can be surrendered early only in writing or by operation of law, so get any early surrender signed.

Cautious course: give written notice before the term ends saying whether you will renew, and if you need the home back state a rent-control ground and serve the 30-day notice to quit.

title: Tenancies Without a Fixed Term in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands statute on tenancies without a fixed term speaks of estates "at will or by sufferance". Either party may end one by three months' written notice; when rent is payable at intervals of less than three months, notice equal to the interval between payments is enough, so a month-to-month tenancy ends on one month's written notice and a week-to-week tenancy on one week's. If a tenant at will neglects or refuses to pay rent, fourteen days' written notice to quit ends the tenancy. A lease for more than one year must be in writing and signed, or it is void; the Virgin Islands Supreme Court has treated an oral month-to-month tenancy as valid even when it continues past a year. A tenant who stays on with your consent after a lease ends is commonly treated as a periodic tenant. No statute separately defines month-to-month or week-to-week tenancies. Notices of 14 days or less are counted in business days. Because the rent-control subchapter may still apply (status unsettled), the cautious course is to give at least 30 days' written notice to quit and rely on one of its listed grounds before filing. Serve notices by hand or leave them at the home; e-mail alone is not enough. See `edu-termination-notice-vi`.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute deals with a tenant's bankruptcy; federal bankruptcy law governs, and the District Court of the Virgin Islands hears bankruptcy cases. FEDERAL rules to follow: (1) the automatic stay stops you from starting or continuing an eviction, collecting pre-filing rent or applying the deposit once the tenant files, unless the bankruptcy court lifts the stay or an exception applies; (2) one exception lets an eviction proceed when you obtained the judgment for possession before the filing (the tenant can delay this in limited cases by depositing rent and certifying a cure right under state law), and another applies to evictions based on endangering the property or illegal drug use, after a certification; (3) a lease clause that ends the lease because the tenant files for bankruptcy or becomes insolvent is generally unenforceable; (4) the bankruptcy trustee or debtor may assume or reject the lease, and rent that comes due after the filing must generally be paid. Cautious course: on notice of a filing, stop all collection and eviction steps and consult a lawyer about relief from the stay. The library offers no bankruptcy-default clause.

title: Damage Caused by a Tenant in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
Virgin Islands law gives a landlord several tools when a tenant damages the home.
- (1) Waste: a tenant for years who commits waste can be sued for treble damages, and the court may forfeit the lease and evict, but only if the injury equals the value of the rest of the term or was done in malice.
- (2) If the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), causing and permitting unreasonable damage is a ground for recovering possession.
- (3) The Housing Code makes each occupant keep its part of the dwelling clean, safe and sanitary and use plumbing fixtures with reasonable care.
- (4) Damage claims go in a separate civil action or small claims, not in the eviction case, and you may apply the security deposit as the lease allows (`security-deposit-use`).

Limits: a domestic-violence victim released from the lease is not liable for damage after the release date, and damage caused by the violence is chargeable to the perpetrator named in a court order, not to the victim's deposit. No Virgin Islands statute gives a tenant a casualty exit or rent reduction, so there is no statutory exception for tenant-caused damage to preserve, and no statute limits a tenant's liability to damage by the tenant and its guests.

The optional shared clause `tenant-caused-damage-nm` makes the tenant pay for damage it, its household or guests cause.

title: When a Tenant Dies in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute says what happens to a residential lease, the deposit or the tenant's belongings when a tenant dies. There is no rule ending the lease at a sole tenant's death, no affidavit procedure for a named contact, and no rule letting the lease name someone to remove property or receive the deposit. Under the general common law a lease does not end on the tenant's death; the tenant's rights and duties pass to the estate, which acts through a personal representative appointed in probate.

Other tenants on the lease remain bound. Entering the home without consent is a crime unless the law provides for it, so do not clear out the unit on your own.

Cautious course: contact the emergency contact named under the shared clause `tenant-death-contact-nh`, secure the unit, and deal with the personal representative (or, for a small estate, the family member handling it) to agree in writing on surrender, removal of belongings and the deposit; if no one comes forward, end a periodic tenancy by written notice to quit and recover possession through the court before disposing of anything, following `abandoned-property-procedure-vi`. A deposit refund no one claims may become unclaimed property.

title: Notice to End a Tenancy in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
Virgin Islands notice rules depend on the type of tenancy.
- (1) Periodic or at-will tenancy: either party may end it by three months' written notice, or by notice equal to the rent interval when rent is paid more often than every three months (one month for month-to-month, one week for week-to-week).
- (2) Fixed term: the lease ends on its last day without a statutory notice, but to evict a tenant who stays on you must serve a written notice to quit at least 3 days before filing (6 months for a farming lease).
- (3) Nonpayment by a tenant at will: fourteen days' written notice to quit.
- (4) Rent control: if the subchapter applies (status unsettled), every possession case needs 30 days' written notice to quit and one of four listed grounds, so the cautious course for any landlord notice is at least 30 days, stating the ground.

No statute says a lease may shorten these periods (do not try), sets a separate rule for tenant notices at the end of a term, requires a notice to mention extension rights, or requires a payment plan before a nonpayment eviction. Notices must be in writing and served by hand or left at the home; e-mail alone is not enough. Periods of 14 days or less are counted in business days, and the cautious practice is to make the termination date the last day of a rental period.

FEDERAL: for federally backed properties the CARES Act requires 30 days' notice to vacate for nonpayment.

The optional clause `periodic-tenancy-notice-vi` puts these rules in the lease.

title: Removing Unauthorized Occupants and Squatters in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no fast-track procedure for removing squatters or other unauthorized occupants outside the courts: no police or Marshal removal on your sworn complaint, no ex parte removal hearing, and no special squatting crime. What the law provides: (1) Entering the land of another without the consent of the owner or the person in charge is a misdemeanor (trespass), and using force to enter or hold property is a separate crime, so you may report a person who has just broken in to the police, who decide whether to act. (2) A person removed from land by legal process who returns to settle or take possession commits a crime. (3) Anyone who claims a right to stay (a former guest, a subtenant, a tenant's former partner, a caretaker) must be removed through a forcible entry and detainer case: serve a written notice to quit on everyone in possession, name them in the complaint, and have the Marshal carry out the judgment. A person in quiet possession for three years may plead that in bar of the eviction case, which leaves you an ordinary action to recover possession. (4) A guest the tenant still welcomes is there with the consent of the person in charge; treat an unauthorized long-term guest as the tenant's lease breach (`guest-policy`, `permitted-occupants`). Never change the locks or remove anyone yourself. Hotels have a separate rule letting the police remove a person illegally on hotel property; it does not reach ordinary residential rentals.

title: Accepting Rent After a Breach or Notice in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute says whether accepting rent after a tenant's breach, after a notice to quit or during an eviction case waives the breach or the notice. That is a common-law question the Virgin Islands Supreme Court decides; many courts treat accepting rent for a period after the notice's termination date as creating a new tenancy or waiving the notice, while accepting rent already owed with a clear reservation often does not.

Statutes nearby: where the old nonpayment statute applies, a tenant who pays the arrears with interest and costs before judgment keeps the lease; and if the rent-control subchapter applies, you can evict for nonpayment only if the rent claimed is no more than the tenant owed for the month before the default.

Cautious course: after serving a notice to quit for a breach other than nonpayment, do not accept rent for periods after the termination date unless you mean to continue the tenancy; if you accept any payment, give a written receipt stating it is accepted without waiving the notice or the case; and use the optional `rent-acceptance-nonwaiver-vi` clause, knowing a court may still find waiver from your conduct.

title: Nuisance and Rental Property in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: Virgin Islands nuisance law reaches rental property in four ways. (1) Private nuisance: anyone whose property or its enjoyment is affected by a private nuisance may sue for damages and, after judgment, have the Marshal abate the nuisance at the defendant's expense, or get an injunction; the defendant may ask for up to 60 days to abate it personally on giving security. A neighbor could sue you or your tenant; you can sue a tenant or neighbor. (2) Public nuisance: anything injurious to health, indecent, offensive or obstructing the use of property so as to interfere with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property by a considerable number of persons is a public nuisance, and maintaining one, or willfully failing to perform a legal duty to remove one, is a crime. (3) Prostitution: an owner who learns after signing a lease that the building has been converted to prostitution must notify the Police Commissioner in writing and has the right and responsibility to seek the tenant's eviction; an owner who does not notify is treated as knowingly leasing for prostitution. Keeping, or having any interest in keeping, a disorderly house or any place of public resort that disturbs the peace, comfort or decency of a neighborhood is also a crime (see `edu-drug-premises-crimes-vi`). (4) Eviction ground: if the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), a tenant who maintains a nuisance, causes unreasonable damage or repeatedly engages in or permits serious misconduct may be evicted on that ground. The Virgin Islands has no nuisance receivership taking the rents, no statute closing or padlocking a building, no neighbor suit to close a building, no drug-nuisance rent escrow, no rule making you a necessary defendant when a third party's conduct is the nuisance, and no requirement that the lease summarize a criminal statute. Cautious course: act promptly on complaints, use the lease's no-disturbance and criminal-activity terms (`no-disturbance`, `criminal-activity-ky`), serve a written notice to quit and go to court; never treat a tenant's calls for police or emergency help in a domestic-violence situation as a nuisance.

title: Taking Back a Rental for Your Own Use in the Virgin Islands
No Possession Bond or Confessed Judgment for Possession in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no statute letting a landlord take a bond or confessed judgment from a tenant at the start of a lease to secure surrender of possession at the end of the term. The bonds the law does know arise in a pending eviction case: a continuance beyond two days requires the tenant to give security for the rent that accrues and costs, and a tenant who appeals a possession judgment must give an undertaking for twice the rental value. The general Code allows a confession of judgment only for money (due, to become due, or to secure a contingent liability), and only by a sworn, acknowledged statement of the facts showing the sum is justly owed, filed with the court; it does not provide for a judgment for possession. Several consumer statutes ban confessions of judgment outright. The library offers no possession bond or confession-of-judgment clause: recover possession by notice to quit and a court case, and secure money with the security deposit and, if you wish, a guaranty (`guaranty-vi`).

title: Belongings and Animals After an Eviction in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: After you win a possession judgment, the clerk issues a writ and the Virgin Islands Marshal carries it out: the statutory form commands the Marshal to remove the tenant from the premises and to levy on the tenant's goods for the costs. When the Marshal takes personal property into custody under a court order, the court's storage rule may apply (it is written for property whose ownership has been transferred, so its reach to an evicted tenant's belongings is not settled): starting five days after written notice to the owner, the owner is charged $10 a day for 30 days and then $25 a day for 15 days, and property not collected may be disposed of by the court after at least 10 days' written notice. No Virgin Islands statute sets your own duties for belongings left behind after the writ (storage, inventory, notice, sale), protects you from liability for executing the writ, gives a warehouse option, or deals with pets left in the unit. A person removed from land by legal process who unlawfully returns to settle, live on or take possession of it commits a crime (fine up to $200 or up to a year in jail): call the police rather than removing the person yourself. Animals: abandoning an animal without providing for its care is a crime by the owner, and peace officers, animal wardens and designated humane-society agents may take possession of a neglected animal; call them or the animal shelter rather than disposing of an animal. For other belongings follow `abandoned-property-procedure-vi` (store, give written notice, allow collection) and see `edu-no-abandoned-property-statute-vi`. Coordinate the date with the Marshal and be present, keep an inventory and photographs, and never remove property before the Marshal executes the writ.

title: Leases and Unlawful Use of the Premises in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute makes a residential lease void, or ends it automatically, because the premises are used for an unlawful purpose. The lease continues until you end it through the normal process: a written notice to quit and a court case for breach of a lease covenant (the residential-use and criminal-activity terms, `residential-use-only` and `criminal-activity-ky`), or, if the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), on the ground that the tenant maintains a nuisance or repeatedly engages in or permits serious misconduct. One statute puts a duty on you: if after signing a lease you discover that the building has been converted to prostitution, you must tell the Police Commissioner in writing and you have the right and responsibility to seek the tenant's eviction; if you do not notify, you are treated as having knowingly leased for prostitution, a crime. Knowingly leasing a place to be used for prostitution is itself a crime, and knowingly maintaining, or helping to maintain, premises used to manufacture methamphetamine or certain other drugs carries 10 to 20 years in prison. Whether a lease made for an illegal purpose is unenforceable from the start is a common-law question. Never treat a tenant's calls for police or emergency help in a domestic-violence situation as misconduct.

title: Paying Up, Partial Payments and Third-Party Payments in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands' only redemption rule lets a tenant sued for possession for nonpayment keep the lease by paying, before judgment, the rent in arrears with interest and the costs of the action and performing the other lease terms; it is printed as suspended while the rent-control subchapter is in force, and that subchapter's status is unsettled (see `edu-forfeiture-redemption-vi`). There is no right to redeem after judgment or up to the eviction, no rule that a fully paid judgment bars the Marshal's removal, no rule on partial payments (no required reservation wording, no rule that accepting part of the rent waives the eviction), and no rule requiring you to accept a payment from a charity or government agency or forbidding you to restrict its method. Whether accepting rent after a notice to quit waives the notice is a common-law question (case law not searched; see `edu-no-waiver-by-acceptance-rule-vi`). Cautious course: accept a full tender of arrears, interest and costs made before judgment, from the tenant or anyone paying for the tenant, and dismiss the case; if you accept a partial payment, give a written receipt stating that it is accepted without waiving the notice to quit or the case (the optional `rent-acceptance-nonwaiver-vi` clause says the same); and accept payment methods as the Payment Options law and the lease require (`acceptable-payment-methods-vi`).

title: Rent Paid into Court and Counterclaims in Virgin Islands Evictions
bodyText: A Virgin Islands tenant does not have to pay rent into court to defend an eviction, and the tenant cannot counterclaim in it. The court rule for summary landlord-tenant and forcible entry and detainer cases bars joining any other claim and bars counterclaims and third-party complaints, while letting the tenant raise any defense; the tenant's own money claims (repairs, return of the deposit, damages) go in a separate civil action or small claims. Money paid into court arises in only a few places: (1) a continuance longer than two days requires the tenant to give security for the rent that accrues and costs; (2) if the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), a stay of an owner-use or demolition eviction is conditioned on the tenant depositing in court, or paying you, a reasonable rent for the stay plus unpaid back rent; (3) a tenant who pays the arrears, interest and costs into court before judgment in a nonpayment case keeps the lease where that statute applies; and (4) an appealing tenant must give an undertaking for twice the rental value. In 2024 the Virgin Islands Supreme Court held that an eviction court could not order rent held in escrow paid to the landlord, because money claims need a separate action. No statute requires a rent deposit for a jury demand or a long adjournment.

title: Ending a Lease Because Repairs Cost Too Much in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets you end a lease, or refuse a repair, because the repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value, and none gives the tenant such a right. The Housing Code forbids renting a building for living, sleeping or cooking that does not comply with the Building Code or the Housing Code, and the owner's duties (plumbing, weathertight structure, roof, wiring, shared areas) continue for the whole tenancy. The Housing Finance Authority may order a non-complying dwelling repaired, vacated or demolished, and the Commissioner of Public Works may order an unfit dwelling repaired or vacated and closed; those are government orders, not a landlord's termination right. If the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), you may recover possession in good faith to demolish the building and build a new one, but only once plans are complete and you are actually ready to build, and the court may stay the eviction and you must offer the unit back before re-letting it. Otherwise, end a periodic tenancy by the statutory notice or wait for a fixed term to expire (see `edu-termination-notice-vi`); after a casualty see `casualty-termination-vi`. The library offers no clause letting you cancel over repair costs.

title: Retaliation Against Tenants in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no general landlord-tenant retaliation statute: none forbids raising the rent, cutting services or evicting because a tenant complained to you or to the Housing Finance Authority about repairs, joined a tenants' group or used a legal right, and none creates a presumption of retaliation. The civil-rights law does forbid retaliation in housing: it is an unlawful discriminatory practice for anyone engaged in an activity the law covers (including renting housing) to retaliate or discriminate against a person because that person complained of or opposed discrimination, or filed a complaint, testified or assisted in a proceeding under the civil-rights law. A tenant who suffers retaliation can sue for compensatory and punitive damages, and the court must award the tenant reasonable attorney's fees and costs. The Code's other anti-retaliation provisions protect employees, witnesses and crime victims, not tenants. Whether a court will refuse an eviction as retaliatory under the common law is a question the Virgin Islands Supreme Court decides. FEDERAL: the Fair Housing Act forbids coercion, intimidation, threats or interference with anyone exercising fair-housing rights, and federally assisted housing has its own protections. Cautious course: do not raise the rent, reduce services or start an eviction soon after a tenant's repair or code complaint or a discrimination complaint unless you have a documented, independent reason, and if the rent-control subchapter applies, every eviction needs one of its listed grounds anyway.

title: Condominium and association documents: no lease disclosure duty
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to disclose a condominium or homeowners association's obligations to a tenant, to deliver the association's documents with the lease, or to put in the lease your own statement that you know the condominium law and the association's bylaws. What the Condominium Act does say: every tenant of an apartment owner, and anyone else who uses the property, is subject to the Act and to the association's declaration and bylaws, whether or not the lease mentions them; each apartment owner must comply strictly with the bylaws, the association's rules and the declaration, and the association may sue an owner who does not; and a lessee counts as the apartment owner (for example, for voting) only to the extent a lease filed with the association's board of directors provides. The Act lists particulars that deeds of apartments must contain, but it does not impose that list on leases. No Virgin Islands statute governing homeowners associations outside condominiums was found; those communities run on their recorded covenants. Cautious course: before signing, give the tenant copies of the declaration, bylaws and house rules, and use the association compliance clause (`hoa-compliance`), because the association can hold you responsible for what your tenant does. If the declaration or bylaws require you to notify the association of a lease or file a copy, do so; that duty comes from those documents, not from a statute.

title: Flood zones and past flooding: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to tell a tenant that the home is in a flood zone or a special flood hazard area, that it has flooded before, or that flood insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, and there is no flood rider or model form and no tenant right to end the lease for a missing flood notice. Flood law in the territory is about construction and planning: the Building Code adopts flood-resistant construction standards and FEMA's flood maps for the Virgin Islands (special flood hazard areas, including coastal high-hazard V Zones), and the emergency management law has the Department of Planning and Natural Resources advise the territory's emergency management agency on structures particularly susceptible to flood. Those rules bind builders and the government, not a landlord's lease. Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. Cautious course: if you know the home is in a mapped flood zone or has flooded, say so in writing before signing, and remind the tenant that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings (renter's flood coverage is available through the federal flood insurance program).
