title: Military installations and airport zones: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to disclose that a rental is near a military installation, in an aircraft noise or accident-potential zone, or in a military impact district, and there is no related tenant right to end the lease. The territory's airport zoning laws for St. Croix and St. Thomas limit the height of structures near the airports; they do not require disclosures to tenants. If the home is close to an airport flight path or another source of serious noise, telling the prospective tenant is the safer practice.

title: Former ordnance sites, planned demolition and shared meters: no pre-lease disclosure
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to tell a prospective tenant about a former military ordnance or munitions site nearby, about a demolition permit you have applied for, or that the tenant's utility meter also serves other areas. Related rules: (1) Demolition. Under the territory's rent control law, whose current force is unsettled, a landlord may recover possession to demolish only in good faith, with plans for the new building completed and ready to build; a court may stay such an eviction, and if you later re-let the premises you must first offer the evicted tenant the unit back at the old rent by registered mail (see `edu-rent-control-vi`). If you plan to demolish, tell prospective tenants before they sign. (2) Shared meters. If you charge a tenant for water or electricity, the charge must be based on the tenant's own use, and unless the lease says otherwise in writing you must install a meter on request (see `edu-utility-meter-vi`). A meter that also records common-area or another unit's use does not meet that rule, so fix the wiring or plumbing, or include the utility in the rent.

title: Landlord's and manager's identity: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to give a tenant, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the owner, of a managing agent, or of a person authorized to receive notices and legal papers, and no statute bars an eviction because you did not. Related rules: (1) Business license. Renting out an apartment house is a licensed business: you need a license from the Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs before you start (an owner who lives in an apartment house of fewer than five units is exempt), and you must display the license conspicuously at the place of business named in it. (2) Real estate agents. A licensed broker or sales associate who rents or manages property for you must make known which party the agent is acting for, give a written agency disclosure before or when the agency agreement is made or before showing the property, whichever comes first, may represent both you and the tenant only with both parties' informed written consent on the agency disclosure statement, and must give each party a copy of any written instrument it signs. An owner managing its own property needs no broker's license. (3) Court. If someone other than you sues your tenant for possession, the tenant may answer that he holds only as your tenant, naming you. Practical course: state your legal name and an address for notices in the lease (the tagged `notices` clause), name any managing agent, and update the tenant in writing if either changes. Your notice to quit and any eviction complaint must name the right landlord.

title: Government tenant rights guide: none required
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute or agency publication you must hand out requires you to give a tenant a government guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, before signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one. The territory has no residential landlord-tenant act, so there is no statutory summary either. The only tenant rights training in the Code is for public housing tenants buying their units. Every residential lease must still be written in plain language, with the front-page statement the territory's plain-language law requires (see `edu-plain-language-vi`).

title: Statement of tenant rights: none required
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a government statement or summary of tenant rights to be attached to the lease, placed as its first page, signed by each tenant, or delivered before you may sue. The one mandatory front-page statement for a Virgin Islands residential lease is the plain-language law's "PLEASE READ THIS" statement highlighting the provisions that restrict the tenant's rights or protect you (see `edu-plain-language-consumer-statement-vi`); the lease builder prints it.

title: No truth-in-renting act
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no truth-in-renting act: no government statement of rights must be given with the lease, and no statute penalizes a landlord simply for offering a lease that contains a term the law forbids. Instead, specific statutes make particular lease terms unlawful or ineffective, for example: a term letting you end the lease or penalize a tenant for calling police or emergency help in a domestic violence situation; a no-pets rule applied to a blind tenant's dog guide; any restriction on use or occupancy because of race, creed, color or national origin; and any waiver of the plain-language law's rights. Two laws can still make a bad term costly. A lease that fails the plain-language law can make you liable for the tenant's actual damages, up to $1,000 in punitive damages, and attorney's fees. And the territory's consumer protection law, if it reaches residential leases (unsettled), treats stating that a transaction involves rights, remedies or obligations it does not involve as a deceptive trade practice. Keep unenforceable terms out of your lease.

title: Bed bugs: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to tell a prospective tenant about bed bugs, to disclose the unit's infestation history, or to treat within a set time. The territory's rules on pests generally are in `edu-no-bed-bug-rule-vi`: each occupant keeps his own part of the dwelling clean, safe and sanitary, you keep openings screened and shared areas sanitary, and the Commissioner of Health may make regulations for treating premises for pests, which must protect the occupants' privacy and safety during treatment. Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. Cautious course: if you know of a current or recent bed bug problem in the unit, say so in writing before the lease is signed, treat it with a licensed exterminator before move-in, and answer tenant questions truthfully. The optional pest-cooperation clause (`pest-cooperation-la`) is tagged for the territory.

title: Mold: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to disclose mold to a tenant, sets mold standards for rentals, or requires a mold notice or pamphlet. The Housing Code still bears on mold: you may not rent a dwelling that does not meet the Building Code and the Housing Code, and you must keep the roof, exterior walls, windows and exterior doors weathertight and the plumbing in good repair, while each occupant must keep his own part of the dwelling clean, safe and sanitary. Water entry after a storm is the usual source of mold in the territory. Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. Cautious course: fix leaks and water damage promptly, remediate visible mold before a new tenant moves in, and disclose in writing any known mold or unrepaired water damage before the lease is signed.

title: Radon: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to test for radon, to disclose radon levels or test results to a tenant, or to give a radon notice, whatever floor the unit is on. The only mention of radon in the Virgin Islands Code is construction-side: the territory's Building Code adopts the International Residential Code's radon-control methods appendix by reference for one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses. That appendix was not read for this library and governs how homes are built, not what a landlord tells a tenant. Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. If you have radon test results for the home, share them on request.

title: Defective drywall: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to disclose defective (corrosive or imported) drywall, or sets any rule about it for rentals. The only mention of drywall in the Virgin Islands Code is a business-license fee category for drywall installation contractors. Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. If you know the home contains defective drywall that has not been remediated, disclose it in writing before signing.

title: Former drug labs: no disclosure or cleanup statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to disclose that a rental was used to make methamphetamine or other drugs, to report a suspected drug lab, to have the unit tested or decontaminated, or bars occupancy until cleanup. The related law is criminal: anyone who knowingly maintains or operates premises used to manufacture methamphetamine, LSD, PCP or a Schedule I or II narcotic drug, or knowingly helps maintain or finance them, commits a serious felony (see `edu-drug-premises-crimes-vi`). Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. Cautious course: if you learn that a unit was used as a drug lab, call the police, do not re-rent it until it has been professionally assessed and cleaned, and disclose the history and the cleanup in writing to the next tenant.

title: Outstanding code orders and condemnation: no pre-lease disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to tell a prospective tenant about an outstanding Housing Code violation notice, a repair or vacate order, or a proceeding to declare the dwelling unfit for human habitation. But the tenant will often find out anyway, because the territory's own procedures give notice to people living there: (1) Housing Code: when the Housing Finance Authority finds a violation it serves written notice on the owner or occupants, and if nothing is done within 90 days it may order repairs, postponed occupancy, vacating or demolition. (2) Unfit dwellings: in a proceeding to repair, close or demolish a dwelling unfit for human habitation, the complaint is served on the owner, mortgagees and everyone in interest, including persons in possession; a copy of the complaint or order is posted in a conspicuous place on the premises and filed in the land records like a lis pendens. It is unlawful to rent out a dwelling that does not meet the Housing Code and the Building Code. Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. Cautious course: do not rent a unit that is under a vacate, closing or demolition order, and disclose in writing any outstanding violation notice or order before the lease is signed.

title: Certificate of occupancy: no lease disclosure
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to state in the lease whether the dwelling has a valid certificate of occupancy, to attach a copy, or bars rent for a period the building lacked one. The territory's Building Code adopts the International Building Code and International Residential Code by reference, and the Code refers to the Department of Planning and Natural Resources issuing a certificate of occupancy when construction is completed; and the Building Code itself bars occupying or using a building that has been constructed, structurally altered, reconstructed or enlarged until the Commissioner has made a final inspection and issued a Certificate of Use. Practical course: before renting a new, converted or substantially renovated unit, make sure any required certificate of occupancy has been issued; renting a dwelling that does not comply with the Building Code or the Housing Code is unlawful.

title: Housing or building code variances: no tenant notice
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to give tenants a copy of a variance from the Housing Code or the Building Code, or to attach one to the lease. Variances in the territory are granted by the Board of Land Use Appeals on appeal from Housing Code or Building Code decisions, where strict enforcement would cause manifest injustice or hardship or would be contrary to the purpose of the code or the public interest, and by the Commissioner of Planning and Natural Resources for public-interest projects such as housing projects. The Board's resolution goes to the agency and the parties to the appeal, not to tenants. If a variance affects how the unit meets a code requirement (for example, room size or a plumbing fixture), telling the tenant before signing is the safer practice.

title: Fire sprinklers: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a lease to disclose whether the building has fire sprinklers, or requires a sprinkler notice to tenants. The territory's Building Code deletes the International Residential Code's sprinkler requirement for one- and two-family dwellings, so many homes have none; where sprinklers are provided, the Code sets the water-supply standard for the cistern or well that feeds them. If the building has no sprinkler system, saying so in the lease is a simple, lawful way to avoid misunderstanding.

title: Landlord liability insurance: not required
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, to show proof of insurance to tenants or the government, or to register rental property with insurance as a condition. (In a condominium, the board must insure the property against fire and other hazards when the declaration, the bylaws, a majority of owners or a first mortgagee requires it.) Carrying liability and property insurance is still prudent, especially for hurricane exposure; any requirement that the tenant carry renter's insurance is covered by the tagged clause `tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca`.

title: Electric submetering: no disclosure regime; utility-status question open
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute sets up a disclosure, form or rate rule for landlords who submeter or re-bill electricity (or gas) to tenants. The rules that apply: you may charge a tenant for electricity or water only on the tenant's own metered use, and unless the lease says otherwise in writing you must install a meter on the tenant's request (see `edu-utility-meter-vi` and `edu-no-submetering-disclosure-rule-vi`). Open question: the territory treats anyone who provides electric power service for compensation as a public utility regulated by the Public Services Commission, and no statute says whether a landlord who re-bills metered electricity to tenants falls within that definition. The cautious course is to bill only the tenant's metered use at no more than the utility's own rate, with no markup or service charge, and to say in the lease how electricity is metered and billed. The public utility definition does not list gas service.

title: Meter conservation charges: none in the territory
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no meter-based energy-efficiency or conservation charge that stays with a utility account for a later occupant to pay, so there is no notice to give a new tenant and no rent deduction rule. The territory's Feed-in Tariff Act deals with payments to renewable-energy producers, not with charges on a tenant's meter. If you bill utilities to a tenant, the own-use and metering rules in `edu-utility-meter-vi` apply.

title: Utility billing disclosure attachment: none required
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a lease to carry a utility billing disclosure, a submetering certificate, or a statement about water or power availability. What the law does set: water and electricity may be charged to a tenant only on the tenant's own use, with a meter installed on request unless the lease says otherwise in writing; a sewer user fee passed on to a tenant may not exceed the actual fee for the unit (see `edu-utility-apportionment-vi`). Good practice: list in the lease which utilities you provide, which the tenant pays directly, which you bill and how each is measured.

title: Wells and cisterns: no test-result disclosure
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to test a private well or cistern serving a rental or to give tenants water test results. Many Virgin Islands homes rely on rainwater cisterns or wells rather than the public water system, and the Building Code and Housing Code govern them: buildings without public water service must have a cistern sized to the roof area, or a well that the Department of Health has certified as safe for drinking; cisterns used for drinking water must meet water-quality and disinfection requirements and be kept watertight and mosquito- and rodent-proof; if an approved well stops supplying safe water, the owner must build a cistern; and the owner must keep roofs, gutters and pipes to cisterns tight and clean and the pump and piping working. Practical course: clean and disinfect the cistern between tenancies and after storms, keep records, tell the tenant whether the home is on a cistern, a well or public water, and share any test results you have.

title: Property tax share of rent: no statement required
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to tell a tenant what part of the rent goes to real property tax, annually or when the rent changes. If you want to pass increases in property tax on to the tenant, the lease must say so (see `edu-tax-escalation-vi` and the tagged clause `tax-insurance-escalation-la`).

title: Condominium associations and rentals
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands Condominium Act governs condominiums (horizontal property regimes); no statute governing homeowners associations outside condominiums was found. The Act binds tenants of apartment owners, and anyone else who uses the property, to the Act and to the association's declaration and bylaws, and decisions lawfully made by the association bind every apartment owner. Bylaws may restrict the use of apartments.

The Act has no rules on association approval of leases, caps on approval or application fees, association-held tenant deposits, rental restrictions that bind only later buyers, limits on what tenant information an association may demand, or home child care. Those come, if at all, from each condominium's recorded declaration and bylaws. Nor does the Act let the association collect rent directly from your tenant, or have the tenant pay rent into court, when you fall behind on common expenses: unpaid assessments are a lien on the apartment, which the association may foreclose like a mortgage, and in that foreclosure you must pay a reasonable rental for the apartment if the bylaws so provide, with a receiver appointed to collect it.

A lease filed with the association's board may make the tenant count as the owner for purposes the lease states, such as voting. On the first sale or lease of each apartment, any blanket mortgage or lien must be paid off or the apartment released from it. If your condominium requires association approval of a lease, use the optional approval clause (`association-approval-la`). Keep your assessments current.

title: Tenants and condominium rules
bodyText:
Your tenant must follow the condominium's declaration, bylaws and rules even if the lease says nothing: the Condominium Act makes them binding on tenants of apartment owners and on anyone else who uses the property. You remain bound to comply strictly with them as the apartment owner, and the association may sue an owner for sums due, damages or an injunction when they are broken. No Virgin Islands statute requires you to deliver the rules to the tenant at signing, makes the tenant's duty depend on delivery, caps association fines, or lets the association collect rent from your tenant when you are behind.

The tagged clause `hoa-compliance` makes the tenant follow the rules and pay fines the tenant's own violations cause. Give the tenant a copy of the current rules before signing so the tenant can follow them. Satellite dishes and antennas: no Virgin Islands statute addresses them, but federal rules protect a tenant's right to install a small dish or antenna in an area the tenant exclusively uses, such as a balcony, and limit restrictions by landlords and associations.

title: Lead-based paint: federal rules only
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no lead-paint law of its own for rentals: no territorial disclosure form, notice, inspection certificate or information packet, no lead-safe certificate to attach to the lease, no abatement duty triggered by a child's lead poisoning, and no territorial rule on peeling paint or retaliation after a lead report.

Federal law applies in full. For housing built before 1978, before the tenant signs you must disclose any known lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards and give any available records or reports, give the tenant the EPA pamphlet Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home, and include the Lead Warning Statement (in the exact federal wording) with signed acknowledgments in or attached to the lease; keep a copy for three years.

Exemptions include leases of 100 days or less that cannot be renewed or extended, housing certified lead-based-paint free by a certified inspector, zero-bedroom units, and housing for the elderly or disabled where no child under six lives or is expected to live. The disclosure is repeated only for a renewal when you have new information. Contractors who disturb paint in pre-1978 housing must follow the federal renovation rules and give occupants the Renovate Right pamphlet.

Use the tagged federal disclosure clause (`lead-based-paint`) for every pre-1978 rental. Peeling or chipping paint is also a Housing Code repair item: you must keep floors, interior walls and ceilings in good repair.

title: Lead-safe certificate: none required
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a lead-safe, lead-free or lead-hazard-control certificate for a rental, or requires one to be attached to the lease. The only certificate that matters is federal and optional: housing certified lead-based-paint free by a certified inspector is exempt from the federal lease disclosure. Otherwise use the federal disclosure for every pre-1978 rental (see `edu-lead-based-paint-vi`).

title: Territorial lead notices: none beyond federal law
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead-based paint disclosure, the Virgin Islands requires no territorial lead notice, tenant-rights notice, inspection certificate or information packet at lease signing or during the tenancy, and nothing to repeat at renewal. Follow the federal rules described in `edu-lead-based-paint-vi`.

title: Sex offender registry: no landlord disclosure duty
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to tell tenants about registered sex offenders living nearby or in the building, to give tenants a notice about the sex offender registry, or to answer a tenant's question about registry information. The territory's sex offender registration law imposes no duty on landlords, though anyone who knowingly harbors an offender who is violating it, or gives police information about one that he knows is false, commits a crime. If you screen applicants using registry information, apply the same written criteria to everyone; the territory's civil rights law forbids refusing to rent because of a protected characteristic, and federal fair housing guidance warns against blanket criminal-record bans.

title: Deaths, crimes and other stigmas: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says whether a landlord must, or need not, disclose that a death, suicide, homicide or other crime occurred in the home, that an occupant had HIV/AIDS or another illness, or that a registered sex offender lives nearby, and there is no statutory safe harbor for staying silent. Two rules bear on it. A licensed real estate agent must disclose to its own client the material facts of the transaction that it knows or should know, so a tenant's agent may pass on what it learns. And the territory's civil rights law forbids refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because of a person's disability; under federal fair housing law, HIV infection is a disability, so never ask about or act on an applicant's or prior occupant's HIV status. Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. Cautious course: answer direct questions truthfully, and disclose events that a reasonable tenant would consider important to the decision to rent, but never disclose anyone's medical condition.

title: Notice of eviction-protection coverage: none required
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a lease or renewal to tell the tenant whether the unit is covered by a just-cause eviction or rent-increase law. The territory's rent control law, which is still printed in the Code but whose current force is unsettled, would itself act as a good-cause rule: it allows an action to recover rented premises only on listed grounds (your good-faith personal use, good-faith demolition to rebuild, the tenant's nuisance, unreasonable damage or repeated serious misconduct, or nonpayment) and only after 30 days' written notice to quit. It does not apply to hotels or transient lodging houses, and it ends only when the Legislature declares the 1947 housing emergency over. Because coverage is uncertain, do not tell a tenant in the lease that the unit is exempt from eviction protections. See `edu-rent-control-vi` for the cautious course.

title: Tenant opportunity to purchase: none
bodyText: The Virgin Islands gives residential tenants no right of first refusal or opportunity to purchase when the owner sells the building or the home, and requires no notice of a sale or of tenants' purchase rights. The nearest rule is different: under the territory's rent control law, whose current force is unsettled, if you recover a unit for your own use or for demolition and later rent it to someone else, you must first offer the evicted tenant the unit back at the same rent by registered mail (see `edu-rent-control-vi`). Government housing programs have their own purchase options for program occupants.

title: Exemption notices for rent caps, just cause or purchase rights: none
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a lease statement that the property is exempt from a rent cap, a just-cause eviction rule or a tenant opportunity-to-purchase law, and there is no exemption a landlord can claim by giving such a notice. The territory has no tenant purchase law (see `edu-no-tenant-purchase-right-vi`), and its rent control law, whose force is unsettled, exempts only hotels and transient lodging houses, without any notice (see `edu-no-good-cause-notice-vi`). Do not put an exemption statement in a Virgin Islands lease.

title: Student housing: no special regime
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute creates a licence, lease certification or special rules for renting to college or university students; students rent like anyone else. The rules that can matter for shared student rentals are general ones: the Housing Code's occupancy limits (floor area per occupant and sleeping-room size) and its rooming-house fixture rules, the business license for renting apartments, and the civil rights law, which forbids refusing to rent because of age or another protected characteristic (see `edu-permitted-occupants-vi`).

title: Leasing when you are not the full owner
bodyText: Virgin Islands property law is common law and does not recognize a usufruct, so the civil-law rule about leases granted by a usufructuary does not arise. The closest Virgin Islands interests are a life estate and an estate for a term of years. A landlord who holds only one of those can lease no more than he holds: a lease granting a greater estate passes only what the landlord can lawfully convey, so a lease signed by a life tenant may end when the life estate ends, even before the lease term is over. If you hold the home as a life tenant, a tenant for years or another limited owner, tell the prospective tenant in writing, and have the remainder owner or co-owners sign the lease if it must bind them. Whether a tenant can recover losses when such a lease ends early rests on case law not searched for this library.

title: Pesticide applications in dwellings: notice to occupants
bodyText: The territory's Pesticide Control Act has notice rules for pesticide use in and around homes. Before applying a pesticide in or on a one- or two-family dwelling, the certified applicator must give the occupants a written copy of the label information, including warnings. In a multiple dwelling (three or more families) the applicator gives that information to the owner or agent, and the owner or agent must make it available to occupants or residents on request at reasonable times; a tenant who hires an applicator for their own unit gets it directly. For a commercial lawn application the applicator needs a written contract with the property owner or agent and must give 48 hours' written notice to occupants of nearby dwellings, and residential lawn treatments over 100 square feet must be marked with signs. The Commissioner of Health's pest-control regulations must also protect the privacy and safety of occupants of premises being treated. No statute requires a pest-control notice in the lease itself. Practical course: use a certified applicator, give tenants written notice before any treatment of their unit or the common areas with the applicator's label information, keep that information on hand for tenants of a multiple dwelling, and follow the lawn-treatment notice and marker rules. Entry to treat a unit follows the lease's entry clause (see `edu-landlord-entry-vi`).

title: Single-family occupancy notice and lease font rules
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a single-family home lease to carry an occupancy notice, presumes that an occupant has no right to be there unless the lease is notarized or signed by a licensed manager, or sets a relative font size for such a notice. The only Virgin Islands rules on lease type size and front-page placement come from the plain-language law, which covers residential leases: conditions and exceptions to the main promises must be in at least 10-point type, and the front page must carry a statement highlighting provisions that restrict the tenant's rights or protect you, in 10-point boldface (not all capitals) under the caption "PLEASE READ THIS" in 12-point boldface capitals. The lease builder prints that statement (see `edu-plain-language-consumer-statement-vi`). To remove someone living in the home without right, use the notice-to-quit and court process (see `edu-eviction-process-vi`).

title: Special districts: no lease statement
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a lease to state that the property is in a special district or that the tenant knows of district laws, charges or plans. The territory has economic-development areas, such as enterprise zones and tax increment financing areas, but their laws set no lease statement for residential tenants. Puerto Rico's district acknowledgments have no Virgin Islands counterpart.

title: What a Virgin Islands residential lease must disclose
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no residential landlord-tenant act and only a short list of required lease disclosures. (1) Plain language and the front-page statement: every residential lease must be clear, simple and easily readable, and its front page must carry the "PLEASE READ THIS" statement highlighting the provisions that restrict the tenant's rights or protect you; the lease builder prints it (see `edu-plain-language-vi` and `edu-plain-language-consumer-statement-vi`). (2) Lead-based paint (federal): for housing built before 1978, the federal disclosure, pamphlet and Lead Warning Statement (see `edu-lead-based-paint-vi`). (3) If a licensed real estate broker or sales associate handles the rental: a written agency disclosure, and written consent of both you and the tenant to any dual agency (see `edu-no-owner-identity-disclosure-vi`). Nothing else is required: no notice of whether the unit is covered by eviction or rent-increase protections, no government form as the lease's first page, and no disclosure of flood zones, mold, radon, bed bugs, past drug labs, code orders, owner identity or other conditions (see the Disclosures rows for each). Adding an option to buy does not trigger a seller's disclosure statement, because the territory has no seller disclosure statute. Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. Disclose known material problems in writing before signing.

title: Pending foreclosure: no disclosure statute
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to tell a prospective tenant that the property is in foreclosure, that you have received a foreclosure complaint or a notice of default, or that a condominium association is foreclosing its lien. What happens to the tenant after a foreclosure sale is covered by federal law (see `edu-foreclosure-tenants-vi`). Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. Cautious course: if a foreclosure action is pending, tell the prospective tenant in writing before signing, and do not take rent far in advance.

title: Contaminated sites and environmental covenants: no lease disclosure
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a residential lease to disclose that the property is contaminated, is a designated brownfield, or is subject to an environmental covenant, or requires recorded environmental use limits to be written into a lease. The territory does have a Uniform Environmental Covenants Act and a brownfields law, under which limits on the use of a cleaned-up site are recorded in the land records and run with the land; a covenant may itself require notice when an interest in the property is transferred, so check any recorded covenant on your property. Even so, the territory's consumer protection law treats a misleading statement, or a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive, as a deceptive trade practice; whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled, and hiding a known defect may also support a fraud or concealment claim. Cautious course: if the property is subject to a recorded environmental covenant or a known contamination problem, tell the prospective tenant in writing before signing and make the lease's use rules consistent with the covenant.

title: California Proposition 65 warnings: not applicable
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warning rules for rental housing do not apply in the Virgin Islands, and the territory has no equivalent law requiring landlords to warn tenants about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, or to post such warnings in rental property. Federal rules still apply where relevant, such as the lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing (see `edu-lead-based-paint-vi`).

title: Shorelines and public beach access: no lease disclosure
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a lease to disclose that the property is on or near the shoreline, that the public may use the beach, or that a public access easement crosses the land. The territory's Open Shorelines Act protects public use of the shorelines and prohibits obstructing them, and coastal zone permits and economic-development benefits can require recorded public access easements to the beach. Those rules bind the property whatever the lease says, so never tell a tenant that a beach is private or let a tenant block public access; if a recorded access easement crosses the property, mention it in the lease.

title: Agreed Ways of Giving Notice in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute defines when a landlord or tenant has "actual notice", and none lets the parties agree on an extra way to give notice, such as a text message, that then counts as notice under the law. The methods that matter are set by the statutes themselves. A notice to quit must be in writing and served by delivering it to the tenant or person in possession, or by leaving it at the premises if the tenant is absent; other periodic-tenancy notices must be in writing. If you recover a unit under the rent-control subchapter for your own use or demolition and later re-let it, your offer to the evicted tenant goes by registered mail. Electronic notice works only where both of you have agreed to deal electronically, a law that requires a specific delivery method still controls, and the tenant may stop dealing electronically at any time; federal law also excludes eviction, default and right-to-cure notices for a primary residence from electronic delivery. Cautious course: you may agree in the lease to send routine notices by e-mail or text as well (`electronic-notice-ma`), but always serve a notice to quit, and any default, cure or termination notice, on paper by hand delivery or by leaving it at the home, and keep proof of service (see `edu-notice-delivery-methods-vi`).

title: Automatic Lease Renewal in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute regulates automatic-renewal terms in residential leases: there is no consumer auto-renewal law requiring bold type, an opt-in or a reminder before a lease renews. A lease may renew itself, or turn into a month-to-month tenancy at the end of the term, if it says so clearly. Three rules shape how you write it. First, the Plain Language Consumer Contracts law covers residential leases: the lease must be clear and readable, and a term that protects you, such as a renewal that commits the tenant to a new term unless the tenant opts out, belongs on the front-page "PLEASE READ THIS" list (`edu-plain-language-vi`). Second, a renewed term longer than one year must be in a signed writing to be enforceable. Third, if the rent-control subchapter applies (its status is unsettled), you may recover possession only on a listed ground and after 30 days' written notice to quit, so a renewal term should never suggest you may refuse to renew or end the tenancy for any reason. A tenant who stays after the term without a renewal holds over (see `edu-no-holdover-damages-statute-vi`), and a periodic tenancy ends on the notice in `edu-tenancy-at-will-vi`.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Virgin Islands Leases
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute authorizes or regulates arbitration clauses in residential leases, and the Virgin Islands Code has no general arbitration act (no Uniform Arbitration Act was found). An arbitration clause in a lease would rest on the federal arbitration law and contract law, and is probably lawful, but the library does not offer one, for three reasons. (1) Possession: eviction is a summary forcible entry and detainer case heard by the Superior Court's Magistrate Division, and a clause cannot send possession to an arbitrator without risking delay and challenge. (2) Money claims: rent and damages are claimed in a separate civil action or in small claims up to $10,000, a fast and cheap forum for both sides. (3) Plain-language law: a clause that takes away the tenant's court and jury rights restricts the tenant's rights and must be highlighted on the front page, and a one-sided clause invites an unconscionability challenge under contract law. A landlord who still wants arbitration may add its own clause after taking advice; it should carve out possession cases and small claims. The library's informal dispute clause (`informal-dispute-resolution-or`) is the lighter option.

title: Other Rules the Virgin Islands Does Not Have
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no residential landlord-tenant act, so many rules common elsewhere do not exist here. Each absence below was searched across the whole Virgin Islands Code and is explained, with what the territory does have nearby, in its own section of this library: no general anti-retaliation statute beyond the civil-rights law (`edu-retaliation-vi`); lockouts and other self-help are unlawful even though no lockout statute exists (`edu-no-lockout-for-rent-vi`, `edu-self-help-eviction-vi`); no possession bond (`edu-no-possession-bond-vi`); no notice-service fee rule (`edu-no-notice-service-fee-rule-vi`); no rent-into-court rule (`edu-rent-into-court-vi`); no defense for late benefit payments (`edu-no-benefit-delay-defense-vi`); no early termination for illness or age (`edu-no-infirmity-termination-vi`); no mitigation statute (`edu-no-mitigation-statute-vi`); no deposit cap or deposit-return statute (`edu-no-security-deposit-cap-vi`, `edu-no-deposit-return-statute-vi`); no late-fee cap (`edu-no-late-fee-limit-vi`); no application-fee rule (`edu-no-application-fee-rule-vi`); no smoke or carbon monoxide alarm statute (`edu-no-smoke-co-alarm-statute-vi`); no tenant repair remedies (`edu-no-tenant-repair-remedies-vi`); no landlord's lien (`edu-no-landlord-lien-vi`); no abandoned-property procedure (`edu-no-abandoned-property-statute-vi`); no holdover-damages statute (`edu-no-holdover-damages-statute-vi`); no eviction-record sealing (`edu-no-eviction-record-sealing-vi`); and no casualty statute (`edu-no-casualty-statute-vi`). Where a statute is silent, common law decided by the Virgin Islands Supreme Court fills the gap, so draft cautiously.

title: Checked Across All of Virgin Islands Law
bodyText: These points were checked across the whole Virgin Islands Code, not only the landlord-tenant chapter. (1) Squatters: there is no special fast removal of squatters or unauthorized occupants; use a forcible entry and detainer case, and report criminal trespass or unlawful entry to the police (`edu-unauthorized-occupants-vi`). (2) Receipts for cash rent: no landlord-specific receipt rule exists, but a business covered by the Payment Options law must offer a receipt for any payment of $5 or more, and a written receipt for every payment, especially cash, is the cautious course (`edu-rent-receipts-vi`). (3) Licensing before eviction: renting apartments is a licensed business (a Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs business license is a condition of doing business, except for an owner who lives in an apartment house of fewer than five units), but no statute was found that bars an unlicensed landlord from bringing an eviction case. Get the license anyway: willfully operating without it is a misdemeanor and can draw administrative fines (`edu-landlord-registration-vi`). Three other filings do bar a suit, though: a landlord renting under a name other than its own must file a trade-name certificate with the Lieutenant Governor before starting business and, until it does, may not bring any court action on that business (11 V.I.C. §§ 1201, 1203, 1212); a corporation may not bring or keep any court action while its annual franchise tax is unpaid (13 V.I.C. § 533(a)); and an out-of-state LLC must have a certificate of authority before it can sue, and owning income-producing real property in the Virgin Islands counts as transacting business (13 V.I.C. §§ 2003(b), 2008(a)).

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations Current in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands lease statute on domestic violence protects tenants without pointing to any other chapter, so no cross-reference has gone stale. It bars a lease term that lets you end the lease or penalize a tenant for calling the police or emergency help in a domestic violence or domestic abuse situation, and it lets a victim end the lease on at least 14 days' written notice with a police report written within the preceding 90 days (`edu-dv-lease-termination-vi`, `edu-dv-eviction-protection-vi`). The statute does not define domestic violence; the definition in the territory's domestic violence remedies chapter (16 V.I.C. ch. 2) is current and other statutes cite it. Protection orders come from that chapter: the court may restrain the abuser from entering the victim's residence and may grant the victim possession of a residence the parties jointly lease, excluding the abuser. Such an order does not change the lease itself, so keep collecting rent under it and do not let an excluded person back in; ask the tenant for a copy of the order.

title: Signing and Sending Lease Documents Electronically in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has adopted the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, so you and the tenant may sign the lease electronically: where a law requires a writing or a signature, an electronic record or signature satisfies it. The Act applies only where each party has agreed to deal electronically, which the shared Electronic Signatures clause records, and a tenant who agreed may later refuse to do further business electronically; that right cannot be waived in the lease.

Send the tenant a copy the tenant can print and store: an electronic record the sender prevents the recipient from printing or storing cannot be enforced against the recipient. The territory's Act does not itself exclude eviction, default or cure notices, but it keeps any delivery method another law requires, and the notice to quit must be delivered to the tenant or left at the premises; federal law also refuses electronic effect to default, eviction and right-to-cure notices for a primary residence.

So sign electronically if you like, but serve notices to quit and default notices on paper.

title: Emergency Contacts for Virgin Islands Tenants
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute requires or regulates an emergency contact for a residential tenant. You may ask for one, and the library's optional shared clause `tenant-death-contact-nh` does so: naming a contact gives that person no right to occupy the home or remove belongings. In a hurricane-prone territory a current contact is worth having for storm preparation and damage, but use it with care. Do not let the contact into the home or hand over the tenant's property without the tenant's consent or a court order, because entering a tenant's home without the tenant's consent is a crime unless the law provides for it.

When a tenant dies, the tenancy and the belongings pass under estate law, not to the emergency contact.

title: No Energy-Data Release Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires energy benchmarking of residential buildings or governs a lease term letting the power or water utility release a tenant's usage data to you. If the tenant holds the utility account, ask the tenant to share usage information or to authorize the utility in writing; the library offers no special clause. If you hold the account and bill the tenant, the bills are already yours, but any charge to the tenant for water or electricity must be based on the tenant's own use, and the tenant may ask for a separate meter unless the lease says otherwise in writing (see `edu-utility-meter-vi`).

title: Changing a Written Lease in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The shared Entire Agreement clause (`entire-agreement`) works in the Virgin Islands as written. No Virgin Islands statute lets you amend an existing residential lease by written notice to keep up with a new law, so a change during the term needs the tenant's signed agreement, or must wait until the tenancy can be ended and a new one offered. Two statutes back the clause's insistence on signed writings. A lease, or a lease renewal, for longer than one year is void unless it or a note of it is in writing and signed by the party to be bound; and an interest in real property under a lease of more than one year can be assigned or surrendered only in a signed writing or by operation of law.

A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy can be changed only by ending it on the required notice and offering new terms; during a declared state of emergency rent increases are restricted.

title: No Blank-Spaces Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires every blank in a residential lease to be filled in, or makes an incomplete lease a breach by the landlord. Good practice still matters. The Plain Language Consumer Contracts law covers residential leases and requires them to be clear, simple and readable, and a lease with blanks left open invites a dispute about what was agreed; a lease longer than one year must be in a signed writing, so its key terms belong on the page. Fill in or strike every blank, have both parties initial any handwritten change before signing, and give the tenant a signed copy (`edu-lease-copy-vi`).

title: What a Virgin Islands Lease Needs to Say
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lists what a residential lease must contain, but several rules shape it. (1) Form: the Plain Language Consumer Contracts law covers residential leases. The lease must be clear and readable, divided into captioned sections, with a table of contents if it runs over 3,000 words, conditions and exceptions in at least 10-point type, and a front-page "PLEASE READ THIS" statement highlighting the terms that restrict the tenant's rights or protect you (`edu-plain-language-vi`, `edu-plain-language-consumer-statement-vi`). (2) Writing: a lease for longer than one year must be in writing and signed by the party to be bound. (3) Terms you may not include: a term letting you end the lease or penalize the tenant for calling the police or emergency help in a domestic violence situation; discriminatory terms; a term denying a blind tenant's dog guide. (4) Terms that work only if written: the tenant's right to ask for a separate water or electric meter applies "unless otherwise agreed in writing" (`utility-meter-request-waiver-vi`). (5) Federal: the lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing (`lead-based-paint`), and the CARES Act notice rules for covered properties (`edu-cares-act-notice`). Rentals of less than 90 days also carry the hotel room tax (`hotel-room-tax-vi`).

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord who signs its own lease to give the tenant a copy, and none makes a missing copy a defense to enforcing the lease. A licensed real estate broker or sales associate who handles the lease is different: failing to give a copy of a written instrument to a party who signs it, at the time of signing, is a ground for discipline by the Real Estate Commission (an owner managing its own property is outside that licensing law).

Give a signed copy anyway, at signing: the tenant needs it to follow the lease, the plain-language law expects the tenant to be able to read the terms, and an electronic copy the tenant cannot print or store cannot be enforced against the tenant.

The optional shared clause `lease-copy-receipt-hi` records the tenant's receipt of a copy.

title: No Lease Initials Requirement in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a tenant to initial particular lease clauses, or makes a clause enforceable only if it is initialed or separately signed. What the territory requires instead is visibility: under the Plain Language Consumer Contracts law, which covers residential leases, the terms that restrict the tenant's rights or protect you must be highlighted in a front-page "PLEASE READ THIS" statement in boldface type (`edu-plain-language-vi`). Initials next to those terms are optional good practice, not a legal requirement; the tenant's signature on the lease is what binds the tenant.

title: Lease Length Limits in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute sets a maximum or minimum term for a private residential lease, and none requires a seal, notarization or other special formality for a long lease. Length matters in three places. (1) A lease for longer than one year from the time it is made is void unless it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the party to be bound or by an agent with written authority. (2) An interest in real property under a lease of more than one year can be assigned or surrendered only by operation of law or by a signed writing, again by the party or an agent under written authority, so if someone signs for the owner on a long lease, get the written authority. (3) Rentals of less than 90 days carry the hotel room tax (`hotel-room-tax-vi`). If the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), the length of the term does not let you recover possession at its end without a listed ground (`edu-rent-control-vi`).

title: Type Size and Layout for Virgin Islands Leases
bodyText: The Virgin Islands sets type-size and layout rules for residential leases through the Plain Language Consumer Contracts law, not through a lease statute. Conditions and exceptions to the main promise must be as prominent as the main promise and in at least 10-point type; sections must be logically divided and captioned; a lease over 3,000 words needs a table of contents or index; and the front-page "PLEASE READ THIS" statement must be in 10-point boldface (not all capitals) under a 12-point boldface capital caption. The library's lease builder applies these rules (`edu-plain-language-vi`). No Virgin Islands statute sets a type size for the whole lease with an evidence penalty for small print, and no other formatting rule reaching residential leases was found.

title: Owners Living Off-Island: Process Agent and Company Rules in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: A nonresident doing business in the Virgin Islands in his or her own name must appoint, in a writing filed with the Lieutenant Governor, a person who lives and has an office in the judicial division where the business is located to receive court papers; if no one is appointed, the Lieutenant Governor is the process agent, and the territory may not grant a nonresident individual a business license until the appointment is filed (11 V.I.C. §§ 1210, 1212). We found no statute requiring the agent to be named in the lease or rent to be withheld for tax. If you own through a company formed elsewhere: an out-of-state LLC must get a certificate of authority from the Lieutenant Governor, owning income-producing real property here counts as transacting business, and until it has the certificate it may not sue (its leases stay valid), while by transacting business without one it appoints the Lieutenant Governor to receive court papers (13 V.I.C. §§ 2003(b), 2008). An out-of-state corporation doing business through agents or representatives here must first file its charter and name a local process agent with the Lieutenant Governor, and is fined up to $500 per offense if it does not; no corporation may sue while its annual franchise tax is unpaid (13 V.I.C. §§ 401, 406, 533(a)). Two more rules matter. First, whoever manages or leases the property for you for pay generally needs a Virgin Islands real estate broker's license (or works as a sales associate under a licensed broker); you, as owner, may manage your own property without one. Second, you need a way to receive and act on tenant notices and repair requests quickly, and the notice to quit and any eviction case must be handled on-island in person or through counsel. List in the lease the local name, address and phone number for notices and emergencies (`notices`), keep your business license current (`edu-landlord-registration-vi`).

title: How Notices Must Be Delivered in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
Virgin Islands law sets only a few delivery rules for landlord-tenant notices.
- (1) A notice to quit must be in writing and served by delivering it to the tenant or person in possession, or by leaving it at the premises if the tenant is absent. No statute says who must serve it, so a marshal or process server is not required for the notice itself (the court's summons is served under the court's rules).
- (2) If you recover a unit under the rent-control subchapter for your own use or for demolition and later re-let it, the offer to the evicted tenant must go by registered mail, or be posted on the premises if the tenant's whereabouts are unknown.
- (3) A tenant ending the lease as a domestic violence victim gives you at least 14 days' written notice.
- (4) Housing Code notices from the government go in person or by registered or certified mail.

No statute makes a delivery method you agree in the lease mandatory for statutory notices. Electronic notice works only where both parties agreed to deal electronically, never replaces a method another law requires, and does not count for default, eviction or right-to-cure notices on a primary residence; the optional shared clause `electronic-notice-ma` is drafted to fit.

Cautious course: hand-deliver every notice to quit and default notice, or leave it at the home if no one is there, note the date, time and person served, and keep a copy; mailing alone is not the statutory method for a notice to quit.

title: No Rule on Move-Out Notice Forms or Work During a Notice Period in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute regulates a move-out form you ask a tenant to sign, requires a warning when such a form adds terms, or bars renovation or other work that makes the unit hard to live in while a notice to vacate is pending. The tenancy and your duties continue until the tenant actually leaves or a court orders possession: the Housing Code duties to keep the unit weathertight, plumbing working and shared areas clean still apply; you may enter only as the lease and law allow and never by force; and cutting services or making the unit unusable to push a tenant out is self-help eviction (`edu-self-help-eviction-vi`). If the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), demolition is a ground for possession only when plans are complete and you are actually ready to build, and the court may stay the eviction. Keep any move-out form to the date and forwarding address; new obligations need the tenant's real agreement.

title: Where Virgin Islands Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Because the Virgin Islands has no residential landlord-tenant act, most terms are for the lease to decide, but a few statutes turn on what the lease says. (1) Meters: a tenant may ask you to install a separate water or electric meter "unless otherwise agreed in writing"; the optional clause `utility-meter-request-waiver-vi` records that agreement. (2) Rent period: when rent is payable more often than every three months, the notice to end a tenancy at will equals the rent interval, so the lease's rent period sets that notice (`periodic-tenancy-notice-vi`). (3) Rent paid in advance: an eviction cannot be brought before the end of any period already paid for, so collecting more than one period in advance delays possession. (4) Electronic dealings: the electronic-transactions law applies only if both parties agree, which the lease can record (`electronic-signatures`). (5) Options the library offers as optional clauses because the law leaves them to the lease (some within statutory limits stated in the clause): a holdover charge (`holdover-rate-vi`), casualty termination (`casualty-termination-vi`), landlord self-cure (`landlord-self-cure-vi`), non-waiver by accepting rent (`rent-acceptance-nonwaiver-vi`), collection costs (`collection-costs-vi`), interest on unpaid amounts (`unpaid-amounts-interest-vi`), a guaranty (`guaranty-vi`), property left behind (`abandoned-property-procedure-vi`), an eminent-domain allocation (`eminent-domain-vi`), reimbursement of government fines the tenant causes (`tenant-caused-fines-vi`), a cap on landlord-paid utilities for a unit with its own meter (`utility-allowance-cap-vi`), moving utilities into the tenant's name (`utility-transfer-vi`), naming you to receive utility shutoff notices (`utility-shutoff-notice-designee-vi`), items you leave but won't maintain (`appliances-excluded-vi`), a designated repairer (`designated-repairer-vi`), care of a tenant's animals in an absence (`animal-care-access-vi`), cannabis restrictions (`cannabis-restrictions-vi`) and firearm rules (`firearm-rules-vi`). Every term that limits the tenant's rights or protects you goes on the front-page "PLEASE READ THIS" list (`edu-plain-language-vi`).

title: Landlord Size Thresholds in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands rule ties landlord duties to the number of units you own across a portfolio, except for the business license fee. Size matters in these places. (1) Business license: an owner who lives in an apartment house of fewer than five units needs no license; otherwise one license covers all your apartment houses, with the fee set by your total number of units (`edu-landlord-registration-vi`). (2) Housing discrimination: the territory's civil-rights law does not apply to renting a unit in a building with housing for no more than two families when you or your family live in the other one. Both conditions must be met: a three-family building, or a two-family building you do not live in, is covered; federal fair-housing law has its own, separate exemptions. (3) Housing Code: an owner of a building with two or more units must keep the shared areas clean, safe and sanitary, and the Code does not apply to owner-occupied rural dwellings under 600 square feet. (4) Payment options: businesses with annual volume under $50,000 need not offer the cash-and-card options (`acceptable-payment-methods-vi`). (5) Rent control does not apply to hotels or transient lodging houses.

title: No Renter's-Insurance Statute in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute regulates a lease's renter's-insurance requirement: none lets the tenant choose the carrier by statute, governs force-placed coverage or a fee for it, or requires a written advisory that you do not insure the tenant's belongings. You may require renter's insurance in the lease; the library uses the shared clause `tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca`, which tells the tenant your insurance does not cover the tenant's property and sets a liability minimum you choose.

Let the tenant pick the insurer and send you proof. If you buy coverage for a tenant who does not, bill only its actual cost, and do not call it rent. Tenant insurance policies themselves are covered by the territory's plain-language law whatever their amount.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute governs what happens to a residential lease when you sell the property or change managers: there is no required notice to tenants, no statutory release of the old landlord, no rule moving the security deposit to the buyer, and no seller disclosure tied to the tenancy. Under general property law a buyer normally takes subject to an existing lease and steps into your place, but that rests on case law not searched for this library. Practical rules: (1) A transfer of your interest under a lease of more than one year must be in a signed writing. (2) Tell the tenant in writing who the new owner or manager is, where to pay rent and where to send notices, and get the tenant's written acknowledgment. (3) Transfer the deposit to the buyer with a written accounting to the tenant, or return it, because no statute releases you from it (`edu-no-deposit-sale-rule-vi`). (4) A sale does not by itself end the lease; if the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), a new owner may recover a unit for personal use only in good faith and subject to its stay and re-letting rules (`edu-owner-move-in-vi`). (5) A new manager who is paid to manage for you needs a broker's license (`edu-no-nonresident-owner-agent-vi`). Foreclosure and court sales are covered in `edu-foreclosure-tenants-vi`.

title: Which Virgin Islands Laws Govern a Residential Lease
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands has no residential landlord-tenant act. Residential tenancies are governed by a short Landlord and Tenant chapter (rent, tenancies at will, domestic violence, eviction by forcible entry and detainer, and a rent-control subchapter whose status is unsettled), the Housing Code, the civil-rights and consumer laws, and common law decided by the Virgin Islands Supreme Court. Scope points:
- (1) One law for all three islands: the Code applies throughout the territory, and there are no county or city ordinances.
- (2) The Housing Code covers all dwellings, hotels, apartment houses, apartments and rooming houses, except owner-occupied rural dwellings under 600 square feet.
- (3) Rent control does not apply to hotels or transient lodging houses.
- (4) Farm leases: a notice to quit must be served six months before suit, and the farm tenant may return to harvest crops planted before the notice.
- (5) Mobile homes: the territory has zoning rules for mobile home parks but no mobile-home landlord-tenant law.
- (6) Short stays under 90 days are taxed like hotel rooms (`hotel-room-tax-vi`).
- (7) Condominium units are also subject to the association's declaration and bylaws (`hoa-compliance`).
- (8) Date gates: the plain-language law applies to leases made on or after October 30, 1984.

No Virgin Islands statute excludes long-term leases or applies only in named places.

title: Severability in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
The shared severability clause (`severability`) works in the Virgin Islands as written. The territory's statutes that police lease terms strike the offending term, not the whole lease: a lease may not contain a term letting you end the lease or penalize the tenant for calling the police or emergency help in a domestic violence situation, and the tenant cannot waive that right; a tenant who agreed to deal electronically may still refuse further electronic dealings, and that right cannot be waived; and a breach of the plain-language law does not make the lease void or a defense to it unless enforcing it would be unconscionable.

A severability clause cannot save a lease that fails as a whole: a lease for longer than one year that is not in a signed writing is void, and a lease made for an unlawful purpose (for example, knowingly leasing for prostitution) may be unenforceable as a whole, a common-law question. The territory's own severability rule applies to its statutes, not to private contracts; how far a court will sever a lease term otherwise rests on case law.

title: No Statutory Lease Form in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands supplies no statutory lease form and prescribes no verbatim text for a residential lease or for landlord notices such as the notice to quit; the statutes say what a notice must do (be in writing, give the required period, be delivered or left at the premises), not its words. The plain-language law gives two related tools: using a model plain-language form from a government agency, the Commission on Uniform Laws or a national trade association is prima facie evidence of good faith, and a landlord without a primary regulator may ask the Attorney General for an opinion on whether its lease complies. The court supplies its own forms for filing an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) complaint and for small claims; those are court forms, not lease text. Federal law supplies the lead-based paint disclosure language for pre-1978 housing (`lead-based-paint`).

title: Tenant Portals and Online Payments in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute regulates an online tenant portal as such, but two laws limit making a portal the only channel. (1) Payments: a business covered by the territory's Payment Options law must offer at least cash and a credit or debit card, the customer chooses the method, and the business may not induce or coerce a particular method; the main pass treats landlords as covered unless their annual volume is under $50,000 (`acceptable-payment-methods-vi`). So a covered landlord may offer a portal but may not require rent to be paid only through it. (2) Documents and signatures: the electronic-transactions law applies only where each party has agreed to deal electronically, and a tenant who agreed may later refuse further electronic dealings; that right cannot be waived. A lease term requiring every signature or notice to go through a portal therefore cannot bind a tenant who withdraws, and notices to quit and default notices must still be served on paper (`edu-notice-delivery-methods-vi`). Records you post must be ones the tenant can print or store.

title: Renter's Insurance and Your Repair Duties in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands uses the library's renter's-insurance clause without a liability disclaimer (`tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca`): it says your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings and requires the tenant to carry renter's insurance with a liability minimum you choose. No Virgin Islands statute forbids, or expressly allows, pushing repairs that are your responsibility onto the tenant's insurance. The Housing Code makes the owner responsible for the building's plumbing, roof, walls, wiring and shared areas as a public-law duty that no statute lets a lease shift, so do not use the tenant's policy as a substitute for your repairs, and do not require the tenant to claim on it for damage the tenant did not cause. The library does not use an unqualified "Landlord is not liable" disclaimer because the common law on such terms was not searched (`edu-no-tenant-insurance-claims-vi`).

title: Changing Rent or Other Terms in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute sets a notice period for changing the rent or other terms of a residential tenancy. During a fixed term you may change the rent or terms only as the lease itself provides (`rent-escalation-la`, `rent-increase-midterm-ky`) or with the tenant's signed agreement. A month-to-month or other tenancy at will can be changed only by ending it on the notice the law requires and offering new terms: a notice equal to the rent interval where rent is payable more often than every three months (one month for month-to-month, one week for week-to-week), or three months otherwise. This applies to any term, including raising a fee, not only rent. Three cautions: (1) if the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), 30 days' written notice to quit is the cautious minimum before any possession case, and a tenant may petition over rent; (2) during a declared state of emergency rents may be frozen and unconscionable increases are crimes (`edu-emergency-rent-pricing-vi`); (3) a pending bill (Bill No. 36-0022) would change these notice rules but is not law. See `edu-rent-increase-notice-vi`.

title: Sunset Dates in Virgin Islands Tenant Law
bodyText: No Virgin Islands tenant protection is on a dated repeal clock, but two sets of rules are tied to emergencies rather than dates. (1) The rent-control subchapter stays in force only while the housing emergency declared in 1947 continues, and stops applying when the Legislature declares by resolution or act that the emergency has ended. No such declaration was found, so its status is unsettled (`edu-rent-control-vi`). (2) The rent freeze and price-gouging rules apply only during a state of emergency declared by the Governor, and for its extensions (`edu-emergency-rent-pricing-vi`). The domestic violence lease protections, the plain-language law and the Housing Code have no expiry date.

title: No Lease Translation Requirement in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to translate a lease or notice, even when the tenancy was advertised or negotiated in Spanish or another language, and none prescribes lease text in more than one language. The plain-language law requires the lease to be clear and readable but says nothing about language. Still, a tenant who cannot read the lease is more likely to dispute it, and the territory's consumer protection law treats misleading statements and omissions as deceptive. Cautious course: if you negotiate in another language, give the tenant a translation for reference, explain the front-page "PLEASE READ THIS" terms in that language, and keep the signed English lease as the controlling text.

title: Which Virgin Islands Notices Must Be in Writing
Cannabis Rules in a Virgin Islands Rental
bodyText:
The Virgin Islands Cannabis Use Act legalizes medical cannabis and adult possession (adults over 21 may possess up to two ounces of cannabis, 14 grams of concentrate and one ounce of cannabis products). What it means for your lease:
- (1) Status: you may not refuse to rent to, or otherwise penalize, anyone solely because the person is a registered medical-cannabis patient (a Qualified Patient), unless not doing so would violate federal law or cost you a federal monetary or licensing benefit. Federally assisted housing therefore follows federal rules.
- (2) Smoking: the Act expressly protects a landlord seeking a smoke-free building, so a ban on smoking cannabis in the lease is safe. Vaporizing cannabis is not "smoking" under the Act, so a lease that means to ban vaping must say so, as the shared `smoking-policy` clause does; whether you may enforce a vaping ban against a patient's medical use inside the home is unsettled, because patients may not be penalized in any manner for possessing or using cannabis items.
- (3) Growing: home growing is allowed only for resident patients (and registered sacramental users), within plant limits, and only with the express consent of the landowner, so you may simply withhold consent. No home-grow right for other adults was found.
- (4) Business: any cannabis business at the property other than a licensed one is unlawful.
- (5) Public use: the Act does not authorize consuming cannabis in a public place.

Because cannabis remains illegal under federal law, do not treat lawful territorial use as "criminal activity" under the lease without advice; use the optional clause `cannabis-restrictions-vi` instead.

title: Guests Displaced by a Hurricane or Other Disaster
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets a tenant house people displaced by a hurricane or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, bars you from enforcing those limits against them, or says when a displaced person's stay becomes a tenancy. Ordinary rules apply: your guest terms (`guest-policy`, `guest-policy-day-limit`), the Housing Code's space-per-occupant minimums, which overcrowding violates (`edu-permitted-occupants-vi`), and a court case to remove anyone who claims a right to stay (`edu-unauthorized-occupants-vi`). Two disaster rules do apply to you: during a declared state of emergency rents may be frozen and unconscionable rent increases are crimes (`edu-emergency-rent-pricing-vi`), and storm damage is handled under the lease's casualty terms (`casualty-termination-vi`). After a major storm, give written consent for longer stays where you can, setting an end date and naming who may stay, rather than enforcing limits strictly.

title: No Guest Access Statute in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives a tenant's guests or service providers (caregivers, home-health aides, delivery or repair workers) a right of access to a residential building, bars a charge for guests, or makes guest access unwaivable. Guests come in under the tenant's right to occupy and the lease's guest terms (`guest-policy`). Three rules still limit you: you may not discriminate in the terms or services of a tenancy on any protected ground, which includes refusing a disabled tenant's caregiver where an accommodation is needed; a blind tenant's dog guide must have full and equal access at no extra charge; and no closed list of fees exists, but a guest fee must be in the lease and reasonable.

title: Police Calls, Crime-Free Leases and Cooperation in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires or regulates a crime-free lease addendum, requires tenants or landlords to cooperate with police investigations, or requires you to give police information about tenants. One firm limit applies: a residential lease may not let you end the tenancy or penalize a tenant for calling the police or other emergency help in a domestic violence or domestic abuse situation, and the tenant cannot waive that right; nor may you evict a tenant solely because the tenant is a domestic violence victim. Draft any criminal-activity term to exclude victims and calls for help, as the shared clause `criminal-activity-ky` does, and treat other criminal activity as an ordinary lease breach (`edu-criminal-activity-vi`). Knowingly leasing premises for prostitution is itself a crime (`edu-drug-premises-crimes-vi`). Do not let police into a tenant's home without the tenant's consent, a warrant or a true emergency; entering a tenant's home without consent is a crime unless the law provides for it. One reporting duty does reach everyone: if abuse of an older or dependent adult involves criminal activity, any person must report it immediately to the appropriate law enforcement agency (34 V.I.C. § 453(b)(2)); the statute's penalties are written for mandated reporters, administrators and supervisors (34 V.I.C. § 453(f)). Reporting child abuse is mandatory only for listed professionals, though anyone may report (5 V.I.C. § 2533), and the duty to report an unnatural death to the Medical Examiner falls on the Commissioner of Health and the Police Commissioner (3 V.I.C. § 115(b)).

title: No Political Canvassing or Sign Right in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or tenant organizers a right to enter an apartment building or knock on tenants' doors, and none gives tenants a right to post political signs that a lease cannot limit.
