Your lease rules decide, within one limit: political affiliation is a protected class under the territory's housing discrimination law, so you may not refuse to rent, or set different terms, rules or services, because of a tenant's political affiliation. Apply any canvassing or sign rule to all candidates and causes alike (see `edu-no-display-rights-statute-vi`).

title: No Portable or Window Air-Conditioner Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives a tenant a right to install a portable or window air conditioner, requires a lease that restricts them to say so, or requires you to provide air conditioning (`edu-heating-na-vi`). Whether a tenant may add a unit is a lease matter: the shared alterations clause requires your consent for changes to the unit (`no-alterations`). In the territory's climate, allow portable or window units on reasonable conditions instead of banning them: require safe installation, no damage to walls or window frames, removal before a hurricane where a window unit would block shutters, and use only on circuits that can carry the load, since the Housing Code makes you responsible for safe wiring.

title: No Recycling Notice Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to tell tenants where or how to recycle, to provide recycling containers, or to post recycling instructions. The Housing Code sets the garbage rules: you must provide garbage storage containers, and each occupant must dispose of garbage in a clean and sanitary manner under the Department of Public Works rules. Tell tenants in writing where the containers are and when collection happens, and add recycling instructions if a recycling service is available to your building.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives a tenant a right to place religious or cultural items (a mezuzah, a cross, a Carnival or holiday decoration) on a door, doorframe, balcony or common area, or limits a landlord's rules about them. The shared `common-area-use` clause's own carve-out for small displays is generous. One rule applies: creed is a protected class under the territory's housing discrimination law, so a display rule must apply alike to every faith and may not single out one religion's items.

title: House Rules in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute governs landlord house rules: none sets conditions for a rule to be enforceable, limits rule changes during a tenancy, or binds a tenant only to rules in force at signing. Rules bind the tenant because the lease says so, so the library uses the shared clause `rules-ia`, which requires rules to be reasonable, in writing and applied fairly, and to take effect after notice. Whether a new rule that substantially changes the bargain binds a tenant during a fixed term rests on case law; the cautious course is to make significant changes only at renewal or with the tenant's signed agreement.

Rules may not discriminate on any protected ground, may not penalize a tenant for calling for help in a domestic violence situation, and may not be adopted to retaliate against a tenant who complained of discrimination. Condominium units are also subject to the association's rules (`hoa-compliance`).

title: Smoke Drifting Between Units in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute addresses tobacco or cannabis smoke drifting between units, or lets a lease make a tenant accept drifting smoke or give up claims over it. Do not use a drift waiver: the library does not use terms that excuse the landlord's own responsibility because the common law on them was not searched. The Smoke-free Act does not reach private homes, but it bans smoking in enclosed areas of places of employment, which include hallways and other areas your employees normally use, and in enclosed areas of places the public is invited, so in a building with staff the enclosed common hallways must be smoke-free (`edu-smoking-policy-vi`). The better tool is a smoking ban in the lease (`smoking-policy`), which the cannabis law expressly allows a landlord to seek.

title: Snow Removal: Not Applicable in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: Snow removal does not arise in the Virgin Islands: the territory is tropical, and no Virgin Islands statute mentions snow. The shared Snow Removal clause is not used for Virgin Islands leases. What matters instead is hurricane readiness. No statute assigns storm preparation between landlord and tenant, so say in the lease who installs and removes shutters, secures outdoor furniture, clears drains and gutters, and removes storm debris; remember that the Housing Code makes the owner keep roofs, gutters and cistern pipes tight and clean; and use the lease's casualty terms for storm damage (`casualty-termination-vi`).

title: Flags and Signs at Virgin Islands Rentals
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives a tenant a right to display a flag, a political sign or a religious item against your wishes, and none bars a landlord or condominium association from restricting them; the territory's flag laws govern official displays only. Your lease rules decide (`common-area-use`), with two limits: political affiliation and creed are protected classes under the housing discrimination law, so a sign or display rule must treat all causes and faiths alike; and a rule should be in the lease or adopted under the lease's rules procedure (`rules-ia`). Separately, putting up advertising for a product on someone else's property without the owner's permission is a minor crime, which covers commercial signs a tenant posts on your building without consent.

title: Barring Non-Tenants From the Property in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands trespass law is simple: anyone who enters the land of another without the consent of the owner or the person in charge of it commits a petty offense (fine up to $50, up to 30 days in jail, or both). The law has no notice element, no posting procedure and no listed defenses, so whether a person lacked consent is a question of fact. As owner of the common areas you can withdraw consent for a non-tenant who causes trouble: give the person a written no-trespass notice, keep a copy, and call the police if the person returns. Be careful with tenants' guests. A tenant is in charge of the tenant's own home and may invite guests to it, so barring a guest from reaching the tenant's door can breach the lease and draw a discrimination or retaliation claim; limit bans to people who have caused real problems and tell the tenant in writing. Entering a tenant's home without the tenant's consent is a separate crime, and a person removed by court process who returns commits a further offense (`edu-unauthorized-occupants-vi`).

title: Waterbeds in Virgin Islands Rentals
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute deals with waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture, so the territory neither protects a tenant's right to one nor sets conditions on it. The lease may forbid or allow them. If you allow one, you may require the tenant to carry insurance covering water damage and to follow installation rules (frame, liner, floor-load limits on upper floors). No statute caps deposits or lists permitted fees, so an added waterbed deposit is lawful if it is in the lease, reasonable and handled like the security deposit (`edu-no-security-deposit-cap-vi`).

title: Foreclosure and Other Proceedings Against the Property: No Notice Statute in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that the property faces foreclosure, a tax sale, condemnation or another proceeding that could affect the tenancy, and none requires notice to tenants when the property is sold. The duty in the library runs the other way: the shared clause `tenant-forward-proceedings-ca` asks the tenant to pass on any legal papers about the property. Even without a statute, staying silent is risky. The territory's consumer protection law treats a failure to state a material fact that deceives or tends to deceive as a deceptive practice, and whether that law reaches residential leases is unsettled; signing a new lease while you know a foreclosure sale is close can also support a fraud or concealment claim. Cautious course: tell an applicant in writing before signing if a foreclosure, tax sale or condemnation case is pending, and tell current tenants promptly. If the government sells the unpaid property tax lien on your building, the buyer of the lien, and anyone who later takes the property through it, is subject to any applicable tenant protections of the rent-control subchapter (whose status is unsettled); the statute also names 33 V.I.C. § 2498, but that section only lets senior and disabled owner-occupants have their tax bills and delinquency notices copied to a person they designate, and protects no tenant. What happens to the tenancy after a foreclosure or court sale is covered in `edu-foreclosure-tenants-vi` and `edu-execution-sale-tenants-vi`; condemnation in `edu-eminent-domain-vi`; the federal foreclosure-notice rules are not part of this row.

title: Business Licenses for Rentals in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no landlord or rental registry, but renting property can be a licensed business. A business license from the Commissioner of Licensing and Consumer Affairs is a condition of engaging in any business on the statutory fee schedule. That schedule names apartment houses by size (four or fewer units, 5-8, 9-12 and more than 12), rooming houses, cottage rentals, hotels and guest houses, rental of non-residential buildings and rent of real property other than buildings, among other categories; it does not name a rented condominium unit, and whether 'cottage rental' reaches a single rented house is not defined. The Department has read the law to cover owners renting a condominium, villa or house, but that reading rests on a Department press release, not the statute, so if you rent out one house or condo, confirm with the Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs whether you need a license. An owner who lives in an apartment house of fewer than five units does not need one. One owner needs only one license, with the fee set by the total number of apartment units owned, and the license must be displayed at the place of business. Willfully doing business without a required license is a misdemeanor (fine up to $500, up to 30 days in jail, or both), and the Commissioner may add administrative fines. No statute was found that makes the license a condition of bringing an eviction case. Other filings can block an eviction case, though: a landlord renting under a name other than its own must file a trade-name certificate with the Lieutenant Governor and cannot sue on that business until it does, and must renew the name every two, six or ten years (11 V.I.C. §§ 1201, 1203, 1212, 1213); a corporation cannot sue while its annual franchise tax is unpaid (13 V.I.C. § 533(a)); and an out-of-state LLC needs a certificate of authority before it can sue, because owning income-producing real property here counts as transacting business (13 V.I.C. §§ 2003(b), 2008(a)). If someone manages or leases the property for you for pay, that person generally needs a real estate broker's license; an owner managing its own property does not (`edu-no-nonresident-owner-agent-vi`). Short stays under 90 days also carry the hotel room tax (`hotel-room-tax-vi`). The territory has no counties or cities, so there is no local registration.

title: When a Virgin Islands Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Under the Virgin Islands statute of frauds, a contract to lease land for longer than one year from the time it is made is void unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party to be bound, or by that party's agent acting under written authority. A separate section adds that an interest in real property, other than under a lease for a term of one year or less, can be created, assigned, transferred or surrendered only by operation of law or by a signed writing (again by the party or an agent with written authority), so an assignment, or an agreed early surrender, of a lease longer than one year belongs in a signed writing too. A guaranty of the tenant's obligations must also be in a signed writing (`guaranty-vi`), as must any other agreement that cannot be performed within one year. An electronic signature satisfies the writing and signature rules if both parties agreed to deal electronically. A lease of one year or less may be oral, but put every lease in writing. The statute does not limit a court's power to order specific performance. Recording is separate from validity: the property title's definition of a conveyance includes any written instrument creating an interest in land, so a written lease that is acknowledged may be recorded with the Recorder of Deeds, and an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good-faith buyer who records first. Whether a tenant in possession is protected anyway is a case-law question not searched here; for a long lease, consider recording the lease or a memorandum of it.

title: Tenant Records and Data Security in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a residential landlord to keep a rent ledger, give one on request, attach one to a nonpayment notice or keep tenant files for a set time. Several rules still make good records essential. (1) Receipts: a business covered by the Payment Options law must offer a receipt for any payment of $5 or more, showing what was paid for, the amount, the date and the business's legal name and address (`edu-rent-receipts-vi`). (2) Eviction: if the rent-control subchapter applies (status unsettled), a nonpayment case needs proof that the rent claimed is no more than the tenant owed for the month before the default, so keep a running ledger. (3) Short stays: if you rent units for less than 90 days and owe the hotel room tax, you must keep separate books showing the taxable rents. (4) Data security: the territory's breach-notice law reaches any person or business doing business in the Virgin Islands that owns or licenses computerized data with personal information, which includes a landlord who keeps applicants' or tenants' names with Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, or bank or card numbers with access codes in a computer system unencrypted. If that data is acquired by an unauthorized person, you must notify each affected Virgin Islands resident without unreasonable delay, in writing or electronically (a police request may delay notice); a vendor or property manager holding the data for you must tell you immediately. Collect only what you need, encrypt or lock it, and shred it when no longer needed. Unclaimed deposit refunds are covered in `edu-deposit-escheat-vi`.

title: Firearms at a Virgin Islands Rental
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute protects a tenant's right to keep a firearm in a rental, makes a lease restriction on firearms unenforceable, protects a licensee from a landlord's rule, or bars a rule about firearms in vehicles in your parking area. Firearms are licensed and regulated under the territory's criminal and firearms laws, which bind the tenant whatever the lease says. Two of those rules matter at a rental: every firearm owner is responsible for storing the firearm safely (locked so it cannot be fired, or in a place only the licensed owner can reach), and it is unlawful to leave a firearm in a motor vehicle unless it is in an approved vehicle firearm lockbox, which applies in your parking area too.

A lease may therefore require tenants, occupants and guests to keep, carry and store firearms only as Virgin Islands and federal law allow (`firearm-rules-vi`). A landlord may also choose stricter rules, such as banning firearms in common areas; that is lawful as far as the Code shows, but apply any rule evenly, list it on the front-page "PLEASE READ THIS" statement, and take advice before banning lawful possession inside a tenant's own home.

title: Portable and Plug-In Solar Devices at a Virgin Islands Rental
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives a tenant an express right to install a plug-in, balcony or portable solar device. But the territory's renewable energy law makes void any covenant, condition or restriction in a deed, contract, mortgage or other instrument pertaining to a conveyance, sale or transfer of real property or an interest in it that prohibits or unreasonably limits installing or using a solar or wind energy system; a restriction is unreasonable if it raises the system's cost, lowers its efficiency or otherwise effectively discourages it. Whether a residential lease is such an instrument is unsettled. So do not refuse consent, or write lease rules, in a way that prohibits or unreasonably limits a tenant's solar or wind device; the library's alterations clause (`no-alterations`) carries a Virgin Islands note to the same effect. You may still set reasonable conditions: safe mounting, no roof penetration or building-wiring connection without your approval, removal before a hurricane, and restoration at move-out. Net metering is a separate matter: it is available only for a system on property the customer-generator owns, so a tenant generally cannot enroll a rental in net metering; a tenant's device can offset only the tenant's own use, and any connection to the grid needs your consent and the utility's.

title: Security Cameras and Video Doorbells at Virgin Islands Rentals
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives a tenant a right to install a security camera or video doorbell, or regulates landlord or tenant cameras at rentals as such. Installing one is a lease matter: a device fixed to the door or walls is an alteration that needs your consent (`no-alterations`); consider allowing battery or peel-and-stick doorbells on conditions (aimed only at the tenant's own entry, not into other units or windows, removed at move-out). Audio is the legal risk. The territory's electronic surveillance law makes it unlawful to use a device to capture the contents of a conversation the speakers reasonably expect not to be overheard, unless the person recording is a party to the conversation or one party has consented beforehand (and not for a criminal or wrongful purpose). Video alone is not covered by that law. So a doorbell that records the tenant's own conversations at the door is generally lawful, but one that picks up neighbors' private conversations in a hallway may not be; ask tenants to turn audio off where the device covers shared areas. Do not install cameras that view inside a tenant's home, and do not record audio in common areas; watching a tenant's home without consent can also violate the tenant's right to quiet possession (`edu-landlord-entry-vi`).

title: No Accessory Dwelling Unit Law in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute deals with accessory dwelling units (a second, smaller home on the same lot, such as a cottage, in-law apartment or apartment over a garage): nothing requires that one be allowed, protects its rental, or requires the owner to live on the lot. The territory has no city or county governments that could pass their own rules; zoning is set territory-wide by the Virgin Islands Zoning Law and administered by the Department of Planning and Natural Resources. That law allows one- and two-family dwellings as of right in its low-density residential districts and treats an ordinary residential accessory building (garage, laundry room, garden shelter) as one not used for a business. Its accessory-use section expressly allows extra buildings for housing tenants or employees only in the agricultural districts, in addition to the main building: up to one in the A-2 district and up to three in the A-1 district. Elsewhere, an accessory use must be on the same lot, subordinate and customarily incidental to the main use, and must not change the character of that use, so a second rental dwelling depends on what your district's table of permitted uses allows (for example, a two-family dwelling where two-family dwellings are permitted). Before renting a second unit on your lot: (1) confirm with the Department of Planning and Natural Resources that your zoning district allows it and how many units it allows; (2) get the building permit the Building Code requires, because the Housing Code forbids renting any building for living, sleeping or cooking that does not meet the Building Code and the Housing Code's own standards; (3) check whether your total number of rental units requires a business license; and (4) make sure the unit has its own kitchen sink, toilet, washbasin and tub or shower and meets the space standards.

title: No Limit on Renting Homes in Residential Zones in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute limits renting out a home in a single-family or other residential zone, and none requires the owner to live on the lot before renting it. The territory-wide Zoning Law regulates how land is used (for example, one- and two-family dwellings are allowed as of right in the low-density residential districts), not whether the occupants own or rent. There are no city or county ordinances in the territory. Two nearby rules matter: a building with more than five guest rooms rented to guests is a hotel or guesthouse under the Zoning Law, which is a separate use with its own district rules, and short stays are subject to hotel room tax (see `hotel-room-tax-vi`); and a landlord may need a business license depending on the number of units (see `edu-no-adu-statute-vi`). Condominium and homeowners' association documents can restrict rentals; check them before signing a lease (see `edu-hoa-vi`).

title: No Smoke or Carbon Monoxide Alarm Tampering Fee Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText:
No Virgin Islands statute sets a fee, fine or charge for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and the Virgin Islands Code has no smoke or carbon monoxide alarm statute at all; alarm requirements for buildings come from the international building codes the territory adopts by reference. The library's optional `detector-care-la` clause lets your lease require the tenant to keep alarms working, test them and not disable them.

If a tenant damages or removes an alarm, charge the actual, documented cost of repair or replacement rather than a fixed "tampering fee": no statute authorizes a preset amount, and a flat charge unrelated to your actual loss risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty, a question the Virgin Islands courts decide case by case. Recover unpaid amounts in a separate civil action or small claims, not in an eviction case.

title: No Asbestos Rule for Rental Housing in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a residential landlord to inspect for, disclose or abate asbestos, or to notify tenants before work that disturbs it. The only mentions of asbestos in the Virgin Islands Code are old fire-code construction details and a zoning listing for the sale and storage of asbestos products. Federal rules still apply to work on buildings: the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's asbestos rules govern renovation and demolition, and federal workplace-safety rules protect workers. If you plan renovation, repair or demolition in an older building, have suspect materials tested by a qualified inspector before work starts, use contractors who follow federal asbestos work practices, and tell tenants about work that could disturb asbestos. If you know of damaged asbestos in a unit, fix it or tell the applicant before signing: hiding a known hazard can expose you to liability (see `edu-no-contamination-disclosure-vi`).

title: No Balcony or Deck Inspection Schedule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires periodic inspections, engineering reports or repair deadlines for balconies, decks, galleries, exterior stairways or other elevated parts of rental buildings. Your general duties cover them. Under the Housing Code the owner must keep every stair, porch and other appurtenance in good repair and able to carry its designed loads, and must keep windows and exterior doors weathertight and in good working order; the Housing Code reaches dwellings, hotels, apartment houses, apartments and rooming houses and their appurtenances (owner-occupied rural homes under 600 square feet are excluded). The Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority enforces it by inspection, written notice and orders, with fines after conviction. New work and alterations must meet the Building Code. Inspect balconies and decks after every hurricane or tropical storm and at least yearly, fix rot, rust and loose railings promptly, and close an unsafe balcony until it is repaired.

title: Steam Radiator Covers: Not Applicable in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires radiator covers, a lease rider about them, or steam heat in rental housing. Homes in the territory are not heated by steam radiators, and the Housing Code sets no heating standard (see `edu-heating-na-vi`). The only radiator rules in the Virgin Islands Code concern heating pipes in dry-cleaning plants and vehicle warranties. If a unit has any exposed heating or hot-water equipment, keep it guarded and in good repair under your general Housing Code duties.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to set a water heater to a maximum temperature, or to reset it before a new tenant moves in. The Virgin Islands Code mentions water heaters only in solar-energy and housing-program provisions. The Housing Code makes the owner responsible for the care and maintenance of each unit's plumbing system, and the plumbing and energy codes the territory adopts by reference (which we did not review) govern installation. Cautious course: set a unit's water heater to a safe setting (many safety authorities recommend about 120°F) at each turnover, keep the relief valve working, and tell tenants not to raise the setting.

title: No Window Guard Rule in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires window guards or a window-guard notice in a lease. The Building Code instead protects emergency escape: for new construction and conversions, jalousie-style windows and openings must meet the Building Code's rules for emergency escape and rescue openings and for wind-borne debris protection, and every habitable room must have a window or skylight that opens. The Housing Code requires the owner to keep every window weathertight and in good working order. If you add guards, grilles or burglar bars, use a type that opens from inside without a key or tool so a sleeping room keeps its emergency escape opening, and consider guards or stops on upper-floor windows in units where young children live.

title: No Residential Pool Safety Statute in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a residential landlord to fence a pool, install a gate or alarm, post rules, give a pool-safety notice at signing, or provide a lifeguard. The Virgin Islands Code mentions swimming pools only in zoning provisions and a drug-free-zone penalty. Pool construction is governed by the international codes the territory adopts by reference, which we did not review, and any Department of Health rules for public pools sit in the Rules and Regulations, which we could not search. Your liability for an injury at a pool rests on general negligence and premises-liability law decided by the Virgin Islands courts. Cautious course: keep a self-closing, self-latching barrier around the pool, post rules and depth markings, keep rescue equipment and the water chemistry in order, and put your pool rules in writing (see `rules-ia`).

title: Fire and Building Codes That Apply to Virgin Islands Rentals
bodyText: Virgin Islands fire and building safety rules come from two places. (1) The Virgin Islands Building Code (Title 29, chapter 5), rewritten in 2024, adopts by reference the 2018 International Building Code (for apartment buildings and other buildings), the 2018 International Residential Code (for one- and two-family homes and townhouses up to three stories) and the 2018 International Energy Conservation Code, each with Virgin Islands amendments, and each later edition takes effect six months after it is published. The Building Code also names the International Fire Code among the codes it relies on, and public housing projects of 30 or more units must have water lines and fire hydrants meeting the International Fire Code and NFPA standards. (2) The Fire Prevention Code (Title 23, chapter 9) applies to new and existing conditions; an existing condition that does not strictly comply may continue only if it is not a distinct hazard to life or neighboring property. The use and occupancy of buildings must follow nationally recognized fire-safety practice, and complying with the National Fire Protection Association's fire prevention code (the 1999 edition and any later edition) counts as evidence of that for matters the chapter does not cover. The fire service director may issue fire-prevention regulations for all places, including homes, which have the force of law once approved by the Governor and published; we could not search those regulations. The construction code has not moved to a new title. The Housing Code separately forbids renting a dwelling that does not meet the Building Code. Keep exits, stairways and hallways clear, keep fire-protection equipment the fire service requires in working order, and get permits for alterations.

title: No Fire Sprinkler Retrofit Duty in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to add fire sprinklers to an existing rental building. For one- and two-family homes and townhouses, the territory's 2024 Building Code amendments delete the International Residential Code's automatic sprinkler requirement, so new homes of that kind do not need sprinklers; where sprinklers are installed anyway, the cistern or well feeding them must meet the NFPA 13D water-supply standard. Apartment buildings and other buildings fall under the International Building Code and the International Fire Code, which set sprinkler requirements for new construction and some alterations; we did not review those model codes. If your building has sprinklers, keep them inspected and working, keep the water supply reserved for them, and do not let tenants hang items from or paint sprinkler heads. Nothing requires a sprinkler disclosure in the lease (see `edu-no-sprinkler-disclosure-vi`).

title: Building Code Editions Update Automatically in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands Building Code is not frozen at a fixed edition. It adopts the 2018 International Building, Residential and Energy Conservation Codes "and any subsequent editions or amendments thereto", and each later edition becomes effective six months after the International Code Council publishes it; the Commissioner of Planning and Natural Resources must publish notice of a new edition at least three months before it takes effect, and may adopt Virgin Islands amendments by rule. The adopted codes apply to new and existing buildings, and an existing building that is enlarged, altered or reconstructed must meet the rules for new buildings to the extent 29 V.I.C. § 310 requires (the whole building when the work or damage exceeds 50 percent of its value, only the altered portions at 25 to 50 percent, and same-strength, same-fire-resistance materials below that; but repairs after a hurricane or other natural disaster that destroys the building, and repairs of any damage that substantially affects its structural integrity, such as the roof or foundations, so that it is unsafe or unfit for occupancy, must meet the adopted codes whatever the cost). Other references are open-ended too: the Fire Prevention Code treats compliance with the 1999 or any later edition of the National Fire Protection Association fire prevention code as evidence of safe practice, and the interconnection between the electric utility and a qualifying cogeneration or small power production facility must conform to the latest edition of the National Electric Code. What this means for you: the edition in force can change during a lease, so check the current edition and any published Virgin Islands amendments with the Department of Planning and Natural Resources before construction or alteration work, and keep records of the code your building was permitted under.

title: Children and Occupancy Limits in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a lease to say anything about children living in the unit. Two sets of rules apply. (1) Occupancy standards: the Housing Code requires at least 150 square feet of habitable floor area for the first occupant, 100 more for each of the next three and 75 more for each additional occupant, and in a bedroom shared by more than one person at least 50 square feet for each occupant 12 or older and 35 square feet for each occupant under 12 (a bedroom for one person needs 80 square feet). A unit with more people sleeping in it than these standards allow is overcrowded and rented in violation of the Housing Code. (2) Discrimination: Virgin Islands law bars housing discrimination because of age, among other grounds, and the federal Fair Housing Act bars discrimination against families with children under 18 (familial status). Virgin Islands law has no separate familial-status ground. So: base any occupancy limit on the Housing Code standards and the unit's size, apply it the same way to every household, count children under 12 at the smaller sleeping-room figure, and never refuse, charge more or set different rules because a household includes children (no "adults only" terms unless the property qualifies as federal housing for older persons). List every occupant, adults and children, in the lease (see `edu-permitted-occupants-vi`).

title: Casualty and Mitigation Terms Are Left to the Lease in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: Some places have statutory rules on fire or hurricane damage (who may end the lease, rent reductions) and on a landlord's duty to re-rent after a tenant leaves early, and say whether a lease may change them. The Virgin Islands has neither: no statute sets casualty rights (see `edu-no-casualty-statute-vi`) and none sets a duty to mitigate (see `edu-no-mitigation-statute-vi`), so no statute says whether they can be waived. The lease therefore governs casualty, and the library offers an optional casualty clause that keeps rent fair for the period the home cannot be used (`casualty-termination-vi`). Mitigation is a common-law question for the Virgin Islands courts; the library does not offer a clause waiving any duty you may have to re-rent, because many courts refuse to enforce such waivers in residential leases, and the cautious course is to make reasonable, documented efforts to re-rent and credit what you receive. Two statutory limits apply whatever the lease says: a domestic-violence victim who ends the lease under the statute owes no termination fee and no damages for later damage to the unit, and the Housing Code's repair duties cannot be shifted by the lease. Any casualty or mitigation term that restricts the tenant's rights must be highlighted on the lease's "PLEASE READ THIS" front page.

title: Rights a Virgin Islands Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no residential landlord-tenant act, so there is no single list of tenant rights a lease may not waive. Instead, particular statutes make particular rights non-waivable or override lease terms: (1) a tenant cannot waive the right to call police or other emergency help in a domestic-violence situation, and no lease may let you end the tenancy or impose a penalty for such calls; (2) a lease cannot waive the tenant's rights under the plain-language consumer contracts law, which covers residential leases; (3) any waiver or modification of rights under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices law is void; (4) a lease term restricting use or occupancy because of race, creed, color or national origin is void, and lease terms that discriminate on any protected ground are unlawful; (5) a no-pets clause does not apply to a blind tenant's dog guide, and no extra charge may be made for it; (6) a tenant who agreed to transact electronically may still refuse further electronic transactions, and that right cannot be waived. Beyond these, the Housing Code's repair and maintenance duties are public-law duties a lease cannot shift (see `edu-no-habitability-waiver-rule-vi`), and statutory steps such as the written notice to quit are conditions of the court case, not something a lease can dispense with (see `edu-notice-to-quit-waiver-vi`). Whether other common-law rights can be waived is for the Virgin Islands courts; draft waivers narrowly, and list each on the lease's "PLEASE READ THIS" front page.

title: Lease Terms Virgin Islands Law Forbids or Limits
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no statute that lists, in one place, the terms a residential lease may not contain; the only section headed "prohibited provisions" for leases is the domestic-violence rule. Terms that Virgin Islands statutes forbid or override: (1) a term letting you end the lease or penalize the tenant for calling police or emergency help in a domestic-violence situation, or charging a fee when a victim ends the lease under the statute; (2) any term that discriminates because of race, creed, age, color, national origin, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability or political affiliation, and any use restriction based on race, creed, color or national origin, which is void; (3) a no-pets rule applied to a blind tenant's dog guide, or an extra charge for it; (4) a term forbidding cable television, charging to allow its installation, or charging more rent to tenants who have it (reasonable installation conditions are allowed); (5) penalizing a tenant solely for being a registered medical cannabis patient, unless federal law requires it; (6) a waiver of plain-language or consumer-fraud rights; (7) sewer charges beyond the actual fee attributable to the unit, and water or electricity charges not based on the tenant's own use (see `edu-utility-meter-vi`). No statute bans confession-of-judgment, jury-waiver, exculpatory, indemnity, attorney's-fee or penalty clauses in leases, but each is limited in other ways: see `edu-confession-of-judgment-vi`, `edu-jury-waiver-vi`, `edu-exculpatory-clauses-vi`, `edu-attorney-fees-vi` and `edu-no-eviction-penalty-rule-vi`. No statute voids a lease for when it was delivered, bars passing a home-warranty deductible to the tenant, or bars repair fees for damage the tenant did not cause; those are contract and common-law questions, and the Consumer Protection Law forbids deceptive statements. Every term that restricts the tenant's rights or protects you must be highlighted on the "PLEASE READ THIS" front page.

title: No Special Penalty for Using a Prohibited Lease Term in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute imposes a special money penalty on a landlord for putting a prohibited term in a lease or knowingly using such a lease. Other statutes make bad terms costly, though: (1) a lessor whose lease does not comply with the plain-language law is liable for the tenant's actual damages plus punitive damages up to $1,000 and the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees and costs (punitive damages in a class action are capped at $10,000 per lessor), although a lessor who tried in good faith to comply has defenses; (2) a person who suffers a loss from a deceptive or unconscionable trade practice may recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, and the Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs may impose administrative fines of up to $5,000 per violation; (3) a discriminatory term exposes you to compensatory and punitive damages and mandatory attorney's fees, and, for race, creed, color or national origin, punitive damages of up to $5,000 per violation plus criminal fines; (4) interfering with a blind tenant's dog-guide rights is a misdemeanor with a fine of $500 to $1,000. Knowingly leasing property for prostitution is a crime. Review your lease for prohibited terms before using it (see `edu-prohibited-lease-terms-vi`).

title: No Statute on Eviction Penalty Clauses in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute specifically voids a lease clause that charges the tenant a penalty or fee because you served a notice, filed an eviction case or won one. Other rules reach most such clauses. (1) The court fees and costs of an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) case are fixed by statute at a total of $2.00. (2) The eviction judgment gives possession only: rent, fees and damages must be claimed in a separate civil action or in small claims. (3) In a civil action the court, not the lease, decides how much the winner recovers toward attorney's fees, and it works both ways (see `edu-attorney-fees-vi`). (4) A fixed "eviction fee" or similar charge unrelated to your actual loss risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty under common law (see `edu-no-liquidated-damages-rule-vi` and `edu-no-notice-service-fee-rule-vi`). (5) You may not penalize a tenant for calling police or emergency help in a domestic-violence situation, or charge a fee when a victim ends the lease under the statute. The library therefore includes no eviction-fee clause; recover your actual, documented costs through the court.

title: Exculpatory and Indemnity Clauses in Virgin Islands Leases
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says whether a residential lease may excuse the landlord from liability for its own negligence (an exculpatory clause) or make the tenant indemnify the landlord for the landlord's own fault, and none voids such terms. Whether a court would enforce one is a common-law question for the Virgin Islands courts, and many courts refuse to enforce these terms in residential leases. The library takes the cautious course: its Virgin Islands clauses do not disclaim your liability for your own negligence or that of your agents (for example, the tenant's-property insurance, parking, storage and services clauses the library uses for the territory). A tenant may still be made responsible for damage the tenant, household members or guests cause. Three rules apply whatever the lease says: the Housing Code repair duties stay with the owner; the tenant's rights under the plain-language law cannot be waived; and any term that limits your liability is a provision designed for your protection that must be highlighted on the lease's "PLEASE READ THIS" front page. If you want a broader liability limit, have a Virgin Islands lawyer draft it and list it on the front page.

title: A Virgin Islands Lease Cannot Waive Housing Code Standards
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute lets a written agreement remove a habitability requirement or lets a tenant accept stated defects in exchange for lower rent, and there is no separate-document rule. The Housing Code's standards are public-law duties: no one may rent a building for living, sleeping or cooking that does not meet the Building Code and the Housing Code, the owner is responsible for the building's plumbing, roof, structure, wiring and shared areas, and the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority enforces those duties whatever the lease says. A lease may restate the tenant's own Housing Code duties (keeping the tenant's part clean, safe and sanitary, disposing of garbage properly and using plumbing fixtures with reasonable care). For details see `edu-no-habitability-waiver-rule-vi`.

title: Jury Trial Waivers in Virgin Islands Leases
bodyText: The federal constitutional right to a civil jury applies in the Virgin Islands through the Revised Organic Act. In a landlord-tenant dispute it matters in the separate civil action for rent or damages, where either side may ask for a jury; the eviction (forcible entry and detainer) case itself is an equitable case for possession that may be tried without a jury. No Virgin Islands statute addresses a jury-trial waiver in a lease or other standard-form contract: none makes it void or presumptively unconscionable, and none requires a separate signed writing. Whether a court would enforce a pre-dispute jury waiver in a residential lease is a question for the Virgin Islands courts, and courts commonly require that a waiver of a constitutional right be knowing and voluntary (Virgin Islands case law was not searched for this library). A jury waiver restricts the tenant's rights, so it would have to be highlighted on the lease's "PLEASE READ THIS" front page. The library does not offer a jury-waiver clause: its enforceability is uncertain, the money claims it would affect are often small claims anyway, and an unenforceable waiver invites a dispute. A landlord who wants one should have a Virgin Islands lawyer draft it as a separate, conspicuous, mutual term and list it on the front page.

title: Confession of Judgment and Virgin Islands Leases
bodyText: A lease clause in which the tenant authorizes you or a lawyer to confess a judgment against the tenant in advance (a "cognovit" or warrant of attorney) does not work in the Virgin Islands. Virgin Islands law allows a judgment by confession only on the defendant's own written confession: in a pending case the confession must be made by the defendant in person (or, for a corporation, by an officer who could accept service), signed and acknowledged and filed with the clerk; without a case, the confession must also be sworn, must be for a particular sum, and must state plainly the facts showing that the sum is justly due or will become due. A lease clause that authorizes you or a lawyer to confess judgment for amounts not yet known cannot meet these requirements, and a judgment for possession cannot be confessed outside a pending case (the no-case procedure covers only money): possession is recovered only through a court case (normally an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) case), in which a tenant may confess judgment only after the case is filed. Statutes ban confession clauses in consumer loans, debt-management agreements and rent-to-own agreements for goods, and no court rule provides for confessed ejectment. If a tenant later admits a specific debt, a confession that meets the statute, or a negotiated payment agreement, is possible; have a lawyer prepare it. The library offers no confession-of-judgment clause.

title: Unconscionability and Virgin Islands Leases
bodyText: Virgin Islands law addresses unconscionability in three ways that can touch a lease. (1) The Consumer Protection Law forbids unconscionable trade practices in the lease or rental of consumer goods or services, meaning practices that unfairly take advantage of a consumer's lack of knowledge, ability, experience or capacity or produce a gross disparity between value and price; but a practice counts only if Virgin Islands law or a consumer-affairs regulation declares it unconscionable with reasonable particularity, and whether a home rental is a consumer "good or service" is unsettled. In an action by the consumer affairs director, the court may strike or limit unconscionable contract clauses. (2) Under the plain-language law a violation does not void a lease or give the tenant a defense unless enforcing the noncomplying lease would be unconscionable. (3) The general common-law doctrine lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable contract or term; the Virgin Islands courts decide how it applies to leases. The Uniform Commercial Code's unconscionability sections cover sales and leases of goods, not housing. No Virgin Islands statute declares any particular lease clause unconscionable or, the other way, fully enforceable, and none lets a court revise a running lease because circumstances made it excessively burdensome. Keep terms balanced, avoid one-sided fees and waivers, and explain unusual terms to the tenant.

title: Virgin Islands Consumer Protection Laws and Residential Leases
bodyText: Two Virgin Islands consumer statutes may reach your leasing. (1) The Consumer Protection Law of 1973 forbids deceptive or unconscionable trade practices in the lease or rental of consumer goods or services (for example, misrepresenting a unit's features, failing to state a material fact if that misleads, or saying a lease gives rights or remedies it does not). Whether a residential tenancy is a lease of consumer "goods or services" is not settled. A consumer who suffers a loss may recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater (outside a class action), and the court may award attorney's fees, and the Department of Licensing and Consumer Affairs may impose fines of up to $5,000 per violation. (2) The Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices law forbids unfair or deceptive acts in any trade or commerce, which it defines to include dealing in real property; it allows consumer class actions with trebled damages, and any waiver of its rights is void. Neither law lists leaving blank spaces in a contract or failing to give the consumer a copy at signing as a specific violation (rules like that appear only for insurance premium finance agreements). Cautious course: treat every advertisement, listing, application and lease statement as covered; fill in every blank before the tenant signs; give the tenant a signed copy; and do not claim rights or fees the law does not give you. The plain-language law also covers residential leases (see `edu-plain-language-vi`).

title: Tenant’s Right to Call for Police or Emergency Help in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: A residential lease in the Virgin Islands may not let you end the lease or impose a penalty on a tenant for calling the police or other emergency help in response to a domestic-violence or domestic-abuse situation, and a tenant cannot waive the right to make those calls. The statute speaks only of domestic-violence situations, but the safe practice is broader: do not write or enforce any nuisance, disturbance, criminal-activity or "excessive calls" term so that it counts a tenant's or household member's calls for police, fire or medical help against them. You may still act on a tenant's own unrelated lease violations, and you may seek possession against the person who committed the violence (see `edu-dv-eviction-protection-vi`). The library's criminal-activity clause for the territory excludes victims and calls for help.

title: No Statutory Confidentiality Rule for Tenants’ Domestic-Violence Information in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires a landlord to keep confidential the information a tenant gives about domestic violence (such as the police report a victim provides to end the lease early), limits how you may use it, or sets up an address-confidentiality program you must honor. Related rules: a victim who ends the lease under the domestic-violence statute must give you a police report written within the previous 90 days; in a domestic-violence case the court waives any requirement that the victim's home address appear on the complaint; and the court may give a victim possession of a jointly leased home and order the abuser out, without changing either party's interest in the home. Cautious course: keep domestic-violence information and reports in a separate, secure file; share them only with people who need them to handle the tenancy or as the law requires; never disclose them, or the victim's new address, to the other household members or the alleged abuser; and follow any court order you are given.

title: Fair Housing Law in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: Virgin Islands civil-rights law makes it unlawful for an owner, lessor, sublessor, managing agent or their employees to refuse to rent, to set different terms, conditions, privileges, facilities or services, or to advertise or use application forms or inquiries that express a limitation, because of race, creed, age, color, national origin, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability or political affiliation. Discrimination because of sex includes sexual harassment. These grounds go beyond federal law (age, sexual orientation, gender identity and political affiliation are added), but Virgin Islands law has no familial-status, marital-status or source-of-income ground; the federal Fair Housing Act separately protects families with children and also applies in the territory. A separate, older chapter bars anyone in the business of selling, leasing or renting houses or apartments from denying a lease because of race (including hair texture and protective hairstyles such as braids, locks and twists), creed, color or national origin, with no small-landlord exemption, and makes a violation a crime with punitive damages of up to $5,000 for each violation; that chapter also bars discrimination against members of the Virgin Islands National Guard. Blind persons with dog guides have their own housing rights, and you may not refuse to lease to someone solely because they are a registered medical cannabis patient. It is also unlawful to retaliate against anyone who complains or takes part in a civil-rights proceeding, or to aid or coerce discrimination. A person discriminated against may sue for compensatory and punitive damages, and the court must award the person's attorney's fees and costs; the Civil Rights Commission may also investigate sworn complaints and order you to stop. The exemptions are covered in `edu-fair-housing-exemptions-vi`.

title: Fair Housing Exemptions and Advertising in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The main Virgin Islands housing-discrimination rule does not apply to: (1) renting a unit in a building with housing for no more than two families living independently, if the owner or a member of the owner's family lives in one of them; (2) restricting all rooms in a housing accommodation to people of the same sex; or (3) renting rooms in a home where the renting occupant, or the owner and the owner's family, live. A religious or denominational organization, or a charity it controls, may limit or give preference in renting its housing to people of the same religion. Unlike federal law, the Virgin Islands exemptions cover the whole rule, including its advertising and application-form ban, so an exempt owner-occupant is not bound by the territory's advertising ban. But the exemptions are narrower than they look: (a) the federal Fair Housing Act's ban on discriminatory advertising applies even to exempt owners; (b) real estate brokers and salespeople get no exemption; (c) owners and agents of publicly assisted housing get none; (d) the older civil-rights chapter barring race, creed, color and national-origin discrimination by anyone in the business of renting real estate has no owner-occupant exemption; and (e) the blind-tenant dog-guide rule applies to all housing offered for rent. Write every advertisement and application without any preference or limitation, even if you think an exemption applies.

title: Real Estate Brokers, Appraisers and Discrimination in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: If you use a licensed real estate broker or salesperson to rent or manage your property, the civil-rights law binds them with no exemption: they may not refuse to rent or to negotiate, say a unit is unavailable when it is available, or advertise or use forms or inquiries expressing a limitation, because of race, creed, age, color, national origin, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability or political affiliation, even where you as an owner-occupant of a small building would be exempt. The territory's licensing law for real estate appraisers separately lets the appraiser board discipline an appraiser whose appraisal work shows a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status or national origin; that rule covers appraisals only, not renting or property management. No Virgin Islands statute bars discrimination against families with children in renting; the federal Fair Housing Act does, and it binds you and your broker or manager. Tell your broker or manager in writing to follow the civil-rights law and the federal Fair Housing Act, and do not ask them to steer or screen out any applicant.

title: Questions and Records About Protected Characteristics in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: Virgin Islands law limits what you may ask applicants and record about them. For most housing, it is unlawful to use an application form, or to make any record or inquiry in connection with a prospective rental, that expresses directly or indirectly any limitation, specification or discrimination as to race, creed, age, color, national origin, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability or political affiliation (the small owner-occupied exemptions apply to this rule; see `edu-fair-housing-exemptions-vi`). For publicly assisted housing the rule is stricter: an owner or agent may not make any written or oral inquiry or record at all concerning those characteristics of a person seeking to rent. Brokers and salespeople are bound with no exemption. Practical steps: do not ask about religion, national origin, birthplace, sexual orientation, political party, disability or health; ask about age only to confirm the applicant is an adult able to sign the lease; if you need information to respond to a disability accommodation request, ask only what is needed for that request; and if a government program requires demographic data, keep it separate from the decision file.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection in Virgin Islands Housing Law
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute forbids refusing to rent because an applicant pays with a housing voucher or other public assistance, requires you to accept vouchers, or requires a lease statement about them. Source of income is not among the grounds in the territory's housing-discrimination law. You may therefore decide whether to take part in a voucher program, but three cautions apply: (1) if you do accept vouchers, your program contract and federal rules govern the lease and the tenancy; (2) a blanket "no vouchers" policy can be challenged under federal fair housing law if it falls disproportionately on a protected group, or if it is used as a cover for refusing people because of disability, race or another protected ground; and (3) owners of publicly assisted housing are bound by the stricter civil-rights rules for that housing and by their funding terms. Apply the same income and screening standards to every applicant, counting a voucher's payment toward the rent.

title: No Rule on Refusing Voucher Program Inspections in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute addresses refusing to rent because a housing-assistance program requires an inspection of the unit, or sets a deadline for program approval. Because Virgin Islands law has no source-of-income protection (see `edu-no-source-of-income-protection-vi`), declining a program's inspection is not itself unlawful under territorial law. If you take part in a voucher program, the program's federal rules and your contract require the unit to pass the program's inspection before assistance is paid; cooperate with it as you would with any condition of the tenancy. Never use an inspection requirement as a pretext for refusing someone because of a protected characteristic.

title: No Immigration-Status Rule for Virgin Islands Landlords
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute bars a landlord from asking about an applicant's immigration or citizenship status, requires a landlord to check it, protects tenants from disclosure of it, or makes it unlawful to rent to a person who is not lawfully present. National origin, however, is a protected ground under Virgin Islands civil-rights law and federal fair housing law, and questions about citizenship or immigration can be evidence of national-origin discrimination. Cautious course: ask every applicant for the same identification and screening information, accept a range of identity documents (passport, driver's license, other government ID), and do not ask about immigration status unless a government housing program you take part in requires it, and then ask everyone in the same way. Federal immigration law has a harboring offense; whether ordinarily renting to someone can fall within it depends on federal law and court decisions we did not review.

title: No Sex-Offender Residency or Occupancy Rule for Virgin Islands Landlords
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute bars a registered sex offender from living within a set distance of a school, child-care center or other place, makes it a crime to rent a dwelling where registered offenders live together, or requires a landlord to check the registry or give a lease statement. The territory's sex offender registration law puts duties on the offender (registering and updating the address where the offender lives) and on owners and operators of child-care and child-residential facilities (background checks of staff), not on landlords; but anyone, a landlord included, who knowingly harbors an offender who is violating the registration law, helps one elude police, or gives police information about one that he knows is false commits a crime. If you screen applicants using registry information, apply the same written criteria to everyone and consider the individual circumstances (see `edu-tenant-screening-vi`). Federally assisted housing has its own federal admission bar for lifetime registrants. Nothing requires you to tell other tenants about a registrant (see `edu-no-sex-offender-disclosure-vi`).

title: Tenant Screening Rules in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: The Virgin Islands has no tenant-screening statute: none limits criminal-history checks or sets look-back periods, requires a conditional offer before a background check, limits minimum-income tests, regulates screening fees or screening companies, or shields a landlord from negligence claims for renting to someone with a record. The rules that do apply: (1) Virgin Islands civil-rights law forbids screening criteria, application forms or inquiries that express a limitation based on a protected ground (see `edu-protected-class-inquiry-vi`); (2) a person whose record has been expunged is treated as never having been arrested, and expunged marijuana-offense records may not be disclosed under any law, so do not ask about or rely on expunged records (the library's `rental-application-accuracy-la` clause excludes them); (3) federal law: if you deny, require a co-signer or extra deposit, or charge more because of a consumer report, you must give the applicant an adverse-action notice, and reports generally may not include most adverse items older than seven years; and federal fair housing guidance warns that blanket criminal-record bans can be discriminatory. Use written criteria, apply them to everyone, look at the nature and age of any offense, and count all of the household's lawful income, including any housing assistance, when applying an income test.

title: No Tenant-Information Privacy Statute in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute specifically bars a landlord from disclosing a tenant's or applicant's personal information, or sets the consent needed to share it. Two nearby rules matter. First, the territory's security-breach law requires any person or business that conducts business in the Virgin Islands and owns or licenses computerized personal information to notify each affected Virgin Islands resident, as quickly as possible and without unreasonable delay, of a breach in which the resident's unencrypted personal information was or is reasonably believed to have been taken by an unauthorized person. "Personal information" means a person's first name or initial and last name together with a Social Security number, driver's license number, or financial account or card number with the code that gives access to the account. A landlord keeping applicant or tenant files with that information on a computer is covered; a property manager or vendor holding your data must tell you immediately of a breach. Notice may be written, electronic (if it meets the federal E-SIGN rules) or, in large cases, substitute notice; law enforcement may ask you to delay it. Second, a real estate licensee acting for both landlord and tenant must disclose information each needs to make informed decisions. Cautious course: collect only the information you need, keep applications, Social Security numbers, bank and income records and domestic-violence information secure, share them only with people who need them for the tenancy or as the law requires, get the tenant's written consent before giving information to anyone else (for example a prospective landlord), and dispose of old files securely.

title: No Employee-Housing Statute in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute governs housing a landlord provides to an employee (a caretaker, property manager or worker living on the property): none requires a signed disclosure of the occupancy terms, an offer of a rental agreement when the job ends, or a special notice period. Whether such an occupant is a tenant or a licensee whose right to stay ends with the job is a common-law question for the Virgin Islands courts. The eviction statute reaches any "person in possession" who stays after a notice to quit at the end of the agreement, contrary to it, or without a written agreement, so an employee who will not leave is removed through the court, never by lockout. Cautious course: put the housing terms in a written agreement separate from (or attached to) the employment agreement, saying whether any rent is charged, that the right to occupy ends a stated number of days after employment ends, and how notice will be given; then serve a written notice to quit and, if needed, file an eviction case, allowing at least 30 days' notice (see `edu-termination-notice-vi`). Wage and labor rules may limit charging housing against wages.

title: No Tenant Organizing Statute for Private Housing in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives tenants of private housing a right to form or join a tenants' association, meet in common areas, or distribute materials, or forbids a landlord from interfering with organizing. Territorial law mentions tenant organizations only for public housing (government assistance to public-housing tenant organizations seeking tenant management, and tenant-resident groups in homeownership conversions). The territory also has no general anti-retaliation statute for tenants; the civil-rights law forbids retaliation only for complaining about or opposing discrimination (see `edu-retaliation-vi`). Cautious course: do not penalize tenants for organizing or for lawful complaints, and apply common-area rules evenly, because a court could treat retaliation as bad faith and because a group complaint may involve fair housing rights.

title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute gives private landlords a tax credit, payment, deposit guarantee or other incentive for renting to veterans. Territorial veterans' housing programs run through the Virgin Islands Housing Finance Authority and help veterans buy, build or improve homes (land for sale to veterans, loan assistance and home construction and improvement loans), and veterans are among the priority groups for some affordable-housing sales and rentals. Veteran status is not among the grounds in the territory's civil-rights law, so a preference or discount for veterans is not itself barred, provided it is offered evenly and not used as a cover for preferring a protected group. Members of the Virgin Islands National Guard are protected from discrimination in renting, and servicemembers have federal rights to end a lease on military orders (see `edu-servicemember-rights-vi`).

title: No Statutory Hunting or Fishing Rights for Tenants in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute says whether a tenant of rented farmland (or of a home) has hunting or fishing rights on the property unless the owner grants them in writing. The lease decides; if it is silent, the question falls to common law. Virgin Islands law does treat farm leases differently in two ways: a notice to quit a farming or agricultural tenancy must be served six months before an eviction case (rather than three days), and after a farm lease ends the tenant may come back to cultivate and harvest crops planted before the notice to quit. The territory's wildlife laws (hunting licenses, seasons and protected species) apply to anyone who hunts. If you rent land with hunting or fishing potential, say in the lease whether the tenant may hunt or fish, and whether you reserve those rights for yourself or others.

title: No Foreign-Ownership or Foreign-Tenant Restriction in the Virgin Islands
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute bars foreign persons, foreign governments or "foreign adversaries" from buying or leasing real property, voids a lease to them, or requires a lease to state that a tenant is a nonresident alien. The Virgin Islands statute of frauds has no such requirement. One territorial rule concerns foreign companies: an alien corporation that wants to acquire personal or real property of record in the territory must first have a registered office and registered agent there and must file a sworn annual report with the Lieutenant Governor; until it complies it may not own, buy or sell property or sue or defend in Virgin Islands courts. That is a registration requirement, not a ban, and it concerns acquiring property of record; an ordinary unrecorded residential lease is unlikely to be affected, but if you rent to a foreign corporation, ask whether it has registered. Refusing to rent to someone, or setting different terms, because of national origin is unlawful under Virgin Islands civil-rights law and federal fair housing law, so do not screen applicants by nationality or citizenship.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: The U.S. Virgin Islands follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (11A V.I.C. § 3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (11A V.I.C. § 1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: The U.S. Virgin Islands' landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (28 V.I.C. ch. 31 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how the U.S. Virgin Islands' courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: No Communal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: The Virgin Islands have no communal, tribal or native land system, and no Virgin Islands statute requires a government officer to approve a residential lease, or voids it, because of how the land is held. A search of the whole Virgin Islands Code for communal, tribal, tribe, native land and ancestral land near lease, lessee or rent found nothing. Land leased from the Government of the Virgin Islands is governed by its own lease and statutes.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: No Virgin Islands statute requires you to record a residential lease. Recording matters for priority. Every conveyance of real property in the Virgin Islands that is not filed for record is void against a later innocent purchaser in good faith and for value of the same property whose conveyance is recorded first (28 V.I.C. § 124). Only a conveyance acknowledged, proved or certified as the Code prescribes may be recorded with the Recorder of Deeds (28 V.I.C. § 122), and it counts as recorded when the Recorder receives it (28 V.I.C. § 123). The recording chapter does not say whether a lease is a conveyance, and that is a question of case law. For a long lease, the cautious course is to have it acknowledged and record it, and to tell any buyer or lender about it in writing.
